en: Preface to the Essential Terms for the Regulations of the Vinaya Garden,
composed by Yuan Jue, Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Grand Master of Ceremonies,
Director of the Drafting of Edicts, and Joint Compiler of the National History.
I lived near Kaiyuan Temple, where the ordination platform was solemn and pure; all who passed by could not help but draw a breath of awe.

Whenever there was an occasion for the conferral of the precepts, I would invariably go to observe it. I saw them sitting cross-legged upon the grass, maintaining a sense of reverent fear while reciting protective mantras without ceasing.
The celestial deities manifested their numinous power to such an extent that some who ascended the platform collapsed and fell, unable to complete the rite. This was because—
I, the stubborn and deluded disciple, have dared not neglect or slacken in this duty. Alas! If one were always to maintain this state of mind, what so-called "hells" could there possibly be?
I, the Vinaya Master Wuxin, have composed these rituals for the formal consecration of the altar and the establishment of the boundary.

I pray that they may be widely disseminated throughout all quarters, so that every person may remain as pure as when first receiving full ordination, and that the ocean of the Dharma may join with the Great Hero.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "There is no difference between this and not being so; how can one overcome the calamities of sin for breaking the Vinaya and violating the precepts?
Written on the Zhongyuan Day of the first year of the Taiding era by the Layman Qingrong, Yuan Zuo, at Mingqing Daxingguo Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture."
The procedural regulations of the Vinaya-piṭaka and the essential terminology for practical application are the pillars and walls of the Chan school.
Master Wugong of Siming, the Heart-Source Patriarch, was deeply devoted to the final instructions of his former master, Master Qinghuyan;

after twenty years of diligent effort, he brought two works to completion, organizing them into ten fascicles totaling over one hundred thousand words, thereby continuing the will and recording the teachings.
While there certainly are those capable of undertaking this task, the expenses for the timber and labor are considerable;
it must therefore rely upon the great virtuous ones—both lay and ordained bodhisattvas—who delight in opening the door of generosity, so that together we may accomplish this sublime endeavor.

The Three Jewels of the Buddha consist of both the Sangha and the Dharma; they are like the rites, music, and institutions that serve as the laws for the virtuous, establishing the standards and regulations for a single school.
Thus, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, there is nothing that is not the Great Way.

Yet, because the Garden of Compassion is so vast, one cannot reach the far-reaching expanse of its fragrant branches. Baizhang gathered and selected [the essentials], yet looked elsewhere for them; the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the Second Patriarch could no longer be employed today.

Then, grasping the collar and nape of the garment, one meets its ultimate purpose; once familiar with it, even wildflowers and weeds each sway in the spring breeze, while clinging rain and foolish clouds do not obstruct the clarity and purity of the mountain scenery.
These more than one hundred thousand words are all the more eloquent for their abundance, and the assembly of twelve hundred is orderly and well-arranged.
Only when the Elder Yixiang finally nods his head will the craftsmanship of the "Carved Dragon" [Liu Xie] truly be realized.
Venturing to employ manual labor, the work has been completed in its entirety; may the merit not be in vain.
On the [blank] day of the third month in the second year of the Taiding era, the scribe for the project was Zhiguan, with Wen Yu providing the calligraphy.
Exhortation for Donations: The Abbot and Head Preceptor of Myōkei Temple,
acting as the general solicitor for donations,

respectfully notes that the Venerable Patriarch Nanshan Deng and the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang adopted the Vinaya regulations to establish the Pure Rules for Chan Monasteries, which have since become widely prevalent throughout the world.
Yet, among those of our own school who study the Vinaya, few have reached this level.

However, the two patriarchs Nanshan and Lingzhi composed their commentaries, sub-commentaries, and records over many years. During the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty, the late Master Si of Jitang at Mingqing Temple petitioned for approval to include them in the Tripitaka;
they were subsequently circulated throughout the world. Truly, they have rendered a great service to the Dharma.
It is a pity that within our own school, the rituals and ceremonies for practice have never been formally recorded in writing.
I have repeatedly received earnest letters from the former abbot of Damingqing, Master Huyan, who repeatedly urged me to compile them.

Recently, while attending the Prajñāpāramitā Gate Dharma Assembly at Wulin, I met with the newly installed abbot of Mingqing, Master Zhelu—a venerable elder among the great masters—along with Yongwen, Yuzhi, and Guanzhi. Furthermore...
He requested that I record his aspirations with a brush; his resolve was most singular. All of these individuals are true "elephants and dragons" within the garden of the Vinaya.

Thereupon, I once again consulted the commentaries and sub-commentaries, inquired of those who have reached the depths of the ocean of the Vinaya, and examined the regulations of the Chan monasteries.

I compiled the *Regulations for the Garden of the Vinaya* (*Lüyuan Shiguī*), along with essential supplementary instructions totaling over one hundred thousand characters. Now, these are combined and set in print, so that they may serve as a model for future generations.
Thus, my realization is merely that of one whose learning is shallow and crude; I still fear there may be omissions.
Should those of lofty insight and long-standing scholarship revise and correct this, and supplement what is insufficient, this would be the profound hope of my humble realization.
Written five days before the Zhongyuan Festival in the year of Yichou during the Taiding era, by the Mountaineer Shengwu of Yanzhong of Siming.

The Ritual for Establishing the Boundary (Sīmā-bandha), including its Preface, compiled by the Bhikṣu Siliang, Abbot of Damingqing Temple in Hangzhou, based on the ancestral traditions.
The matter of establishing the boundary is a fundamental pillar for the monastic community;
in this age of the semblance dharma, the Buddha’s teachings rely upon it for rectification and support. It is a rite performed collectively through *karmavācanā*.
The reason for relying on this as the fundamental manual is that those who govern these affairs are few, resulting in a scarcity of those well-versed in the practice.
During the Xiǎnchún era of the Song dynasty, the monk Dùn'wēng Wénīng Lǜshī of Sìmíng compiled the *Jièjiè Lìlì* (Record of Boundary Rituals).

Herein, I have extracted its format and appended twenty chapters—including the general discourse (*pǔshuō*), the opening address (*báixí*), the incense offering (*zhùxiāng*), and the closing remarks (*jiézòuyǔ*)—as essential supplementary instructions.
I have drafted these as rules for future students and do not dare to present them for official approval; I hope you will not find fault with them.
Regarding the chanting of boundary markers (*sīmā-bandha*), practitioners have traditionally found it difficult to understand;

therefore, I shall now explain it by using the earthen walls and stone thresholds outside the temple to mark the inner and outer boundaries, aligning the cardinal directions at the four corners, and beginning the recitation from the left front corner of the temple—hence there are two parts.
Diagram.
First, the Ritual for Binding the Three Realms.
On the first day at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), first recite the scriptures and offer prayers.

Before the site is formally consecrated, strike the bell to assemble the congregation at the Great Buddha Hall. Make a formal announcement and offer prayers, reciting the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī twenty-one times.
First, consecrate sand and water, circumambulate the hall, scatter flowers, sprinkle water, and strew sand.

Next, recite the Śūraṅgama-dhāraṇī once and dedicate the merit to the devas, nāgas, and the three realms, as well as to the local landowners and spirits belonging to the jurisdiction of the prefecture and county, both those who have passed away and those yet to come.
Having completed the offerings to the deities of the transformed lands and realms, the assembly dispersed.
At mid-afternoon, for the purpose of chanting and prayer, the bell was struck to reconvene the assembly;
they once again proceeded from the Great Hall to recite the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī, scattering flowers, sand, and water throughout the temple.

Having entered the temple and circumambulated it externally, following the boundary markers of the great precinct (*mahā-sīmā*) and returning to stand before the Land Hall (*bhūmi-śālā*), one performs the dedication of merit to the assembly of holy ones of the monastery;
having completed this, one disperses. (This is the practice of the Master Shangweng; it does not deviate from the Vinaya regulations.)

○ The Procedure for the Initial Reception (The Vinaya regulations state that the assembly should be bound during the day so that everyone may be accounted for; however, nowadays the boundary is often bound at night because wandering monks are few).

First, at the beginning of the night, the method for striking the gong to assemble the assembly: the Head Dharma Master ascends the high seat and performs the incense offering (as detailed above), then sits.

Next, the two ranks of officials from the home temple perform their inquiries. Then, the various members of the assembly form the boundary and come forward to inquire. The *vinayadhara* (Vina) chants the *brahman* chant.
[The Master] concludes his general discourse (as detailed in the *Beyong Yaoyu*). Upon completion, he descends from the seat for a brief rest.

At midnight, the formal assembly for the three realms [concerning the robes and food of the Sangha] is convened (the procedures for gathering the assembly and transmitting the incense are fully detailed in the *Bosayi*).
A great drum is struck to assemble the community, who take their places standing before the Sangha Hall. When the drum ceases, the *Vina* intones the verse for hearing the bell: [Verse omitted]
Having subdued the enemy of Māra’s power, And having eliminated all fetters without remainder, The bhikṣu strikes the *gaṇḍī* in the open air;
All those who wish to hear the Dharma, To cross the flood of the ocean of birth and death—
Upon hearing this wondrous sound, They shall all assemble here like clouds.

The procedure for the sequential assembly in the Dharma Hall: standing in their respective positions, they perform three full prostrations with robes spread wide, then kneel to recite the outer verse:
"Observing the precepts with purity like the full moon, Body and speech are bright and stainless, free from blemish;
The great assembly is harmonious, without conflict— Only then can we together establish the boundary."
The assembly each gathers their implements and sits to perform the ritual. Three persons rise, scatter flowers and water, and recite the verse:
Scattering flowers, pure radiance is adorned; Adorned with precious flowers, they form a canopy.
Scattering various precious flowers throughout the ten directions, I offer them to all the Tathāgatas.
The *karmadāna*, performing the duties of the *brahman* chant, takes a censer in his sleeve and carries his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) out from the assembly to the great incense burner.

He performs prostrations and kneels before the burner, offering three pinches of incense and bowing. He waits for the *brahman* chant to conclude, then raises his body to kneel in the *hu-kuei* (half-lotus) posture and recites the verse:
The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, and the fragrance of liberation— Cloud-palaces of radiance pervade the entire Dharma-realm, making offerings to all infinite Buddhas;
Seeing or hearing them, one is universally perfumed and realizes quiescent extinction.

[At this point, as required by the liturgical manual: The Master of the Dharma, presiding over the newly established Great Boundary, addresses the assembly (concluding with): "Now, we invite [Name] to chant the Great..."
[The person responsible for the boundary markers] answers regarding the dharmas to be established: [Name] respectfully informs. Venerable Saṃgha, listen:
the establishment of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) does not permit the transmission of *kṣānti* (consent). [Thus it is said... Questioning the assembly; questioning the harmony;
sending away those who are not fully ordained. [The presiding master says: "A certain bhikṣu shall rise and proclaim the characteristics of the fourfold great boundary for the Saṃgha."
Next, the boundary-designator is called forth from the assembly to perform the rites and stand in place.
He proclaims: "Venerable Sangha, listen! I, the bhikṣu, shall proclaim for the Sangha the characteristics of the great boundary of the four directions...

(as detailed in the *Yao-yu*). Having proclaimed this three times, the designator returns to his seat. The presiding master asks: "The Sangha is now in harmony; what shall we do? [The response is: "We shall establish [the boundary]."

The Ritual for the Great Boundary (The Master says): "I rely upon the venerable assembly to join their palms, unify their minds, and bear witness as to whether this ritual for binding the great boundary is accomplished or not.
Venerable Sangha, listen... (The proclamation and the ritual formula for binding the boundary are both contained within the *Karmavācanā-sūtra*, ending with the words: "It is performed."

Once the Dharma for establishing the boundary has been completed and perfected (the announcement, the *karmavācanā*, and the words of the formal establishment are all accomplished through question and answer;
hereafter, all cases follow this pattern), the preceptor next establishes the *cīvarasaṃgraha-sīmā* (the boundary for collecting robes). The preceptor announces to the assembly:
"I now request [Name] to respond to the Dharma to be accomplished. "[Name] respectfully announces."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen to the inquiry regarding the assembly; the inquiry regarding harmony; the dispatching of those not yet fully ordained; and the solicitation of consent. (The questioner says:

"The Saṃgha is now in harmonious assembly; what is being performed? (The respondent says: "The formal act (*karmavācanā*) for establishing the boundary for the storage of robes (*cīvarasaṃstaraṇa-sīmā*), performed with the entire assembly in agreement and with mutual testimony."

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen... (as detailed in the *Karmavācanā* [Karmavibhaṅga]; the formal announcement and the wording for the *karmavācanā* for the establishment of the boundary are both contained in the *Karmavibhaṅga*).

Subsequently, when first establishing the *saṃbhojanīya-sīmā* (the food-eating boundary), the presiding master makes the formal announcement at the assembly (concluding with): "I now request [so-and-so] to proclaim the characteristics of the pure ground;
[so-and-so] shall respond regarding the dharma to be accomplished. [So-and-so] respectfully announces.

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Inquiry regarding the assembly; inquiry regarding harmony; sending away those who are not fully ordained; requesting the consent (*chanda*) of absent members. (The Preceptor says:
"A certain bhikṣu shall proclaim the boundaries of the pure ground for the Saṃgha. The proclaimer of the boundaries steps out from the assembly, performs the full prostrations, and proclaims, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, a bhikṣu, shall proclaim for the Saṃgha the location of the pure ground... (and so forth, as in the *Karmavācanā-sūtra*). (3)
When the chanting is finished, the presiding master returns to his seat and says: "The Sangha is now in harmony; what shall we perform? [The respondent] replies:

"The *karmavācanā* for establishing a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*). The master says: "We rely upon the great assembly to establish this *karmavācanā* for establishing a pure ground; may you join your palms and with one mind bear witness to the ritual."

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen: regarding this dwelling place... (the *jñapti* and the formal motion for the *karman*, including the concluding words of the binding, are as found in the *Karmavācanā-sūtra*).
The above concludes the establishment of the three great boundaries (*mahāsīmā*) for the clothing, food, and dwellings of the Saṃgha.
Once the boundary has been formally established by the *karmadāna*, the assembly reflects upon it with joy, reciting this verse:
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is the foremost joy; hearing the Dharma and practicing it is the joy of peace and stability.
The harmony of the great assembly is the joy of nirvana; sentient beings being free from suffering is the joy of bliss.
The Preceptor stands up on the purified ground and, holding the incense burner, says: "Above, we have respectfully followed the Vinaya rules to perform the *bandhana* (binding)."

The vast merits gathered through these Dharma activities of the various realms are specifically intended to pray for the Emperor’s ten-thousand-year reign of peace, for the Empress Dowager and the Empress to enjoy equal longevity, and for the Crown Prince to attain a thousand autumns of wisdom.

May the civil and military officials likewise increase their fortunes and life-spans; may the state be prosperous and the people at peace, and may the seasons be harmonious and the harvests bountiful. We offer our boundless prayers for these excellent causes.

We offer this to the various devas who protect the Dharma, to repay the four debts of gratitude, and for the sake of the true lords of the *gārala* who guard the teachings and bring peace to the Sangha, so that all sentient beings in the *dharmadhātu* may together realize the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).

With these reflections as the causal condition, [recite] the names of the Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha, the ten titles of the Buddhas, followed by the titles of the two Great Wisdom Patriarchs of the Southern Mountain, up to the *pāramitās*.
When this is completed, the assembly of monks performs three full prostrations with wide-spread mats; the ritual master strikes the wooden mallet and chants the Three Refuges.

(As stated in the ritual for the *śīla*, change "poṣadha" to "delimiting the boundary"). Once the assembly has finished, they collect their requisites and return to the front of the Sangha hall, where they perform a *vaṃdana* and disperse.
On the second day, the delimitation of the three boundaries is dissolved. At the first watch of the night, the delimitation of the three boundaries is dissolved in sequence.

At dusk, the bell is struck to assemble the community in front of the Sangha hall; they recite the verse for entering the hall (as before), collect their requisites, take their seats, and perform the walking meditation.
To serve the three masters, they rise and scatter flowers and water while reciting verses (as before). The *vinaya-dhara* performs the *brahma-karma*;

one person steps out from the assembly, prostrates three times, and, holding the incense burner, completes the *brahma-karma*. He then transmits the three pinches of incense, and the assembly recites the verses (as before).
Next, the purification of the ground and the robes, as well as the two boundaries (*sīmā*), are established; the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) are performed in their proper sequence.

First, the master who performs the ritual for purifying the site (*śuddhasthāna*) makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*). [The announcer] says: "I now request [Master So-and-so] to respond regarding the dharma to be accomplished.

[Master So-and-so] respectfully announces: "I shall inquire, harmonize, and solicit the consent," etc. (as before). However, the response should simply state: "The *karmavācanā* for purifying the site. [The words are as follows:]
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This residence is for communal dwelling and communal *poṣadha* (the wording for the motion and the formal act of *karmavācanā* is as found in the *Karmavastu*).

Next, the preceptor who shall dissolve the robe-boundary (*cīvarāvadhi*) makes the formal announcement at the assembly (concluding with): 'I now request [Name] to respond to the dharma to be accomplished. [Name] respectfully announces.
[The preceptor] asks for harmony and seeks consent (as before); one simply replies: 'The formal act for dissolving the non-loss-of-robe boundary (*acīvarāpattibhūmi*)' (the wording is as follows)."

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This dwelling place is a single residence with a single *poṣadha* recitation (*yathā karmavastu*). [The formal motion and the *karmavācanā* for the boundary-binding are as in the *Karmavastu*].

Subsequently, the master who shall dissolve the great boundary makes the formal announcement at the seat, concluding by saying: 'I now request [Name] to respond regarding the dharma to be accomplished. [Name] respectfully announces."

Question: Requesting the dissolution of the boundary (the procedure is the same as before, with the following response). Response: Recite the *karmavācanā* for the dissolution of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā-bandha*).
[The formal motion and the *karmavācanā* for the binding are as found in the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! At this residence, the bhikṣus... [and so forth].

Once the *vinaḥ* has completed the ritual for dissolving the world-boundary (*lokasīmā*), the assembly recites verses of self-congratulation (as before). Rising from their seats, the master who dissolved the boundary takes up the hand-incense burner.

(As stated above) ... Having respectfully followed the monastic rules to perform the ritual for establishing the boundary (*sīmā*), the vast merit thus accumulated is dedicated solely to praying for the Ten-Thousand-Year Peace and Security of the Emperor’s Life.
(As before) ... With this intention, [recite] the ten Buddha names plus the two Patriarchs as usual.
Upon completion, the assembly performs three prostrations; the ritual officiant strikes the mallet, chants the Three Refuges, collects the implements, and returns to the Sangha Hall.
[The assembly] bows and disperses.
○ During the formal ritual for binding the three realms at midnight, the abbot strikes the *daqi* (striking board) to assemble the community before the Sangha Hall;
they chant the verse for hearing the bell (as before). They enter the Dharma Hall, perform prostrations, and chant the verse.
Once seated, scatter flowers, offer water, chant in the Brahma-voice, and recite verses (all as in the original *kṣetra-bandha*).

First, for the formal binding of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the presiding master announces the proceedings, concluding with: "I now request [Name] to proclaim the characteristics of the great boundary;

[Name] shall respond regarding the dharma to be accomplished. [The respondent] respectfully announces: "I humbly announce. Then, the assembly asks for harmony and solicits the consent (*chanda*) to appoint the person to proclaim the boundary marks (all as before, three times). Having finished the proclamation:

Question: What is it? (Answer: The *karmavācanā* for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā-bandha*). (The ritual formula for binding the boundary is as previously described in the section on the initial establishment).

Next is the formal binding of the robe-reception boundary (*cīvara-saṃvartanīya-sīmā*). The master announces the assembly (*jñapti*), saying: "I now request [Name] to respond regarding the dharma to be accomplished. [Name] respectfully announces. Question:
To solicit the consent (*chanda*) and appoint the person to designate the boundaries (*sīmā-nidarśaka*). The *karmavācanā* questions and answers (are all as in the initial establishment). Correct.

Concluding the Binding of the Three Realms; A Brief Expression of Gratitude for the Master of the Dharma; Closing the Session (as in the *Ruyu*); the *Liao* Venerable concludes the ritual of the world and the Brahma-kṣetra;
the assembly recites a verse of self-congratulation; they rise and the Master of the Dharma, holding the incense burner, prays for the Sage and recites the Buddha’s name (all as in the *Chuangjing*);
thereafter, he addresses the Buddha, requesting the Sage’s empowerment so that the boundaries of the realm may be firm and secure.
The assembly recites the formal liturgy together and performs three full prostrations. The ritual master strikes the mallet and chants the Three Refuges;
they then return to the front of the Sangha hall, perform a bow, and disperse.
○ On the third day, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is recited in full (the ritual procedures are detailed in the *Poṣadha-vidhi*; as this method is widely practiced today, it is appended here).
○ One person for extensive recitation; one person for the formal announcement (*śukra-vācanā*); one person for the *brahman* chant; four or more persons for the ritual procedures.

Regarding the sequence of boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandha*), if many practitioners are present, it is permissible to divide the roles for binding and releasing the boundaries and the formal announcements.

However, if there is only a single presiding master and the others are unacquainted with the rites, one cannot avoid simplifying the procedure. Thus, the four types of formal announcements for the seating arrangement (*āsana-śukra*) are herein described.
As indicated in the "Essential Discourse" (Yao yu), each chapter of the *Karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) should be performed separately for future use.

Regarding the proclamation of the boundaries (*sīmā*) for the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), this was previously handled according to established precedent; however, in the present case, the proclamation of the boundaries is omitted as the robes are being adjusted.
The sequence of the ritual procedures is now set forth below.

General Announcement for the Initial Establishment of the Two Boundaries: the Boundary for Gathering Robes and the Boundary for Gathering Food (Concluding with "Liao yun"): "I now request [Name] to respond regarding the dharma to be accomplished. [Name] respectfully announces.

Questioning for Harmony and Soliciting Consent (as before). The general response states: "The *karmavācanā* for establishing the boundary for gathering robes; the *karmavācanā* for establishing the boundary for gathering food.
First, perform the *karmavācanā* for establishing the boundary for gathering robes. Next, perform the *karmavācanā* for establishing the boundary for gathering food.

Karmavācanā. For the collective resolution to dissolve the two boundaries of food and robes, the general announcement for the sitting is as follows: [End of recitation] "I now request [Name] to respond regarding the dharma to be accomplished.
[Name] respectfully announces. Questioning for harmony and soliciting consent (as before); however, respond collectively by saying: "The karmavācanā for dissolving the boundary of food."

The Ritual for Dissolving the Boundary for Storing Robes (*cīvara-sīmā-bandha-karman*): First, perform the ritual for dissolving the boundary for storing food (*piṇḍapāta-sīmā-bandha-karman*). Next, perform the ritual for dissolving the boundary for storing robes (*cīvara-sīmā-bandha-karman*).

For the formal announcement (*jñapti*) regarding the simultaneous binding of the two boundaries for storing robes and storing food, the presiding officer says: "I now request [Name] to respond to what is to be accomplished."
The Dharma [Name] respectfully informs: Regarding the inquiry for consent (as previously stated), the general response is as follows:

the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for binding the robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*) and the formal act for binding the food-boundary (*piṇḍapātasīmā*). First, one shall perform the formal act for binding the robe-boundary; second, one shall perform the formal act for binding the food-boundary.

The Community of Monks, having collectively understood [the matter of] food and robes, makes a general announcement regarding the seating mat (concluding with): "Now we invite [Name] to respond to the dharma to be accomplished. [Name] respectfully announces. Question:

Requesting the consent of the assembly (as before). General response: Announcing the *karmavācanā* for the dissolution of the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*). Announcing the *karmavācanā* for the dissolution of the robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*).
Announcing the *karmavācanā* for the dissolution of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). First, perform the *karmavācanā* for the dissolution of the pure ground; next...
First, perform the *karmavācanā* for the boundary of the robe-keeping area (*cīvaradhāraṇasīmā*). Next, perform the *karmavācanā* for the dissolution of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
Regarding the ritual for establishing and dissolving the *śīmaṇḍala*:
For the initial establishment of the *śīmaṇḍala*, the presiding officer (*viniścayin*) says: "Now I request [so-and-so] to proclaim the boundaries of the *śīmaṇḍala*. [So-and-so] replies as follows:

The Dharma-attainer (Name) respectfully informs: Having requested the harmony and sought the consent, the boundary-designator shall emerge from the assembly and perform the ritual (the words for the *karmavācanā* for designating the boundaries are the same as those in the *Yao yu* [Essential Words], identical to the procedure for binding the great boundary).

Next, the procedure for the announcement (*jñapti*) regarding the dissolution of the *sīmā* (precept boundary). [The presiding monk] says: "I now request [the assembly] to designate someone to respond to the ritual to be performed; I respectfully announce this.
[He then] asks for harmony and solicits consent (as previously described), but simply responds by saying: "The formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the dissolution of the *sīmā*."

The formal announcement for the conclusion of the boundary of the *śīma* (the *śīma-vidhi-śrāvaṇa*). [At the end, it says: "I now request [Master] So-and-so to chant the characteristics of the *śīma*;

[Master] So-and-so shall respond regarding the dharma to be accomplished. [The proponent] respectfully announces: "I seek the consent; I ask for harmony. The master who chants the characteristics steps forth from the assembly (as in the procedure for first establishing the boundary).
However, he should respond by saying: "The *karmavācanā* for concluding the *śīma*. (The *karmavācanā* text is as found in the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*).
Circular Notice on the Sequence for Establishing the Boundary:
Regarding the Place for Establishing the Great Boundary (for now, the sequence of five monks shall be determined; if there are more or fewer, they shall be arranged as appropriate).
On the first day, the assembly gathers in the morning to perform circumambulation and prayers at [Name] Temple; the Vinaya Master of the temple performs the dedication of merit for the meal.
In the afternoon, the assembly gathers to circumambulate the temple and perform circumambulation and prayers; the Master of [Name] Temple performs the dedication of merit for the refreshments.
In the first watch of the night, the Vinaya Master of Temple A offered incense and gave a general discourse;
in the middle watch, the Vinaya Master of Temple B established the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*);
in the fourth watch, the Vinaya Master of Temple C proclaimed the boundaries (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*), and the Vinaya Master of Temple D responded according to the Dharma.
The Vinaya Master of Temple Bing initiates the delimitation of the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*); the Vinaya Master of Temple Wu responds with the Dharma.
The Vinaya Master of Temple Ding initiates the delimitation of the pure ground (*śuci-sthāna*);
the Vinaya Master of Temple Wu chants the boundary marks (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*); the Vinaya Master of Temple Yi responds with the Dharma and the marking of points.
On the second day,
during the first watch of the night, Vinaya Master A of Temple B explains the purification of the site; Vinaya Master B of Temple C responds regarding the Dharma (medicines, food, and meals).
The Vinaya Master of Temple Yi explains the boundary for the *saṃkakṣikā* robe; the Vinaya Master of Temple Ding responds with the ritual procedure.
The Vinaya Master of Temple Bing chants the *mahā-sīmā*; the Vinaya Master of Temple Wu responds with the ritual procedure.
At the midpoint of the night, the Vinaya Master of Temple Jia formally establishes the *mahā-sīmā*.
The Vinaya Master of Temple Bing chants the characteristics [of the boundary]; the Vinaya Master of Temple Yi responds with the ritual;
the Vinaya Master of Temple Ding formally binds the robe-boundary (cīvara-sīmā); the Vinaya Master of Temple Bing responds with the ritual;
the Vinaya Master of Temple Wu formally binds the food-boundary (piṇḍapāta-sīmā).
The Vinaya Master of Temple A chants the ritual form; the Vinaya Master of Temple B responds with the Dharma (regarding medicine, food, and medicinal gruel).
On the right, we humbly submit that the Piṇī-piṭaka is the teaching that prolongs the life-span of the Buddha-Dharma.

Since the power of the Sūtras and Śāstras has diminished, the Bhikṣus on the ground of the Karmavācanā naturally become weak and frail in their observance of the communal laws. Regarding this monastic precinct, although...

How can one excel in this? Before the Dharma has been fully applied, one seeks to avoid the transgressions of overnight cooking and separation from the Sangha; one delimits the boundaries for the clothing and food of the community.
When devas and humans revere their teacher and divine dragons provide protection, one should solemnly compose the body and mind to chant the secret edicts of the three sections.
With diligent incantations and vows, may the borders of the realm remain firm for ten thousand years, perfecting both the beginning and the end. Do not...
May there be no negligence; may the teachings of Nanshan flourish.
I pray for the sagely longevity of the Emperor at the Northern Gate. This day, the [blank] month of this year, the proclamation.
*Rules for Rituals in the Garden of Vinaya*, Fascicle Two.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Xingwu, Abbot of Yanzhong Lushi Temple in Siming.
Section: The Ritual for Tonsure.
For one who wishes to leave the household life, the *vinaya* prescribes a formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize with the Saṃgha so that the great assembly may know [the request].

If they are in harmony, it is well; otherwise, one should go from room to room to inform them. Once this has been done, one should grant the tonsure. First, one should invite the Upādhyāya, and next, the Ācārya.
One should approach the Upādhyāya with full decorum, perform three prostrations, kneel with palms joined, and request him [to serve as preceptor]. An attendant should be appointed.
First, consider the words of Master Tou:
"The Confucianist attends to his father, placing primary importance on the perfection of the self; the Buddhist disciple relies upon the teacher, making the cultivation of the Way his essential task.
Thus, the four modes of deportment serve as the standard by which one refines oneself, and through this, the fivefold Dharma-body is established."
Since one must serve with utmost sincerity, you should resolutely set forth your petition; fearing that you may not yet know how, I shall now instruct you.
(The petition states:
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], now request the Virtuous One to act as my tonsure preceptor. May the Virtuous One..."
"Venerable One, please act as my preceptor for the tonsure; by relying upon your virtue, I shall be able to shave my head and leave the household life out of your compassion. (Three times.
The Preceptor replies: "Since you have made this request, I shall serve as your preceptor for the tonsure. (Then he leads him [to the place]).
[The attendant, after the preceptor has performed the prostrations and mutual kneeling, says:

"Now, one who grows weary of the common stream of worldly existence and rejoices in participating in the precious rank [of the Sangha], desiring to sever mundane habits, ought by principle to discipline the deluded mind.
Since this is a matter of personal responsibility, it must be entrusted to a master of renown. I now request [Name] to serve as your tonsure master."
How much more so for this Ācārya, who instructs others without weariness and engages with sentient beings through skillful means;
therefore, one must single-mindedly maintain a focused heart and respectfully present three requests (the words being as follows).
"Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], now request the Venerable Sir to serve as my hair-cutting preceptor (*keśacchedana-ācārya*).
May the Venerable Sir act as my hair-cutting preceptor; through the Venerable Sir, I shall obtain the shaving of my head and go forth into homelessness.
Out of compassion for me... (Request three times.)
The Ācārya replied: "Since you have made this request, I shall serve as your hair-cutting preceptor (śramaṇera-ācārya).
The Holy Patriarchs of the Southern Mountain said: "One should establish the ritual for leaving the household life by combining the clarifications from various sections [of the Vinaya].

On an open space, one sprinkles scented water around it to a circumference of seven feet, hangs banners at the four corners, and places a single seat therein intended for the candidate who is to leave the household life."

Furthermore, two superior seats were prepared to serve as the seats for the two masters. The one seeking ordination, having put on his original lay garments and completed his prostrations and farewell to his parents and elders, spoke this verse:
"Transmigrating within the three realms, One cannot escape the bonds of affection; I cast aside these affections to enter the unconditioned."

One who truly repays the debt of gratitude shall cast off secular clothing (*from the Qingxinshi duren jing*). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that one should bathe with fragrant water to remove the scent of white robes, then don the garments of a renunciant (the present-day *bianshan*) and approach the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
Kneeling with both knees on the ground, one should request [the preceptor] to speak of the hair, body hair, nails, and so forth.
Why is this so? Because there was once a person who, having observed these five things, immediately upon shaving his hair, triggered his past karma and attained enlightenment.

Just as Rāhula attained Arhatship before his shaving was even finished—like a ripe abscess waiting for the needle, or a lotus flower waiting for the sun—after the Dharma had been preached, he sat before the Ācārya. (From the *Samantapāsādikā*). He was then bathed with warm water.
The eulogy says:
Excellent, O Great Man! You have been able to realize the impermanence of the world; Abandoning the secular life to proceed toward Nirvana—this is rare and inconceivable.
Having paid homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, the practitioner recites this verse:

I take refuge in the Great World-Honored One, Who can deliver one from the sufferings of the three realms of existence; May all sentient beings likewise universally enter the bliss of the unconditioned.
The *ācārya* then shaves the hair, while others chant the verse for leaving the household life (*pravrajyā-gāthā*):
"Altering one's appearance to maintain the vows, Severing attachment so as to have no kin, Abandoning the home to propagate the Holy Way— May all people be delivered. (From the *Duren jing*)

When shaving the hair, one should leave three or five *cūḍā* (small tufts of hair) on the crown of the head—“three or five” being used merely as a conventional expression—and approach the *upādhyāya*, kneeling with legs crossed.
The *upādhyāya* then asks:

"Now I shall shave the hair from your crown; is this acceptable? [He answers: "Yes. (Alternatively, there is a method for submitting a written request for the tonsure, as detailed in a separate document.)
It should be understood that the primary purpose of shaving the hair is for the *upādhyāya* to act on behalf of the candidate, fearing that the process might take too long;

therefore, he instructs the *ācārya* to remove the remainder, leaving only a small amount, which the *upādhyāya* then shaves himself. In current practice, one first shaves the hair oneself into small tufts, which is not the intent of the original teaching.

Once the hair has been removed, the *upādhyāya* bestows the *kāṣāya* upon the candidate, who receives it by placing it upon his head in veneration. Having received it, he returns it to the *upādhyāya*. Thus it is done.
The preceptor puts it on three times (as recorded in the *Samantapāsādikā*). He then recites this verse:
"How great is the robe of liberation! The signless field of merit garment. Wearing it as one observes the precepts, May I extensively deliver all sentient beings."
Having finished paying homage to the Buddha, he circumambulated him three times and recited this verse of self-congratulation:
"How wonderful it is to encounter a Buddha! Who would not rejoice? May my merit and vows coincide with this moment;
I have now obtained the benefit of the Dharma."

Having paid respects to the great assembly and the two masters, one takes a seat below to receive the prostrations and congratulations of the six types of relatives regarding one’s renunciation and departure from desire;
with a mind set on the far-reaching and great, the parents and others all perform prostrations to express their joy in one’s resolve for the Way.

Prior to midday, one shaves the hair (as stated in the *Duren jing*). The *Vinayamātṛkā* says: "Only after shaving the hair and donning the *kāṣāya* does one then confer the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts."
The Ritual for Receiving Full Ordination and Arousing the Resolve (Xuan Shoujujie Ce fayi).
First, the lay attendant strikes the drum, and the śrāmaṇeras and two attendants assemble in the Dharma Hall. They proceed to the master’s quarters to pay their respects;
one holds an incense burner while the other rings the leading chime. Leading the candidate, they arrive at the Dharma Hall to burn incense.

Upon the conclusion of the ascending to the seat, the śrāmaṇeras perform the circumambulation and burn incense. They join the assembly in performing three prostrations. The attendant instructs the śrāmaṇeras to sit and strikes the mallet once.

The *Banyin Shi* (Master of Chanting) performs the *brahma-svara* chant; when it is finished, the assembly recites the "Verse for Transmitting Incense" (*chuanxiang jie*) in unison (as in the Ritual for Establishing the Boundary).
When the verse is finished, the mallet is struck once more. The attendant recites the invitation to the Master, beginning with: "The Head [of the Assembly] says..."

Now, just as carving and adorning the myriad features depends upon the skill of a master craftsman, so too does the education and completion of a person of great talent require the power of an enlightened teacher.

If one does not reverently request [his guidance], how could he ever grant his compliance? We now, with one mind, respectfully request such-and-such a person to serve as the *ācārya* for your ordination;
moreover, this master never tires of instructing others and possesses skillful means in dealing with sentient beings. Therefore—
One must single-mindedly maintain a focused heart and respectfully present the three requests.
After striking the wooden gavel once, chant the precepts in a loud voice, while the candidate follows along in thought, saying:
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], now request that the Virtuous One act as my *adhiṣṭhāna-ācārya* (empowerment preceptor). May the Virtuous One..."
"Please act as my *pravrajyā-ācārya* so that, by relying upon your venerable virtue, I may receive full ordination out of compassion.

(Having made this request three times, each time with a prostration, the attendant descends from his seat. The *pravrajyā-ācārya* replies: "Since you have made this request, I shall act as your *pravrajyā-ācārya*.
You must listen attentively to all my instructions."
The procedure for the *caila* (robe-offering) ceremony and the preaching of the Dharma (as in the *Yao yu zhong*). Having finished the preaching of the Dharma (one rises with a single bow and says):

"The vast merit gathered through the performance of the *caila* ritual, conducted in full accordance with the monastic rules above, is dedicated solely to the long life of the Emperor—ten thousand years and more" (and so forth).
(As in the *Jie jie yi zhong*). Descending from the seat, the ritual for purifying the world (*chu shi jie fan*) is completed and the assembly disperses.
The Ritual for Receiving the Five Precepts: 1. Invocation (in Sanskrit);
2. Requesting the Preceptor; 3. Invoking the Holy Ones; 4. Formal Announcement; 5. Exhortation; 6.
Inquiry regarding Obstacles; 7. Repentance of Sins; 8. Administering the Dharma; 9. Explaining the Characteristics; 10. Making Vows.
First, the initial pure attendant strikes the drum to assemble the śrāmaṇeras in the Dharma Hall. Two attendants go to the Ten Masters’ Hall to pay their respects;
one holds a hand-incense burner while the other rings the leading chime to welcome the Five Precept Master.

They proceed before him to the Dharma Hall, where he burns incense and ascends the seat. The śrāmaṇeras perform the circumambulation of the hall burning incense, and the attendants ring the leading chime for the assembly.
The śrāmaṇeras perform three prostrations together; the attendant instructs the śrāmaṇeras to sit and strikes the mallet once.
Once the *brahmaghoṣa* master has finished the *brahmaghoṣa*, the assembly recites the incense-offering verse (*dhūpa-gāthā*) in unison (as in the *Sīmā-bandha* ritual).
When the verse is finished, the mallet is struck once, and the attendant strikes the ruler once while reciting the invocation for the masters of the hall.
Second, the Request for the Preceptor: Since you have originally received the Three Refuges to overturn the erroneous conditions of the past, you are now granted the Five Precepts;
this is like first ascending the heavy turrets of the initial story. Without a clear master, it is difficult to transmit the supreme Dharma.
Therefore, on behalf of you all, we now with single-minded reverence request that Master [Name] in the hall serve as the Upādhyāya and Karmavācanā-ācārya for the Five Precepts.

Moreover, since this master teaches people without weariness and engages with beings through skillful means, one must single-mindedly maintain a focused heart and respectfully present the three invocations (with a *chī* strike followed by a high chant).
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, [Name], now request the Venerable sir to act as my preceptor for the five precepts.
May the Venerable sir act as my preceptor for the five precepts; through reliance upon the Venerable sir, I shall receive the upāsaka precepts.

Out of compassion, [please grant this]. (Recite this three times, each time lowering the hand by one chi. For a woman receiving [the precepts], she says: "Upāsikā, [Name], preceptor of the five precepts. The teacher replies: "Since you have made this request, I shall act as your [preceptor]."
"Listen attentively to all the instructions of the Preceptor for the Five Precepts (the Attendant shall descend from his seat). ○ Third, Invoking the Holy Ones (The Preceptor says):

'In all cases where one wishes to transmit the Dharma of the Precepts, one must first invite the eternally abiding Triple Gem and the various devas who protect the Dharma to descend upon this ritual site to bear witness and bestow their empowerment. The majesty and gravity of the Triple Gem are peerless.'"
Those who may sit should rise when invited; following my words, invite with utmost sincerity. (One *chi* [pace] below, all chant in unison:
"I, [Name], bow my head and take refuge, single-mindedly and respectfully inviting the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm."
The Vairocana Buddha of the pure Dharma-body; the Roshana Buddha of the perfect reward-body; the Shakyamuni Buddha of the thousands of millions of transformation-bodies;
the Honored Maitreya Buddha descending to be born in the future; the Amitayus Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; and the entire Vinaya-pitaka of the precepts of both the Mahayana and Hinayana vehicles.
Dharma Jewel Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva,
all the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, the holy masters of the Southern Mountain, the Bodhisattva Vinaya Master of Great Wisdom,
the Dharma-transmitting patriarchs of India and this land, the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all true monks who have attained the Way: we pray that you...
The Triple Gem, having heard this, is now respectfully invited to descend together to this ritual site to bear witness to the reception of the precepts. (One strike of the gong, then recite).
*Namo* to the Buddhas of the ten directions who abide eternally. (Recite "Dharma" and "Sangha" likewise, three times each, with one strike of the gong after each.
I, [Name], with a single-minded and devout heart, respectfully entreat all the devas who protect and uphold the True Teaching, and all the myriad spirits of the triple world, to take their seats.

Now, for the year’s cycle of merit and demerit among the assembly of sages, for the great original deities of the local territory, for the various ancient benevolent spirits, for the incense-offering shrines of the prefectures and counties, for the intelligent beings present here, for the natal star-deities of this assembly, and for the Protector of the Monastery of this dwelling place:
we pray that upon hearing our current invitation, you will descend in splendor to this ritual arena to bear witness to and receive our ordination. (One strike of the gavel.)
Namo to the Dharma-protecting devas and bodhisattvas (recite three times, each at one *chi* [cubit] and one *xiang* [inch], then conclude by sitting).

Fourth, the Invocation: We have respectfully invited the Triple Gem above; may you deign to descend. We pray that you extend your auspicious light and look down with compassionate mindfulness upon the present assembly.
We now wish to proceed to receive the five precepts as a means of departing from the household life and entering the Way.
Fundamentally, I am concerned that the faculties of sentient beings are shallow and thin, and that demonic obstacles may suddenly arise;

therefore, I first take refuge in the Buddhas and devas, praying for their empowerment so that at this very moment when the transmission is being correctly performed, this entire assembly may remain with a single, undistracted mind, all phenomena may be orderly, subject and object may merge in harmony, and the transmission and reception may be clear and unclouded.
I look up to your majestic spiritual power, earnestly hoping for a manifest response. (Recite.)
Namo to the Buddhas who eternally abide in the ten directions (recite "Dharma" and "Saṃgha" three times each).
Namo to the various devas and bodhisattvas who protect the Dharma (three times, each with one strike of the *chī*, then sit).
○ Fifth: The Preceptor for Encouragement and Guidance explains the cultivation of the resolve based on the objective conditions (as in the *Yao yu*).
Sixth, the Refutation of Obstacles: Having already explained for you how to generate the resolve by taking an object as its condition, it is further necessary that the physical vessel be pure.
If there are obstacles or impediments, the precepts will not be generated. I now ask you; you should answer truthfully.
First, I shall ask regarding the grave obstacles.
1. One-sided offenses; 2. Corrupting a nun; 3. Living as a thief; 4. A follower of external paths;
5. A eunuch; 6. Killing one’s father; 7. Killing one’s mother; 8. Killing an Arhat; 9. Causing a schism in the Saṃgha; 10.
Shedding the blood of a Buddha; 11. A non-human being; 12. A dragon or an animal; 13. A hermaphrodite.
Furthermore, ask concerning the minor prohibitions (without asking about age; the requisites of robes and bowl are limited to thirteen prohibitions).
Ask as follows: "What is your name now? What is the name of your preceptor for the five precepts? Have your parents given their permission?
Are you not in debt to others? Are you not a servant or a messenger? Do you have a name, rank, and official status? Are you a man?"
The five ailments of a husband.

○ Seventh, the confession of offenses: Since you have already been questioned regarding the obstacles and disqualifications (*antarāya*) and found to be free from them, it is further necessary that the roots of your offenses be purified before you are fit to receive the transmission.
Follow my words and perform the rite of repentance.
I, [Name], with a sincere heart, repent of all evil karma created in the past (as recited three times according to the separate text, each time measuring one chi and one cun).
○ Eighth, since the root of the offense regarding the administration of the Dharma has been purified, the essence of the precepts may now be manifested.

The Ritual for Receiving the Ten Precepts:
1. Invocation; 2. Requesting the Teacher; 3. Invoking the Holy Ones; 4. Formal Declaration; 5. Exhortation; 6.
Inquiry on Obstacles; 7. Administration of the Dharma; 8. Explanation of the Characteristics; 9. Enumeration of Virtues; 10. Dedication of Merit.
First, the initial pure attendant (śuddhakarman) beats the drum to assemble the śrāmaṇeras.
Two attendants then proceed to the Hall of the Ten Preceptors (daśācārya-śālā) to pay their respects—one holding a hand-incense burner and the other ringing the lead chime (pravāla).

The Preceptor of the Ten Precepts and the Ācārya approach the Dharma Hall together before the two masters and burn incense in unison. Once the Ācārya has ascended the high seat, the Preceptor sits below it.
The śrāmaṇeras perform the ritual path while burning incense; they follow the attendant, who strikes the gong to lead the assembly. All the śrāmaṇeras together prostrate three times.
The attendant instructs the śrāmaṇeras to sit and strikes the mallet once. The *brahmasvara* master performs the *brahma* chant;
when it is finished, the entire assembly chants the Incense Transmission Verse (*dhyāna*) in unison (as in the *Sīmā-bandha* rite). (When the verse is finished, strike the mallet once more.)
Second, the two chief attendants of the various masters strike the wooden gavel once; the head of the recitation assembly then says:
"Just as gold is refined and cast into objects so that images arise from the original mold, so too do humans act according to their nature and thereby manifest ritual propriety."
If the teacher is not held in profound reverence, how can one be moved to develop the higher precepts? It is essential to use this ritual to resolve the doubts of the ignorant.

Now, for your sake, we single-mindedly and respectfully request [Name] of [Temple Name] to serve as the Upādhyāya for the ten precepts, and [Name] of [Temple Name] to serve as the Ācārya for the ten precepts.

(Having requested this three times, each time with one bow.

[As stated below:

Out of compassion, [the candidate] requests three times (each time measuring one chi).
The *ācārya* replies: "Since you have made this request, I shall act as your *daśa-śīla-ācārya*.
You must listen attentively to all my instructions. (The attendant descends from his seat.)

○ Third, Invoking the Sages (The Acharya says): "In all cases where one intends to transmit the Dharma of the Precepts, one must first invite the eternally abiding Triple Gem and the various devas who protect the Dharma to descend upon the site of practice (*dōjō*) to bear witness and bestow their empowerment. The majesty of the Triple Gem is such that it cannot be summoned while seated;
you must rise and, following my words, invoke them with utmost sincerity and devotion. (One strike of the *shaku*; the *śrāmaṇera* [responds]).
[They] chant in unison: "I, [Name],

prostrate and take refuge, single-mindedly and reverently entreating the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm" (the words of entreaty are as in the Five Precepts).
Fourth, the Announcement: Having respectfully invited the Triple Gem above, may you deign to descend and extend your auspicious radiance;

we pray that you look down with compassionate mindfulness upon this assembly present here. We now wish to proceed to receive the Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera, which serve as the fundamental basis for leaving the household life and entering the Way.
Fearing that our spiritual faculties are shallow and thin, and that demonic obstacles might suddenly arise, we first take refuge in the Buddhas and devas.

I pray for your grace and empowerment, so that at this very moment when the transmission is being correctly bestowed, the entire assembly may maintain single-mindedness without distraction, all phenomena may become orderly, subject and object may merge in stillness, and the act of bestowing and receiving may become flavorless.
I look up with hope that your majestic spiritual power will decisively manifest its awe-inspiring response. (Recite.)
Namo to the Buddhas of the ten directions who abide eternally (Dharma, Sangha), and to the various devas and bodhisattvas who protect the Dharma (recite each three times;
one *chi* [measure] below, then sit). ○ Fifth, the exhortation, etc. (as in the *Yao-yu*).
○ Sixth, the Interrogation: Now, this dharma of the precepts must require that the vessel of the body be pure before one is fit to proceed to receive them.
I fear deeply that you may be burdened by obstacles or impediments that would hinder the precepts;
therefore, I shall now question you one by one, and you must answer truthfully. (First Question)

(Question: "Virtuous son, have you not committed a pārājika offense? (Answer: "No. [These thirteen difficulties (*antarāyikadharma*) and the following thirteen prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*) are as set forth in the *Karmavibhaṅga*.]
1. A nun who has committed a grave offense; 2. One who dwells as a thief in the community; 3. A follower of a non-Buddhist path; 4. A eunuch; 5. One who has killed his father; 6.
One who has killed his mother; 7. One who has killed an Arhat; 8. One who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha; 9. One who has shed the blood of a Buddha;
10. A non-human being; 11. A nāga or an animal; 12. One with both sexual organs.

Since the heavy obstacles have already been resolved, one must answer truthfully regarding the minor obstacles that obstruct ordination (excluding questions concerning age, robes, and bowl, one asks only about the thirteen obstacles).

"Virtuous son, what is your name now? [Answer: "I am so-and-so. "What is the name of your Upādhyāya for the ten precepts? [Answer: "He is so-and-so. "Is your Upādhyāya your teacher? "Did your parents give their permission?
"Do you owe debts to others? "Are you a slave? "Are you a eunuch? "Are you a man of high stature? (Note: *zhàng* refers to a person of great height.)
Regarding the five impediments:
as previously asked of you, if there were no grave obstacles before and no minor prohibitions after, the precepts could be received.

Following my words, take refuge in the Triple Gem (bow once with the hands at the chest; recite along with the voice):
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha... (as in the *Karmavācanā Sūtra*). Recite this three times (bow once with the hands at the chest after each).
○ Eighth, the Exposition of the Precepts (the text explaining the precepts is as found in the *Yāyǔ*).
1. Not killing; 2. Not stealing; 3. Not engaging in sexual misconduct;
4. Not speaking falsehoods; 5. Not drinking intoxicants; 6. Not wearing perfumes or anointing the body with unguents; 7. Not performing singing, dancing, or theatrical displays.
9. One must not sit on high, wide, or large beds. 10. One must not eat at improper times. 11.
One must not handle raw gold, silver, money, or treasures.
These are the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras, which one must not violate for as long as life lasts. Why are only ten precepts enumerated?
Because one frequently commits transgressions, these ten precepts—whose essence is non-action—are the merit of untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*).
You must protect and uphold them; do not violate them. The Ninth:
The Tenfold Five Virtues (as in the *Yao yu*). Regarding the five virtues: first, one who has resolved to leave the household life cherishes and wears the Way upon their person.

Therefore, there are five virtues that constitute the essentials of leaving the household life: first, to destroy one's physical beauty; second, to accord with the dharma robes; third, to cast aside body and life to revere the Way;
fourth, to forever sever affection for kin, being without partiality toward anyone; and fifth, to resolve upon the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering all beings.
These five virtues are the great requirements for renunciation.
The ten categories are: first, all sentient beings rely upon food for sustenance; second, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); third, sensation, perception, and volition (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra*);
fourth, the Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*); fifth, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); sixth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*);

seventh, the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-bodhyaṅga*); eighth, the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); ninth, the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*); tenth, [the ten powers].

These ten universal bases (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) and the ten numbers mentioned above are each paired with their opposites to refute the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), so that you may concentrate your minds to discern and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
(The names and meanings of these ten numbers are found extensively in the Vinaya texts; they are not cited here at length.

**The Altar Ritual for Receiving Full Ordination** (including the addition of robes and the declaration of purity).
First, having received the ten precepts on the previous night, the ten masters assemble together with their attendants.
The masters shall have a *jñātipuruṣa* (lay attendant) strike the drum to gather the *śrāmaṇeras*. Next, two attendants go to the hall to inquire after the assembly;

one carries an incense burner and the other strikes the *yin-qiṅ* (leading gong) while lighting lamps to welcome the masters to their seats in the Dharma Hall. The *śrāmaṇeras* then sit in a single row below the masters.

When the incense-burning procession is completed, everyone performs three prostrations together and kneels facing one another. Next, the attendant distributes the portions, the *śrāmaṇera* leads the way with the markers, and once the ten masters have finished, the leader strikes the signal bell twice.
Then, he recites the invocation for the head of the assembly, saying:
Now, a bright mirror on its stand reflects whatever form it encounters; a great bell on its frame resounds when struck.
To perfectly accomplish the Three Jewels, one must rely upon the three masters; to investigate and rectify the seven transgressions, one must depend entirely upon the seven witnesses.

This being so, since these various masters possess both realization and conduct and are fully versed in both the *Sūtras* and the *Vinaya*, one must single-mindedly maintain a focused heart and present each of the three requests (first requesting the Preceptor for Ordination, and next...).
Next, the *karmavācanā* master (following behind the *śikṣamāṇācārya* and before the *sākṣin*) instructs the śrāmaṇeras to each bare their right shoulder, place their right knees on the ground,
and make this request as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], now request the Venerable sir to act as my Preceptor for the attainment of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
May the Venerable sir act as my Preceptor for the attainment of full ordination. Through reliance upon the Venerable sir, may I receive the full ordination.
Out of compassion, [please do so]. (Request three times.)

Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], now request the Venerable sir to act as my *karmācārya* (the teacher who presides over the ritual and serves as the witness for the subsequent instruction).
May the Venerable sir act as my *karmācārya* (the teacher who instructs and serves as the witness for the ritual). It is by relying upon the Venerable sir that I shall receive the full ordination;
therefore, out of compassion, please grant this.
After each has made three requests, the ten masters should speak to arouse joy in them, responding in unison:
"So be it; we shall instruct you in purity; do not be negligent. (The śrāmaṇera replies: "I shall bear this upon my head and serve you.

The attendant then leads the ten masters back to the hall of the ten masters. On the day of the *chen* fast, they enter the dining hall at the time of the empty mind (*śūnyatā-citta*) and take their places accordingly.

Once the Buddha-recitation session is concluded and the meal of gruel for the assembly of monks has ended, one should first invite a monk to serve as the *kāṣāya-pradāna-ācārya* (robe-bestowing master).

Next, the śrāmaṇeras are assembled to hold their robes and bowls and proceed to a designated location. The attendant instructs the śrāmaṇeras to perform three prostrations and sit to listen as the master expounds the Dharma.

The Preceptor adds the robe and preaches the Dharma (as detailed in the *Yao yu* [Essential Words], concluding as follows): He has the śrāmaṇeras kneel facing one another while holding the robe, instructing them with these words.

Regarding the addition of the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*)—which properly consists of three types: the cut-and-sewn (*khaṇḍa-sīva*), the folded-leaf (*pattāvalī*), and the pleated-leaf (*paṭṭāvalī*); below this is the seamless robe (*saṃghāṭī*), which has twenty-one types according to its use; these are to be modified accordingly.
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], receive this five-strip *antarvāsa* robe—one length and one short—cut and sewn, to be worn as a formal possession.
(Recite three times.)
[Add] seven strips (there are actually two types: the cut-and-sewn and the folded; down to the plain robe, there are twenty-two types according to variations).

"Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, [Name], accept this seven-strip *uttarāsaṅga* robe, consisting of two lengths and one shortness, as a cut-and-sewn garment" (recite three times).

[For] the *saṃghāṭī* (there are exactly eighteen items: nine pieces of cut-and-sewn cloth and nine layers of folded cloth; down to the plain cloth, one should modify according to the number of large items):
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], accept this *saṃghāṭī* robe consisting of [number] strips;
it is [number] spans long and [number] spans short, a robe of cut-and-sewn cloth. [Recite] three times."
Kālapātra (Sanskrit: *pātra*; Chinese: *bōduōluó*, here translated as "proper vessel"), Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, [Name], accept this *pātra* because it is of the proper measure and for the purpose of constant use. (Recite three times).
Next is the sitting mat (Sanskrit: *niṣīdana*; translated here as "the cloth for sitting according to the occasion").

"Virtuous One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind: I, [Name], have made this *niṣīdana* according to the prescribed measurements; I now accept and maintain it. (Recite three times. The ritual site should be oriented facing south.

The procedure for donning the robes above follows. If there is no person present to whom one can address the rite (*pratimukha*), it is permitted to perform it through mental recitation (*manasikāra*).
[The robe and bowl are placed] upon the altar. The *jìngrén* (lay attendant) beats the drum, and two *shìzhě* (attendants) go to the hall, continuing to beat the drum as they lead the way.
Holding censers and lifting lamps, they welcome the Ten Masters out from the hall.

Chanting "Namo to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha," they proceed to the altar site, circumambulate the altar from the east to the west, and ascend the second tier of the western steps. Facing east toward the altar, they cast [the items] down.
Standing in a single file, they perform three prostrations to the presiding master.

After the opening announcement and the prayer for the longevity of the Emperor are completed, the ritual implements are withdrawn. Once again, they recite the name of their own Master. Then, circumambulating clockwise around the second tier of the altar, they proceed to the western steps and perform three prostrations upon the altar.
Next, they pay homage to the Four Holy Ones who established the altar with three prostrations, burning incense and reciting the name of their own Master.
From the west, proceed northward to enter behind the Buddha and exit southward, standing in their respective positions. The attendant rings the bell twice to lead the procession;
everyone performs a simultaneous inquiry and sits below the altar. The mallet is struck once, and those with voices complete the *brahman* chant.

The assembly then recites the verses for transmitting the incense and scattering flowers (as in the Ritual for Establishing the Boundary). The master of the altar strikes the ruler once and announces the altar (in current practice, this blessing of the sacred space is often omitted).
Having performed the prostrations, [the candidate] does not use the pure Brahma-voice and does not address the *karmavācanā* directly; he simply raises his hand.
The *karmadāna* (preceptor of the rite) addresses the assembly (as detailed in the *yuyu zhong*).

When this is finished, the *karmadāna* draws lots for the *śrāmaṇera*, writes down his name, and with upright mindfulness, subsequently appoints the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) and the *śikṣācārya* (instructor). The *karmadāna* says:
First, the novice (so-and-so, so-and-so, so-and-so), about to ascend the precious altar, requests from the Sangha to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

We now invite the Preceptor of [Name of Temple] as the *karmavācanā* master (the second position), the Preceptor of [Name of Temple] as the *śikṣācārya* (the third position), and the Preceptor of [Name of Temple] to respond to the dharma to be accomplished (the fourth position).
The sequence being complete, the *karmavācanā* is performed by means of a formal motion (*jñapti*).
The appointed instructor should first ask: "Who is able to serve as the instructor for that śrāmaṇera? (This question is sometimes placed after the question regarding the harmony of the assembly.
[If the instructor replies: "I, [Name], am able," [the presiding monk] should say: "Venerable sir, since you have consented, the formal act of appointment shall now be performed."

Questioning on the root offenses (*ānantarya*): violating a nun, living as a thief, being a heretic, being a eunuch, killing one's father or mother, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, shedding the blood of a Buddha; [questioning on] non-humans, dragons, animals, and those with two sexual organs;
