Having finished the inquiries of greeting, proceed to the front of the Dharma seat and briefly inquire after the master’s health. Ascend the seat;

once seated, inquire before the incense burner, burn three pinches of incense, and then release the remaining incense. Inquire once more, place the sitting mat (niṣīdana) at its proper position, turn the body to inquire, and sit cross-legged.
The second, third, and fourth officiants perform the same actions: they rise, inquire, and [the second person] [performs the same].

Go before the incense burner and stand in the center; this is the third position. Go to the right and stand there; this is the fourth. Go to the left and stand there. All together, perform a greeting (*monshin*).

Advance three steps forward and perform a brief greeting. Kneel cross-legged (*kogai*) facing one another. The second person takes the flower tray, while the two persons on the left and right take up the soup bowls and water bowls respectively.
Rising, they perform a brief hand-greeting (*shochō*), then retreat three steps and join their hands in prayer (*sashu chō*). At this point, the temple gate is oriented toward the front.

The person holding the water vessel at the south end first proceeds to the east; both individuals follow along, sprinkling water and scattering flowers, while the person holding the white staff recites:

"Scattering flowers, I shall recite a verse... (as in the ritual for establishing boundaries, the entire assembly joins their palms and recites it). The person holding the white staff strikes the wooden mallet once, and the assembly...
All joined their palms and, in Brahma-sounds, said:
"We prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas, as well as to the Dharma and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.
Now, you shall expound the Vinaya rules so that the True Dharma may long endure. With Upāli at your head, and the others who have realized the body-witnessing [of the truths]."
Instructing on the Essential Meaning of the Recitation of the Precepts: May all the virtuous ones listen together.
[The officiant] scatters flowers while three people circumambulate the Dharma seat; they scatter them throughout the hall (as in the *Muk-tsi-i*).

Returning to the southeast corner, the three people circumambulate again and stand facing each other with one person kneeling. The person scattering flowers must face south; the person holding the hot water slightly tilts the vessel.
The person holding the water vessel lifts it from within the basin and places the vessel upon the flower tray;
as everyone rises together, the person scattering flowers steps back and sprinkles water, filling the center with flowers.

The two persons carrying the hot water vessels proceed together to the incense burner, bow in unison, take three steps forward, and after a brief bow, kneel facing one another and place the hot water vessel upon [the stand].

Rising from one's original position, perform a brief greeting; retreat three steps and perform another greeting. As the fourth person proceeds first, all return together to their positions to greet and sit.
When the person filling the flower offering reaches the southeast corner, turn the body so that the flower tray faces north.
Return to the incense burner, face it with hands joined, advance three steps forward, perform a brief greeting, kneel crosswise, place the flower tray and water down, and depart.
The *yu* (officiant) rises from his place at the head of the hall, performs a brief inquiry (*wenxun*), steps back three paces to perform another inquiry, and returns to his seat.
As the first person to perform the ritual, he waits for the *fan-yin* (chanting leader) to utter the words "All Worthies" (*zhu xian*).

He then rises, takes up his sitting mat (*zuojù*) and tucks the incense case (*xianghe*) under his arm, performs an inquiry, and proceeds to the incense burner, where he performs another inquiry (the large burner is not used for burning incense). He spreads his mat and performs three prostrations, waiting for the appropriate moment.

As soon as the Brahma-voice has finished, everyone rises and kneels with their bodies facing one another, holding incense burners (the person presiding over the recitation of the precepts on the seat also holds an incense burner). Holding the white announcement, they raise their voices to say:

"The transmission of incense and the recitation of the verse" (the verse is as in the ritual for establishing the boundary). The assembly all join their palms and recite it; the person offering incense [begins] at the first phrase.

After reciting the verse, burn three incense sticks; holding the hand-incense burner, perform prostrations. When the verse is finished, release the hand-incense burner, rise, and perform one prostration.

Withdraw the ritual implements, inquire after the assembly’s well-being, and return to your seat to sit. The presiding official strikes the mallet once, then returns to his seat to inquire after the assembly’s well-being and sits.
The person administering the precepts holds the hand-incense burner and recites as follows:

*The Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra (Preface Concluded)* The presiding monk (zhuchi) releases his hands from the incense burner and joins his palms to bow to the assembly. The assembly all join their palms to receive the bow.

The presiding monk asks: "Virtuous Sangha, listen! Is the Sangha assembled? Is there harmony? He then dispatches those who have not yet received full ordination to seek the consent (*chanda*) of absent members.
(If there are those receiving consent, they unfold their sitting cloths, kneel with one knee raised, join their palms, and say: [End of excerpt]
Venerable Saṃgha, listen: I, the bhikṣu [Name], have received the consent (*chanda*) and purity (*śauca*) from him regarding the legal matter of the Saṃgha;
I give this consent and purity. (Recite once, collect the implements, and return to one's place. Question on the Instruction: What is it for? (Answer: It is for the *Poṣadha* ritual (*karmavācanā*).
Please bear witness. Perform the *jñapti-karman* (as in the *Sifen lü jieben*).
Having asked whether it has been accomplished, once it is declared so, the high seat proclaims the precepts (*śīla*). (The proclaimer joins his palms. He recites the precepts in a level tone;

however, those who recite with a melodic chant follow the practice of the *Wufen lü*, which is a discarded teaching. The recitation proceeds until the abbreviated precepts of the Seven Buddhas, at which point the great assembly [responds].

The *zhai* (preparatory rite) is performed by joining the palms and striking the bell in front of the Sangha Hall twice to summon the *śrāmaṇera*. The person who recites the precepts takes up the hand-incense burner and proceeds until the end of the "Postscript" (*houxu*).

Then, rising from his seat, he withdraws his ritual implements, tucks the incense case under his sleeve, performs a formal greeting (*wenxun*), and descends from the seat. The *fanzhi ren* (person in charge of the *brahman* chant) then announces: "The chanting begins."
The five supernatural powers of the gods and seers were established through incantations; for those who possess shame, they restrain the shameless.
The Tathāgata has established the prohibitions and precepts, reciting them every half-month. Having spoken thus of the benefits of the precepts, I bow my head in homage to all Buddhas.
Like space, you abide in the world; like a lotus, you are unsullied by water. Your mind is pure, transcending all else; I bow my head in homage.
In the ritual for the Unsurpassed Honored One, when the one who recites the precepts reaches the incense burner, both the reciter and the person on duty stand up.
The three together perform a greeting and prostrate three times while unfolding their mats. The one who recites the precepts first withdraws the mat and proceeds to the place of the mallet;
the person on duty likewise withdraws his mat and stands at his original position. Only the reciter waits for the rhythm of the *brahman* chant, whether slow or fast.
As soon as this is concluded, they rise and kneel facing one another, saying:
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], pay my respects at the feet of the assembly of monks and respectfully thank the assembly for the assignment to recite the precepts.
My three karmas have been lax and I have frequently committed lapses; I pray that the Sangha, out of compassion, will grant me joy. Having risen, he performs one prostration.

[The officiant] tucks away the incense case in his sleeve, folds his sitting mat, and bows to inquire after the assembly before returning to his original position. The person on duty [leads with two strikes of the mallet]. The entire assembly rises;

they tuck away their incense cases in their sleeves, fold their arms, and stand in unison with their sitting mats folded. [With two strikes of the mallet], the assembly all bows and stands with their mats unfolded.
The person in charge recites the Verse of Self-Rejoicing (as found in the *Jiejie yi*). When the assembly has finished reciting the verse with palms joined...
Holding the white staff, strike the mallet once and join the palms, saying:
"Everyone, with all reverence, take refuge in the Buddha. (Strike once; lead the assembly in bowing.
"May all sentient beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind. (Lead one strike; the assembly stands, and strike the mallet once.)
Taking refuge in the Dharma (bowing with the *dazhong* call): May all sentient beings Penetrate deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
(Strike the mallet once and say: Taking refuge in the Sangha (bowing with the *dazhong* call):
May all sentient beings Govern and lead the great assembly. The foregoing *poṣadha* ceremony constitutes An infinite cause for supreme merit.
Sprinkle [the water] throughout the Dharma-realm; pay homage to the assembly of sages. (Lead two steps, descend.
The assembly all withdraws their implements and stands. (Lead two steps, descend. The assembly all offers greetings to the person on duty for the day (strike sparsely).
The assembly proceeds first from the small hall. Upon reaching the front of the Sangha Hall, they stand in a single row at the original place of assembly, facing straight ahead.
When the sun is still at its original position (strike the signal), wait for the Abbot to arrive; then the assembly shall all perform a greeting and disperse.

The Rector (Vina) shall have the attendants of the Hall Office (Tangsi) go in advance to invite the seven persons, including the one who recites the precepts, to offer hot water (according to the usual custom).
Furthermore, he shall have the attendants of the Hall Office collect the items and return them to the quarters, ensuring that each and every thing is accounted for.

Compiled by the monk Xingwu, Abbot of Zhongli Temple in Siming: The Ritual for the Summer Retreat (Huang Anju Yi).

[In some monasteries following the Vinaya, sand and water consecrated with mantras are kept in the Main Hall three days prior to the retreat and sprinkled along the corridors on the day of the retreat.
On the eighth day of the fourth lunar month, the *Vina* (Chamberlain) displays the plaque inscribed with the words for the retreat (hanging it on the right side in front of the Sangha Hall).
Plaque for the Proclamation of the *Poṣadha* on the Fifteenth Day (to be hung on the left side in front of the Sangha Hall).
Text for the *Varṣā* (Rainy Season Retreat) (to be written out as on the *Poṣadha* plaque):

"Virtuous One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the Bhikṣu [Name], now, within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) of [Name] Monastery, during the first three months of the summer retreat..."

Because the dwelling for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is dilapidated, it shall be repaired. (Recite this three times. [Addressing the person before them: "Be aware; do not be negligent. [The other] replies: "I shall uphold it. [The first] asks:
"Upon whom do you rely as a master of the Vinaya? [The other] replies: "Upon Master So-and-so" (one should state the name of the Abbot).
[The first] instructs: "If you have any doubts, you should go and ask him."
On the [day] of this month, the Hall Superintendent Bhikṣu [Name] respectfully reports to the Venerable Karmadāna.
Furthermore, the Venerable Abbot shall issue a wooden plaque for the lecture (to be hung on the left side of the Sangha Hall);
one must first go to the Abbot’s quarters in advance to inquire about the specific section and volume of the scripture to be lectured upon, and record these details on the plaque.

The *vina* (ritual director) shall also, prior to the summer retreat (*an-gyo*), calculate the number of monks and prepare in advance the seating chart for the precept assembly (*kai-shō shi-soku zu*,

to be hung in the Hall Office), the liturgical repentance chart (*rai-san zu*— to be hung on the right pillar of the Repentance Hall, or alternatively, two separate charts for chanting and repentance may be made and hung in their respective locations), and the chart for days of reduction (*ken-nichi zu*, to be hung on the left pillar of the Repentance Hall).
*Patwei-tu* (Bedside Chart for the Alms Bowl; currently handed down in written form and posted on the bed). These are all hung on the evening of the fifteenth day.
Furthermore, one must carefully calculate the number of people who will serve as *zhirì* (duty-day holders) within the ninety days of the summer retreat.

First, determine the total number of persons and the number of days per person, report this to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), and then have the storekeeper of the Hall Office (*tangsi*) invite the appropriate duty-day holders according to these numbers to offer hot water (*xiàn tāng*).
The Rector (Vina) shall withdraw, join his palms, and bow to the assembly to announce the principle of taking turns according to seniority.

He must inform those whose turn it is to serve that if they have reasons for requesting leave, they must each personally arrange for someone else to act on their behalf; no other excuses shall be made to cause clamor or dispute.

(In all matters concerning the *yuezong*, one must be tactful and conciliatory to win the hearts of the assembly; otherwise, human relations will not be harmonious. On the evening of the fifteenth day, the Office of the Hall (Wantangsi) shall prepare hot water and issue the command.
The practitioner requests the assembly (such as the Brahmā-like ones) to offer hot water (first, one must harmonize and settle this).
Then, the person on duty for the first day of the month arrives (fearing they may not yet know the regulations, they should be instructed).

When the morning bell tolls on the sixteenth day, go to the Hall of Repentance and place a single table in the center, upon which set the diagram for the ritual of repentance and illuminate it with a candle. As for the ritual of repentance:
There are also fifteen meditation cushions (pútán) arranged in advance according to the diagram; one must not fail to attend to this at the last moment.
After the morning gruel, the rector (weina) orders the temple attendants and the hall stewards to sweep and sprinkle the Great Hall together.
They shall spread the meditation cushions before the Buddha, arranging them all horizontally with the right side serving as the "length," and they shall also provide small low tables (xiǎojī).

Place one [incense burner] before the abbot’s meditation cushion; prepare a flower tray and set it upon a small table or desk (the whisk, *jingchi*, and hand-incense burner are delivered by the head attendant of the Abbot’s Quarters).
Place the *jingchui* (striking mallet) to the right of the Buddha image.

Establish the seats for the two masters, Nanshan and Dazhi, on both sides of the Buddha image in front of the pillars, with incense, flowers, censers, and candles as offerings (or this may also be done within the Dharma Hall).

When the arrangements for both corridors have been completed and the meal has concluded, the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) orders the attendants of the hall to ascend to the various shrines with incense and candles.
The hall administrators’ attendants first notify the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and then notify the Abbot’s quarters, saying: "We inform the Venerable Master to strike the bell.
All bells are struck in sequence starting from the small board; next, the bell in front of the Sangha Hall is tolled, and the assembly of monks each prepares their seats.
Equipped with incense cases and wearing their robes, they assemble in orderly fashion at the Great Hall according to the ritual for recitation, standing in rows.

Once the large bell has been struck and its tolling ceases, they wait for the great drum to be beaten. Upon the signal, the Abbot ascends the hall, burns incense in the large incense burner, and withdraws to stand in his place as the drum falls silent (strike two rolls).
The Rector then intones the *Sutra on the Elimination of Calamities* and leads the chanting of mantras while circumambulating the Buddha.

The person on duty for the day arrives first at the exterior lower edge of the hall and stands waiting. When the *jūji* (abbot/resident master) reaches the entrance, he turns before the Buddha to perform a bow (*monshin*).
[The attendant] leads him down [the steps] (II). He then turns and exits the threshold of the hall;

the person on duty bows as the *jūji* proceeds ahead, keeping slightly below his shoulder. [The attendants] strike the gong intermittently (or, in some cases, two attendants sprinkle sand and water before him). They proceed in order, circling the corridor to the right.

Proceeding to the various halls and chambers, burn incense; finally, go before the Hall of the Local Deity (Tǔdìtáng) to burn incense and perform the circumambulation (*xiàngxíng*) for one or two circuits.
Once the assembly has taken their places, the *Weina* strikes the *qìng* bell to conclude the recitation of the sutra. When the sutra is finished, chant the *Mahā-āyuṣya-mantra* one hundred times.
The *Weina* then goes before the Local Deity to burn incense and perform the dedication of merit (*huíxiàng*), which consists of four or six lines of prose (addressed to the assembly).

Regarding the intent behind the reliance on the *vassa* (summer retreat), there may be a ritual procedure in which the *vinaya* master first recites the liturgical verses, followed by circumambulating the corridors while chanting mantras.
The assembly chants in harmony with the Buddha as usual; the *karmadāna* enters his position and leads the chant "Namo to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha" (with two prostrations).
The assembly recites this in unison. The official of the day strikes the signal gong, leading the way to the Great Hall, whereupon the head monks take their places.

Outside the hall, they stand in separate lines according to the order of their precepts. Upon entering the hall, they proceed from the center toward the great incense burner and before the Buddha image, burning incense and circumambulating to the right.
The abbot enters through the first row of cushions and stands at the first position on the western side.

Once the assembly has all taken their places, the *zhirì* (daily duty officer) leads the way; the assembly bows in greeting, spreads their sitting cloths (*zàojù*), and ceases all sounds, including those of the Buddha-recitation.
Perform three prostrations; the attendants of the Hall follow suit. Strike the *qing* once, then sit cross-legged until the next day.
Stand facing outward at the place of the mallet and wait for the assembly to be seated. Strike the mallet once; the assembly joins their palms.

The *fanren* (chant leader) raises the *jishou li zhufu* (Prostration to All Buddhas) [as recited in the *busha*]. When the chanting ceases, the Abbot takes up the hand-incense burner, performs three incense-twirls, and raises the *chuan* (transmission).

Recite the Incense Verse (as in the Ritual for Establishing the Boundary). Release the incense burner and take up the flower tray; recite the Verse for Scattering Flowers (as in the Ritual for Establishing the Boundary).
When the verse concludes, strike the mallet once. The attendant on duty returns to his seat.

The Abbot strikes the ruler twice, takes up the whisk, joins his palms, bows to the assembly, and addresses the presiding officer (either in four-character or six-character prose, as one chooses). Having declared the intent for the summer retreat and its diligent practice, conclude by saying: "The Mountain Dweller, [Name]..."

A) Having respectfully informed the assembly, everyone turns around to face their respective partners and performs the *pratyekapratimukha* (face-to-face) *anvaya-vāsa* (residence) ritual (each reciting three times).

Each asks and each answers (the person of highest rank always acts first; however, when the abbot faces his partner, there is no questioning or answering). Once the assembly has completed the ritual, they turn and stand up, maintaining solemn composure until the day’s end.
They proceed directly to the place where the mallet is kept and stand there (prepared to strike the mallet while reciting the Buddha’s name).

The Abbot, holding the hand-incense burner, performs the dedication, saying: "The vast merit accumulated through the above performance of the *an-guo* (rainy retreat) ritual in strict accordance with the Vinaya precepts is dedicated solely for the long life and peace of the current Emperor.
[Dedication as in the *jie-jie yi* (Boundary-binding Ritual)]... up to the *pāramitā* [verse]. Strike the mallet once more."

[The *vīnā* intones] the *bhāṣya* in the Brahma-voice at the place where people perform [the ritual], as in the *Poṣadha* rite. (If the two methods of *pravāraṇā* are being performed, the *bhāṣya* is used after;

however, for the single method of *varṣā* [rainy-season retreat], it is not used. The *vīnā* proclaims: "Namo to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. [The assembly] stands, collects their implements, and moves toward the large incense burner.

They inquire after one another’s well-being, burn three pinches of incense, and then withdraw to their seats to arrange their implements. The *vīnā* proclaims: "His countenance is most wondrous and sublime."

(As stated above) After three prostrations and standing, next recite the names of the Ancestral Masters of the Southern Mountain and the verses of the awakened ones who appeared in succession (as stated above).
Next, recite the name of the Great Wisdom [Bodhisattva] and the verse "Endowed with Perfect Dignity" (as stated above; the aforementioned verses are as found in the ritual text).

Each time, offer incense and perform three prostrations (as described above). Again, recite the names of all the great ancestral masters and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, performing three prostrations for each.

(No incense is burned. As the assembly enters the hall together, the attendants follow in bowing and striking the *qing* bell. The assembly collects their sitting cloths (*zuoju*) and waits until all are properly arranged.

(The *yin* bell is struck three times. When the assembly has completed their mutual salutations (*wenxun*), the Abbot proceeds first, followed by the assembly, circumambulating to the right and saluting each other one by one before the Buddha before exiting.
The attendant on duty remains outside the hall as before (striking the *yin* bell as above) and leads them to the Dharma Hall.
Circumambulating the hall clockwise, they stand in formation. The abbot shall offer several words regarding the purpose of the ninety-day assembly;

having done so, he performs three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*). Once the abbot has finished speaking, the assembly likewise performs three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths.
Then, after bowing in greeting (*wenxun*), they disperse.
When the Abbot ascends the sedan chair, the attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi Xingzhe) shouts loudly:

"I request the two classes of officials, the elders, and the assembly to each carry incense and proceed immediately to the Abbot’s Quarters for a formal greeting. (The Rector [Weina] has previously prepared two candles, which are first placed at the incense burner in the Abbot’s Quarters; the same applies to the seat in the office.
The assembly gathers in front of the Abbot’s Quarters. The Rector orders the attendant of the Hall Office to enter and inform the Attendant (Shizhe), who then...
Lead [the guest] before the Abbot and say: "Prostrate to the Abbot, the two classes of officials, and the assembly.

The Abbot descends the steps to receive the Head Seat (Shouzuo), the Administrators (Zhishi), and the Heads of Departments (Toushou). [The guest] steps forward and requests them to be seated. The Abbot declines;

each person burns incense, and after the customary greetings are concluded, they escort [the guest] down the steps. The West Hall (Xitang) and the Senior Elders (Qijiu) proceed [to meet him] as above. The assembly follows.

If one does not receive the assembly [as the presiding monk], one must ascend the steps; the *shangzuo* (the "senior seat," so called because there is no specific personage designated for it) acts as the leader (*candou*). Approaching [the master], he requests:

"Please, Venerable Master, sit cross-legged to allow us to pay our respects. The *weina* stands on the right as the head of the procession, leading three members of the assembly forward to burn incense and perform three prostrations.
The rest of the assembly then lines up in order from east to west, proceeding in the same manner, with the appropriate announcements made throughout.
Regarding the admonitory speech, if the abbot is modest and does not accept this ritual, he shall join the assembly to burn incense, offer thanks for the lecture and instruction, and then conclude.

The abbot shall see him down the steps, and the assembly shall proceed to pay respects to the various officials. Among the administrators (*karmadāna*) and heads of departments (*śreṣṭhin*), each shall act as a host in turn and prepare incense and verses.
(If it is an elder *vaihāyasika* serving as the head seat, he may accept the incense; however, if someone of lower rank occupies this position, he must not accept it. If the abbot is modest...)

[The guest] must not accept anything at all. Thereafter, the assembly may engage in private social interactions (such as requesting instruction from a teacher, exchanging greetings with peers, or meeting fellow dharma-relatives), each according to their own convenience.

Once the assembly has returned to their quarters to rest, they await the abbot’s inspection of the dormitories (*luāo*). If the officials have their own private quarters, they may receive [the guest] there, provided they yield the seat of honor to the host. If the reception takes place in the two corridors, three or five rooms should be drawn together to establish a single location for the formal reception.
The abbot first dispatches an attendant to the quarters of the Head Seat (*shouzuo*), the Administrative Officers (*zhishi*), and the Head Monks (*tou-shou*).

The Announcement for the Departure [of the Abbot]: The Abbot of the Vihara returns the greeting. If the various quarters along the two corridors are involved, the announcement is made at the location where the seats have been set;

the most senior by years of ordination (*lǎ*) is appointed as the leader (*cāntóu*). (The invitation says: "Please sit cross-legged. The Abbot declines, saying: "I have already witnessed your grand ceremony.

Thereafter, they exchange pleasantries regarding the weather and seasonal conditions. The administrative officers (*zhīshì*) and heads of departments (*tóushǒu*) must likewise perform this announcement once.
Regarding the etiquette for the various quarters, the attendant in charge of the ritual hall announces: "The two classes of officials are making a circuit of the quarters to offer their thanks.
If a person holding an office receives private honors, this shall also be announced separately; the formal rites of the monastic community must not be treated with negligence or arrogance.
On the seventeenth day, the gong is struck once in the gruel hall, and it is said:
He announces to the assembly: "The summer retreat has already passed one day; eighty-nine days remain. You should exert yourselves with diligence and be careful; do not be negligent.

(In this manner, the days are added at the beginning and subtracted at the end as each day passes. When a month with fewer days has ended, the remaining days are added to the count of days already passed and announced. This continues until the fifteenth day of the seventh month, at which point it concludes.
On the sixteenth day of the seventh month, there is only the announcement for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, as no further days can be subtracted.)
The attendant must report to the Abbot on the evening of the sixteenth day, saying: "Tomorrow, the Master will specially provide tea and soup for the Head Seat and the assembly.
The Abbot replies: "So be it. The attendant then assumes a dignified demeanor and goes to the Head Seat’s quarters to inquire after him, saying:
"The Abbot of the Vihara intends to prepare tea specially for the Head Seat tomorrow after the morning gruel; we humbly hope for your compassionate presence."
The Chief Seat (Shouzuo) replied with humble courtesy: "How could I, of such meager virtue, presume to accept such a distinguished invitation? I shall attend accordingly.

On the following day, at the time for the morning gruel, the attendant (Xingzhe) in charge of hosting guests in the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang) goes to the gruel hall and, while circumambulating the hall, invites the two classes of the assembly, saying:
"The Abbot, the Honored One, requests that you all proceed to the Dharma Hall to receive tea. This continues until the striking of the bell signaling the end of the session.

The tea board is struck three times as a signal; the Abbot first arrives and stands at the central seat, while the Attendant stands in the southeast corner facing west, awaiting the arrival of the Head Seat and the assembly at the Dharma Hall.
The Attendant steps forward to inquire after their well-being and leads them to the steps.
Once they have descended the steps, the Abbot receives them and exchanges greetings with the Head Seat, followed by [greetings with] the rest of the assembly.
The assembly inquires after the health of the Abbot, bows to the Head Seat (Zhuzuo), and returns to their respective positions.
The assembly stands in order and bows together before sitting down. The Attendant (Shizhe) stands facing north in the southeast corner, waiting for the assembly to be seated.
He then leaves his position, passes before the incense burner to bow, and proceeds to bow before the Abbot (to signify the request for incense; the incense case must have been prepared in advance).
Place [the incense] upon the desk. Pass before the Head Seat (Shouzuo) to inquire after his well-being (this is called "bowing while seated"), then turn and exit.

Before the incense burner, briefly inquire after his well-being, take one pinch of incense, and once again ascend the hall from the east. Arriving before the Head Seat, inquire after his well-being (this is called "bowing for the incense"), then turn and exit as before.

Stepping back before the burner, inquire after his well-being with hands joined, and stand still. (In some traditions, there is a further burning of one stick of incense in the interim; this is not the proper ritual.)
The two attendants each hold a tea bowl and stand by the sides of the abbot and the head seat, waiting for their instructions.
When the abbot raises his hand to signal the assembly, the attendant strikes the tea gong twice and passes the tea to him. Next, they serve tea to the rest of the assembly;
once it has been distributed to all, the attendant returns to the center to perform a brief inquiry (wèn-xùn), then proceeds from the east to the front of the head seat.

Inquire after [the guest’s] well-being (this is called "yielding tea"), then return to the center to inquire after [the host’s] well-being and burn one incense stick (called "light-accompanying incense").

Ring the board once to collect the cups; ring the board a second time. (According to Chan regulations, for the morning and evening tea services, first ring the long board until the attendant has yielded the incense; when drinking the tea, ring the board twice; when collecting the cups, ring the board once;

when withdrawing from the seat, ring the board once—thus totaling five board strikes. If it is a special tea service, first ring the drum once; when withdrawing from the seat, ring the drum three times. Reside.
Carry the Head Seat (Shouzuo) to the incense burner (the assembly all turn toward the west and stand behind the Head Seat).
The Head Seat bows to express his gratitude for the tea; the Abbot bows in return to escort him. The attendant steps forward, bows again to escort him, and then disperses.
When the meal is finished, the attendant returns to the Head Seat’s quarters to invite him [to the next service].
The Abbot again orders the guest-inviting attendants to invite the assembly for the *tang* (hot water offering; the ritual for the *tang* is identical to that of the tea).
This matter must be supervised by the attendant (*shishi*), while the administrative servants prepare the *tang* pitcher, cups, saucers, tea spoons, and trays, ensuring they are all orderly.
Alternatively, they may notify the various quarters to prepare them, and then arrange the seats, incense burners, flower vases, and candle stands within the Dharma Hall.

To ensure there is something worthy of observation: on the eighteenth day, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) and the Abbot’s Attendant (Dusi) shall each take turns serving tea and soup once (or, as may be the case, serve the three-day tea and soup for the monastery).

all must arrive early, before the wooden fish gong has sounded (or having been invited the previous night), and personally visit the Abbot’s quarters to inform the Attendant and wait in attendance.

He then instructs the attendant of the Hall Office to go around the hall and invite the assembly to perform the rites (as above), with the exception that the Head Seat ascends to the west.
Upon reaching the abbot’s quarters, one should inquire after his health; the only difference is that one exits from the west.

the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) shall request the appropriate liturgical sections for the day, and the Head of the Assembly shall offer hot water. First, prepare a sheet of paper.

After the *rāula* (monastic administrator) has explained the purpose of the preliminary categories, he instructs the practitioners to set out a single desk and place upon it a brush, inkstone, and ink cakes.

Having completed the preliminary preparation for the recitation, the *Vina* (Monastic Administrator) shall present the text from the beginning to the Abbot for his signature;
this is done so that there may be no hesitation regarding the performance of the recitation.

The lot used for selection must be kept in the public domain so that those scheduled for the lecture day do not fall into negligence.

If the affairs of the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) are busy, the rector (weina) should temporarily cease his duties and must not act rashly;

It is appropriate to proceed with the preliminary rites first. Regarding the Chan regulations for the closing of the retreat (*jie-zhi*), there are three special days for serving tea:
on the first day, the Abbot personally serves tea for the Head Seat and the assembly; on the second day, the administrative office (*kusu*) serves tea for the Head Seat and the assembly;
and on the third day, the Head Seat serves tea for the assembly of the Rear Hall. All of these take place in the Sangha Hall.
For all formal ceremonies, a tea notice is posted before the Sangha Hall.

Regarding the Opening of the Summer Retreat: The myriad phenomena of the universe are the realm of the One True Reality. Night after night, the blue sky and bright moon; morning after morning, the green trees and singing orioles.
These fully manifest the Samantabhadra Monastery and reveal the essence of the pure precepts. For ninety days, the prohibitions are observed.
One must deeply guard against the criticisms of the mundane world; during the three-month summer retreat, one constantly protects the lives of sentient beings.
This cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed by the mouth; how could it be contained within the pursuit of forms or sounds?

Whether in terms of nature or prohibitions, neither maintaining nor violating, it is perfectly round and brilliantly radiant, illuminating the past and resonating through the present. Pure, naked, and vividly clear, it supports heaven and upholds the earth—how can it be compared to anything else?
The "Wild Goose Protects the Thunder" and the "Wax Man in the Ice" are tested by others; here, neither is of any use.

Now, respectfully adhering to the sacred regulations and following established precedents, we shall dwell together in peaceful retreat. Each shall present their confession before the assembly. I, the mountain dweller [Name], respectfully announce this.
Dedication at the Land Hall for the Closing of the Retreat: The three-month *an-gu* (summer retreat) follows the solemn regulations of the Tathāgata;
our dwelling in this region relies entirely upon the vast grace of the divine and sacred powers. We humbly entreat your spiritual wisdom to look down with clear discernment upon us.
Now, we assemble our fellow practitioners to circumambulate the Dharma abode, chanting the *Vidyārāja Dhāraṇī Sūtra for the Elimination of Calamities* and reciting the name of the Mahā-Buddhamātṛ.
I dedicate the merit of this collection of sacred names to the local deities (various positions) of this mountain, the presiding spirits of the entire hall, and the holy sages of this temple.

I pray specifically that all demons be extinguished, that the entire assembly may enjoy peace, that the six sense organs and three karmas be purified like ice and water, and that the seven groups of offenses and five articles of discipline be cleansed as white as snow.
In walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, may the four requisites never fail; regarding fire, theft, public or private matters, may all be free from calamity.
May there be no disturbance even as much as a hair’s breadth; may all such prayers be granted through manifest response.

"Each of you recite the pure and wondrous verses from the Vinaya (as in the *poṣadha*). Once the assembly has finished their mental recitation and the formal announcement has been made, the person presiding over the rite should stand up and strike the wooden mallet.

The *brahman* chanters perform the *brahman* chant (as above). Once completed, there is no further need to announce the transmission of incense; the verse concludes, and the abbot simply remains in place.

The seat is not the seat for attaining enlightenment; it is a seat of grass. Second, the two *pañcavarga* (groups of five) rise, collect their implements, and exit to both sides.

I alone admire the fragrant name (Cloud-Mind), where a single thread of incense (drifts with sweet moisture, piercing the heavens) and tenfold great drenching (brings clarity and brightness).
May the Buddhas and Devas grant rain; the Buddha’s compassion has been moved by our sincerity, and His Holy Virtue is impartial.
It stirred the Nine Heavens below, immediately releasing the parching heat of the tortoise-shell divination; three days of rain have sufficiently moistened the auspicious signs of the fish-dream.

The Compassionate Father Avalokiteśvara, the Guide who vows to rain down salvation from suffering, took the pure water from his precious vase and sprinkled it everywhere with willow twigs, reviving the parched and withered earth.

In an instant, the crops were restored; for three days a single rain poured down in a deluge of grace, filling tens of thousands of granaries and hundreds of thousands of storehouses as the sound of joy permeated all.

O Dragons, we pray that you will send down rain. We beseech the Creator above and invoke the Dragon Lords to swiftly raise the clouds of compassionate intent and pour down the rains of sorrowful mercy.
May the five grains flourish daily and the hundred crops ripen in their season; may the people rejoice in perpetual abundance, and may the records of the year show a great harvest.

Prayer for Clear Skies: Śākyamuni, World-Honored One; Avalokiteśvara, Compassionate Father—grant the power of fearlessness and employ your great compassionate heart to sweep the azure heavens clear, lest deluded clouds bring further calamity.
Disperse the bright sun and suddenly cause the entire earth to shine with radiance.

May the five grains no longer suffer from the dread of being submerged by floods, and may the six types of crops hold the hope of a bountiful harvest. Grant your grace immediately in response to this earnest prayer.
The response was manifest.

○ Regarding the prayer for snow: if one receives snow throughout the winter, the year may be blessed with successive bountiful harvests; if the "three whites" present their auspicious signs, then Heaven bestows its wondrous grace through great artistry.
Thus, [the monks] from near and far gathered together, and in the Sangha hall, Daozhao made this announcement to the deities above and below and to Heaven.
Though the Way is remote, the human heart can be moved; Śākyamuni, the Tamer, and Avalokiteśvara, the Guide, with the hearts of parents, fulfill the vows of sentient beings.
Through the vast application of the three wheels of activity, they boil the waters of the four great oceans until every drop becomes a flower;
manifesting the supernatural powers of the ten strengths, they pervade the borders of the unified realm, where white jade accumulates in towering piles.

During the winter, at the Great Hall or the Treasury Hall, for the ritual of offering prayers for the Emperor on the first and fifteenth days of the month, prior to the morning repentance, the assembly recites the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* once.

After the Abbot has finished burning incense and reciting the incense mantra, the Rector (Vina) leads the chanting of the name "Namo Amitābha Buddha" three times. The Rector then makes the formal announcement.

[Cloud] Address to the Buddha: (As before) [Name], Abbot of [Name] Temple in [Name] Prefecture of [Name] Province, a monk and subject, on this day of the [first/fifteenth] day of the month, has respectfully assembled the monastic community to reverently approach the precious hall, chanting secret mantras and extolling the names of the Buddhas.
By the vast merit thus accumulated, I pray for the long life and prosperity of... (In cases where the abbot performs the dedication himself, he may say: ...for the benefit of all beings.
May the current Emperor’s holy life be ten thousand years of peace; may the Empress Dowager and the Empress live as long as the Emperor;
and may the Crown Prince’s wisdom and fortune endure for a thousand autumns. Gazing afar upon Your Majesty’s person, we pray that you be joined with the celestial count of years.

[We recite] the *Vajra*, the *Amitāyus Sūtra*, the *Āyuṣpati-rāja Bodhisattva*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; having finished reciting these, we do not recite the minor sūtras, but instead perform the rite of repentance. Having completed the repentance, [the ritual continues].

After the early morning gruel service has concluded, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community; the drum is struck, and the *zangxing* (Tripitaka reciter) strikes the *fuo* (cymbals).

[The striking of the drum and cymbals is not exempted. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) intones the *Xiuzai Jing* (Sutra for Averting Disaster) while circumambulating the Tripitaka three times to symbolize the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma, praying that the imperial way may flourish far and wide.
Having stood still and finished the sutra, the *vinaya-dhara* intones: "Namo..."
Amitāyus Buddha (Dedication Verse):
Within the Great Perfectly Radiant [Mirror] lies the Flower Treasury Ocean; its merit transcends all transformation, its Way is beyond name and speech.

The three lights roll like lightning, yet the true mark remains tranquil; the six realms thunder forth, yet it is profoundly still and silent. This inconceivable Dharma is difficult to praise to its full extent.

Through the recitation of the *Sūtra of the Dharani for the Elimination of Calamities and the Majestic Virtue*, the turning of the Dharma-treasure wheel of the Celestial Palace, and the chanting of the Buddha’s name,
these accumulated vast causes are solely for the purpose of offering prayers for [the Emperor’s] longevity (as detailed above).

It is further said: "The Wheel of Dharma was turned thrice throughout the great chiliocosm; that wheel is inherently and eternally pure. That devas and humans have attained the Way serves as its witness;

from this, the Three Jewels have appeared in the world. (At present, on the eighth day of the month and the twenty-third day—the days of the fast—one also practices the recitation of the *Tripitaka*.)

Upon arriving at the imperial court for prayers, whenever performing rites of incense-burning and supplication, one must be reverent and purified through ritual bathing. The offerings of flowers and fruits must be fresh, and the incense and candles must be of the finest quality.

The temple halls must be swept and sprinkled with water at all times, and the monastic community must maintain solemn and dignified deportment. When officials offer incense, they should do so with added reverence.
The abbot and administrative officers shall welcome and see off guests with propriety, remaining free from extraneous affairs.

The quarters for the senior monks must always be kept strictly clean, ensuring that their efforts bear fruit and that the mountain gate’s prayers are fulfilled. The storehouse office shall first consult the abbot’s intention and present it in advance to the rector;

the hall office attendants shall then notify the various lodgings and post the notice boards. The assembly shall gather twice daily to chant, concluding the service with formal dismissal. Strictness is required.
Having established the offerings, we set a fixed period for their efficacy, each hoping for single-minded sincerity. As the summer—
the anniversary of the Tathāgata’s birth—
is approaching, the hall administrators and attendants shall lead the assembly to deliver various provisions to the treasury office to prepare these offerings.

The ancient method is as follows: while the Abbot delivers the discourse, the Rector (Vina) orders the preparation of the following text (if the ritual text of Dharma Master Xi-xi already exists, it need not be composed).
All signatures on the petition are to be handled together with those for the Sacred Festival.

The administrative office (Ku-si) shall in advance instruct the attendants to solemnly set up the interior of the Vimala Garden, install a bronze statue of the Prince, prepare fragrant decoctions, place two small ladles within the basin, and arrange [offerings] before the Great Buddha.

The offerings are presented until the hour of the day (the eighth hour). The assembly, each assuming their proper dignified demeanor, proceeds together to the Great Hall and stands as if in recitation.
The Abbot burns incense, returns to his position, and stands firm. The Rector (Vina) recites the Verse for Bathing the Buddha (the text of which appears below;
in many instances, the Head Seat recites the Sutra or the Buddha’s name, according to local custom).
To the right, prepare copper coins for the Buddha-bath ceremony. Each person returns to their seat upon the *pútuán* mat and spreads their ritual implements.

The Abbot offers incense, returns to his position, and together with the assembly performs three prostrations without withdrawing the implements. He steps forward to offer hot water and food. When the attendant has finished serving, he returns to his position;

the assembly performs three prostrations, offers incense, distributes monetary gifts (*xiān zhǐ*), and serves tea. The assembly performs three prostrations. (In the Chan regulations, the drum is struck three times; in the Lecture Hall, it is specifically struck for the *lǎo*). The assembly kneels.
The Abbot holds the incense burner; the Rector recites the two verses for the incense and flowers (as in the Ritual for Establishing the Boundary).

When finished, the Abbot recites the general announcement from the opening salutation through the three requests. Once completed, the assembly rises. The Abbot recites the Buddha-verses (from the ritual text: "In the heavens above and the heavens below, none is equal to the Buddha...").

When finished, the Rector steps forward to proclaim the memorial text (*śāstra*). Having finished, he recites the mantra for transforming food and returns to his place. The assembly performs three prostrations.

Perform the prostrations (as in the ritual text; hereafter, all shall be chanted by the *vinaya-dhara*). Once the prostrations are completed, the assembly puts away their implements and recites either the *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Legacy of the Teaching) or the "Anle-xing-pin" (Chapter on Peaceful Conduct).

(Alternatively, one may perform the dedication of merit, or simply recite the verse beginning with "May the three obstructions and all afflictions be extinguished," etc. At the conclusion, recite: "In the ten directions and three periods of time...

(etc., up to "...pāramitā"). Then, disperse while circumambulating to the right. (The Dedication says: "The merit from the above recitation of the sutra is dedicated toward the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
May this adorn the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit, universally repay the four debts of gratitude, provide sustenance for all beings in the three realms of existence,
and cause all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu* to together perfect the seed-wisdom. To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time,
and to all Honored Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, [homage to] the Mahāprajñāpāramitā (and so forth).
A verse addressed to the Buddha:
The single moon dwells in the sky, its reflection contained within all waters; The one Buddha appears in the world, each seated upon a flower.
The white tuft of hair radiates light, illuminating the three realms; Nectar is sprinkled, nourishing the four modes of birth.
Bathing Buddha Gāthā:
I now bathe all the Tathāgatas, The mass of merit adorned by pure wisdom;
May sentient beings of the five turbidities be freed from defilement, And together realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Statement: [Name] of [Road], [County], [Temple] respectfully reports:

On the eighth day of this month, the anniversary of the birthday of our Great Preceptor Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the Abbot Bhikṣu [Name] and the assembly of bhikṣus have prepared these modest delicacies to extend our offerings.

Now, I humbly submit that while in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he never rose from his seat yet constantly preached this Dharma; within the Lumbinī Garden, he manifested birth through the power of his great vows.
Looking upward, downward, and in the four intermediate directions, he is proclaimed the Sole Honored One among the three realms.

As the fragrant influence of the Dharma realm flows through the era of the Image Teachings, this day marks the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth; auspicious signs surge from the Dragon Abyss, manifesting the merit of the ceremonial ablution performed in former times.
We, the disciples of the Great Monk, the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Tathāgata, humbly pray that you shall employ the ocean of your profound wisdom to turn back the surging, turbulent waves.
May the radiance of this glorious age further extend the boundless longevity of the Sovereign, and may all sentient beings, as numerous as motes of dust, attain liberation.
Together we realize the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body. Respectfully annotated.

Regarding the ritual texts for the anniversaries of the Tathāgata’s Parinirvāṇa and Attainment of Enlightenment, Master Xi溪 (Xi) has produced them; yet the rite for the Attainment of Enlightenment likewise must not be omitted, and as for Chan... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary liturgical note or preface. The final characters "禪" suggest the text may have continued with a discussion on Chan practice.)
The Forest Tradition contains an ancient saying recorded hereafter: On the appointed day, the abbot prepares the ritual texts and leads the assembly in providing offerings.

The assembly gathers to offer incense, performing three prostrations; they present hot water and food, performing three prostrations; they offer incense again, distribute monetary gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), and present tea, performing three prostrations. (In the Chan regulations, the drum is struck three times; for the Lecture tradition, this is a special rite.
The assembly kneels and recites two verses on incense and flowers (as in the Ritual for Establishing the Boundary). The abbot holds the incense burner and recites the liturgical text.
The presiding head recites the memorial for the transformation of food and performs prostrations (following the ritual eulogy of Master Yue).

Upon completion of the prostrations, the assembly collects their implements, recites the *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Bequeathed Teaching Sutra), turns to the right, and disperses (all in accordance with the rituals for the Buddha’s Birthday).
The verse offered to the Buddha:
“The body of the pure Dharma-realm originally has no appearing or disappearing; through the power of great compassion and vows, it manifests coming and going.
Furthermore, [the account of] his attaining enlightenment:
Before Mount Bodhi, he beheld the morning star and awakened to the Way; within the great trichiliocosm, he drove the sun of wisdom to radiate its brilliance.
(The preceding words are from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*; they were extracted by the Vinaya Master Dazhi as found in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Zhīyuán jí*, and are not reproduced here.)
The prose commentary describes the circumstances as being identical to the Buddha’s birth, with the sole difference that "celebrating his birth" is changed to "entering nirvana.

(Regarding the Attainment of Enlightenment: Snow covers the thousand mountains, yet spring returns to the cold valleys; the stars shine brightly at midnight, awakening the heavens as clouds disperse across the vast sky.
This demonstrates the cause of six years of ascetic practice and realizes the fruit of cultivation throughout kalpas. We, [Name] and others, have received this grace...

In this final age, I am humbled to have inherited the ancestral legacy; I harbor deep feelings of shame regarding my diet of hemp and wheat, yet I find it difficult to forget the service of offering the simple *pingfan* (water and herbs).

I prostrate before my Root Teacher, the Great Monk Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and pray that his radiant light may descend upon me to open my ignorance and delusion, and that the great chiliocosm may enjoy eternal longevity.
May the Holy Sovereign enjoy longevity, prosperity, and peace, and may all sentient beings fully realize the wisdom and virtuous marks of the Tathāgata.
[Seal] *Qiū Lánpén Xiàngōng* (Autumn Offering for the Ullambana):
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the attendants of the Ullambana Hall shall first lead the assembly to prepare the necessary materials and deliver them to the storehouse in advance.

The administrative staff prepares offerings to repay the kindness and virtue of their parents. The draft of the memorial and the collective memorial (are performed the same as for the Buddha’s Birthday).
On the day of the ceremony, before the Great Buddha, the offerings are laid out; the assembly each dons their ceremonial robes and proceeds to the hall (as in the ritual for the Nanshan Memorial).

The Abbot offers incense, and the assembly performs three prostrations without withdrawing. They advance to present hot water and food. When the attendant has finished serving, the assembly returns to their positions.

Three prostrations, incense offered, and the distribution of alms; tea is served. The assembly performs three prostrations and kneels without withdrawing their ritual implements (according to the *Changuī*, the drum is struck twice for this special tea ceremony held during a lecture).
The Abbot holds the incense burner while the Rector presents the incense and flowers with two verses (in some places, it is the Head Seat who recites these).

When finished, the Abbot recites the ritual text from the general announcement (*zǒngbái*) through the invitation to the Buddhas. The assembly stands and chants the "Praise of the Triple Gem" and the prayer of blessing. The Rector then [proceeds].

The master proclaims the ritual manual to transform the food; the assembly returns to their seats and performs three prostrations (as in the ritual text of Lingzhi). When this is finished, the assembly withdraws their implements. Once the *Ullambana Sūtra* has been recited, the assembly performs the dedication of merit, saying:
"By means of these practices, may we cultivate roots of goodness to repay the labor and virtue of our parents: for those who remain, may there be boundless blessings, joy, and longevity;

for those who have passed away, may they leave suffering behind and be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*). [May this merit extend] to the four debts of gratitude and all beings within the three realms of existence."
May all sentient beings suffering in the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions be universally graced;

may their obscurations be cleared away and their ailments and defects washed clean, so that they all emerge from saṃsāra and are born in the Pure Land throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time... (as above), dispersing [the flowers] while circling to the right.
The aforementioned words (from the *Lanpen Shu*; extracted by Dazhi Lushi as found in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Zhishuan Ji*). Compiled:
The Ritual Text for the Anniversary of Master Lingzhi of Nanshan (compiled by Gushan, Chexi, and Kāṇa Lushi).
The Ritual Text of Lingzhi (compiled by An Lushi). As the anniversary of the master’s death approaches, [the assembly gathers] in the hall.

The Scribe shall issue the order for the dyeing of the *shū* (memorial tablets) at the same time as the Imperial Birthday ceremony (the aforementioned instructions regarding the route to the *zhāi* hall are as follows).
The Abbot shall focus his sincerity; the officers of the Mountain Gate shall prepare everything; the *weina* of the East Zhejiang Vinaya Garden shall preside over the memorial service for Nanshan;

the *zhikě* shall preside over the memorial service for Lingzhi. All requirements for the offerings and meals shall be provided from the funds of the incumbent officers of the respective memorials, so as to serve as the foundation for their transcendence. If...
Who among these would truly take the time to attend to the ancestral texts? How tragic!

When those who observe the prohibitions first entrust the affairs to the attendants to borrow and arrange the ritual vessels for division of duties, the *Tidien* (Director of Ceremonies) shall prepare the Dharma Hall and lay out the ritual implements.

During the day, the head of the *Zhan* (Duty) shall dispatch acolytes to arrange the guardians and straighten the Dharma Hall, hanging the portraits and solemnly setting out the sacrificial banquet, the incense burners, vases, and incense tables.
In each instance, according to the ritual protocol: in the upper section, a meditation chair, whisk, and clothing rack shall be set out for hanging the dharma robes;
in the lower section, a chair, scripture stand, incense burner, vase, incense, and candles shall be arranged as prescribed by the relevant texts. It is improper to simply set up folding beds.

The attendants of the Hall Office shall notify the Abbot’s quarters and all the various monastic offices that they must recite sutras that evening and prepare for the half-day vegetarian meal the following day, each assuming their proper dignified demeanor.

The ritual for the *sanji* (memorial service): Chant the sutra before the altar; ring the bell at the front of the Sangha Hall to assemble the assembly; strike the drum to offer the special hot water (*tetui tang*).

The Abbot offers incense and performs three prostrations without withdrawing his sitting cloth (*bujū*). He steps forward to receive the hot water; once the attendant has finished pouring it down, he returns to his position and performs three prostrations.

He steps forward again to bow for the hot water and inquire after the Abbot’s well-being, then performs three prostrations and withdraws his sitting cloth. The person on duty rings the *yinzǐ* (introductory bell), and the *Weina* (Venerable of Affairs) leads the recitation.

Upon the conclusion of the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) of the *Śāstṛśāsana-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching), the assembly disperses. When the evening bell tolls, the assembly gathers to chant the sutra;

the Abbot offers incense, and the Rector leads the chanting until the dedication is completed. Next, the head of the hall leads the assembly forward in a line to enter the hall (*chán*), where they prostrate and chant the sutra.

The residents of the quarters arrange themselves in rows, respond with a formal greeting (*shēnyuò*), and perform prostrations while chanting the sutra. On the following day, after the morning gruel has been consumed...
The Abbot performs the usual rites of offering incense and hot water; the Rector (Karmadāna) intones the scripture and dedicates the merit.

At the half-meal, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community as usual for chanting. The assembly stands in formation awaiting the Abbot, who burns incense and returns to his position.

Once he is settled, the Rector intones "Namo" [to the Patriarchal Master of the Southern Mountain, the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master]. The assembly circumambulates to the right and each returns to their seat upon the meditation cushions.

The participants unfold their sitting cloths and perform three prostrations; they do not fold the cloths back up. Soup is served, followed by food. Once the attendants have finished distributing it, everyone returns to their positions and performs three prostrations.

Incense is burned, followed by the distribution of monetary offerings (*dakṣiṇā*) and tea. After the assembly performs three prostrations and does not fold the sitting cloths, the drum is struck three times.

For this special tea ceremony, the assembly kneels. The Abbot holds the incense burner, while the Rector recites the verse for lighting incense and the verse for scattering flowers. Having finished, the Abbot recites:

In the ritual text, after the general announcement from the white head down to the three requests has been completed, the assembly rises. The Abbot makes the announcement to the *zhen* (the bell), [or, if acting on behalf of a realized person, one says]:

"The sublime marks are fully perfected," and so forth. The assembly recites this in unison. The Rector steps forward to proclaim the memorial text (*shu*). Having finished, he intones the mantra for transforming food (*bian shi zhou*) and returns to his place.

The assembly performs three prostrations with full obeisance. (As in the ritual text below, all subsequent parts are chanted by the Rector. When the rites are concluded, the assembly puts away their implements and recites the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa Sūtra* (*Yijiao jing*).
[The verse] "Wishing to extinguish the three obstructions" (concluding the verse on the ten directions and three periods of time, etc. ends. The assembly disperses, circling to the right.
At the mountain gate, an offering is prepared; there is no monetary gift (*dakṣiṇā*), but there is a distribution of food.

Dedication of Merit for the First Watch of the Night: The compassionate vows are profound and the Way is vast beyond naming; having humbly received the nourishment from the residual waves, my descendants have attained some luster.
I look up with hope for your true compassion and pray that you will deign to cast your gaze upon me.

On this day—the third (or first) day of this month—it coincides with the anniversary of the passing of the Great Master (Nanshan Lingzhi). We have prepared incense and offerings to extend our veneration in advance, chanting the sacred scriptures.
By extolling the holy name, may the extraordinary merit thus accumulated serve as a supreme requital for the compassionate protection [of our parents].

We humbly pray that all sentient beings may rely upon it to propagate the family tradition of [Taoyi Zhiyuan], and that through inexhaustible wondrous wisdom, they may perfect the faculties required to realize the Perfect Teaching. [Ten Directions and Three Periods...
Furthermore, the dedication of merit states: "The merit from the recitation of the sutra above is respectfully offered for the sake of the Great Master [Nanshan Lingzhi]."

Adorning the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time (*etc.*, as before; the verse for extinguishing the three obstructions may also be used).

The above words [are from] the *Nanshan Zhaiji Su* (Ritual Manual for Fasting and Memorial Services of the Southern Mountain School) by Vinaya Master Dazhi, and the *Lingzhi Su* (Ritual Manual of Lingzhi Monastery) by Dharma Master Xiyan; both are contained within the *Zhiyuan Ji* (Collection of the Zhi Garden).

Winter: Regarding the anniversary of the founding patriarch’s death, one should adhere to the ancient rites and never forget one's ancestors; this may be practiced with diligence. If a donor establishes a temple and requests a founding patriarch, it is customary to observe the memorial rites;
however, those who have performed meritorious deeds for the mountain gate need not be restricted by this rule. This must be done in accordance with the Dharma.

In the center of the hall, mats are spread for the assembly to chant scriptures and perform prostrations, following the same ritual as the memorial services for the Nanshan school. The dedication (pariṇāmanā) states:

"The precious, luminous ocean of emptiness is tranquil amidst the surging waves of birth and death; the gate of great quiescent concentration merges the phenomena of past and present, coming and going.
We look up to Your true compassion and pray that You will graciously grant Your illumination. On this day of this month, it coincides with the anniversary of the founding patriarch [Name]..."
On the occasion of the Venerable Master’s passing into *nirvāṇa*, the monastery has prepared offerings of food to extend its veneration.
As the assembly of bhikṣus recites the sūtras and extols the holy names, may the extraordinary merit thus accumulated be dedicated to the True Compassionate One to further elevate his station.

We pray that the *dharma*-flower may blossom once more, reopening the springtime of the Garden of Enlightenment, and that the Sun of Wisdom may shine forever long, eternally illuminating the dark alleys of the world.

On the night of [the anniversary of] the passing of the patriarchs of the ten directions and three periods (etc.), the various patriarchs’ memorial services are held with great reverence for their spiritual conduct and meritorious governance of the mountain gate.
The arrangements in the Dharma Hall must be made on the day preceding the service; it is not permissible to deviate from this precedent. If it is according to precedent...

For the anniversary of the Patriarch’s death, as is customary, recite the sutras after the gruel meal. One should request the ancestral plaque and seat, arrange them in the Dharma Hall, and perform offerings according to the ritual rules while burning incense.
The Abbot and the two classes of officers prostrate; the attendant prostrates at the end of the row, or the entire assembly may prostrate.

In some places, they merely serve one portion of food directly in the Patriarch’s Hall and recite the sutras; this is highly improper. Dedication of Merit: We look up with hope that the True [Ancestor]...

May Your Compassion look down and take heed. On this day of this month, at the mountain gate, we have encountered the anniversary of the passing of the former abbot of this mountain, the late Venerable [Name], who served as the sixth successor.
We have prepared incense and offerings to extend our veneration, reciting sacred scriptures and chanting the holy names.
By the merit accumulated through these deeds, we dedicate them to Your True Compassion, praying that Your rank be further exalted within the ten directions and three periods.
[The text continues as follows:
Regarding the anniversary of the late Dharma Master Rùn:

The former masters held that one should solely propagate and expound the vehicle of the school (zōngchéng), clarify one’s own nature, and instruct those yet to come, so that they may know there is a transmission of the Dharma.

To repay their virtue, in recent times at the Zen monasteries of Daichuan for the anniversary of Master Zhe’ung and Xianchuan for the anniversary of Master Tianmu, the abbot prepares a seat and sets out a portion of food, burns a single stick of incense, and performs nine full prostrations;
the chanting of sutras is not permitted. These two great elders had profound intent in this; yet, in honoring one's teacher and revering the Way, ritual propriety must not be deficient.

On the anniversary of the passing (jichén), one must prepare offerings within the robe-closet (yigé). Anticipate the necessary funds and goods to be returned to the monastery’s permanent endowment for the purpose of performing the memorial service.

The arrangement of the Dharma hall and the seating of the Dharma seat, as well as the hanging of the portrait, are the same as for the anniversary of the Southern Mountain (Nánshān). However, no prostrations are performed.
One must invite a person of renowned virtue from the West Hall to serve as a companion; he takes his seat to the right [of the abbot]. If none is available, the abbot performs the rites himself.

When the drum is struck three times, the assembly withdraws from their seats. The Hall Attendant (Tangsi) and the ritual assistant (Xingzhe) announce the upcoming recitation of the sutra by hanging up the notice board and notifying all the quarters;

they also announce that there will be a midday meal the following day and instruct everyone to assume their formal dignified demeanor for the memorial service. When the evening bell tolls, the assembly gathers for the recitation of the sutra.

The Attendant directs the Chief Guest Master (Ketu) to invite the two classes of officials and the senior elders in advance to attend the offering of hot water and fruit to accompany the True Body (the deceased). At the Dharma [Hall],...
In the hall, seats are arranged according to rank; the practitioners set out the mats in accordance with the Dharma. Relatives, elders, and brothers from the same lineage must all be invited.
Junior disciples and grand-disciples may not eat together. When the assembly chants the sutras, the attendant bows and invites the two classes of officials and the venerable elders.
The Abbot leads them into their seats. Once they are seated, the Abbot leaves his place, steps forward, and ascends [to the high seat].
The incense-bearer ascends to the bathhouse and returns to his station; the attendant burns incense and descends to serve the bathwater, followed by the distribution of bath-fruit.

The next morning, after the breakfast gruel has been finished, the abbot offers incense and serves the bathwater, prostrating before the assembly of monks as they chant the sutras and perform the dedication of merit. Laypeople and Dharma relatives then immediately join in the chanting for half a meal-period.

The bell in front of the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community, and the abbot, together with those observing the anniversary of the death of Nan-shan, offers incense and performs prostrations.

The head official (tou-shou) goes to offer the bow, and once seated, incense is burned.

(According to Chan regulations, each person should return one prostration; those who do not do so now are doing so because the full prostration would interfere with their robes. **Vinaya:** When a head monk of the West Hall (*xitáng*), a chief administrator (*zhǔzhí*), or a special envoy arrives at the monastery, they first visit the guest master (*zhīkè*). Together, they are led by the attendant (*shìzhě*) to have an audience with the Abbot (*fāngzhàng*).

They offer incense, perform prostrations, and exchange formal greetings according to the prescribed ritual; this includes the sequence for serving tea and seeing off the guests. Go to the Abbot’s quarters to seek formal instruction: "At [Name] Temple, we now invite [Name] Person to serve as the abbot.

that evening, the Abbot invites the special envoy of the new appointee specifically for the medicinal broth and the stone-broth with fruit, accompanied by both the *gwanban* (monastic officials) and the *bangban* (lay attendants).

The Method for the Head Official (Lǚ) to Receive the Dharma Robe from the Abbot:
If the head official is a dharma heir, he first recites the formal report from the Attendant’s Office requesting the abbot to bestow the dharma robe.

On the appointed day, he goes to the Abbot’s Quarters to wait for the abbot’s emergence; upon greeting him, the abbot presents the dharma robe, and if there is a dharma discourse, it is delivered to the newcomer.

Regarding the robes, there is also a procedure for withdrawing them and then donning the *dharmakāya* (Dharma robe). After the abbot has sat cross-legged and performed three full prostrations with the robes fully spread out, he recites the following:
"Throughout my life, I have sought only to settle my own affairs, and I look up with shame at the sages of old. Since the invitation was so earnestly extended, I cannot evade this superior command;
my humble heart is filled with the utmost trepidation. He then performs another three prostrations and recites: "On this day, at this auspicious hour, I respectfully contemplate the Hall..."

[He] first bows three times to the Abbot, the Great Monk, saying: "I hope you are in good health and enjoying many blessings. He then withdraws his implements, steps forward to inquire after the Abbot’s well-being, and says:
"The needle in the bag has already been revealed; the falling flowers and rain cannot conceal it. It is fortunate that this person [the Abbot] is present; I pray you accept my congratulations.

Next, he presents the memorial and the notice, each with its respective formal address. According to the established rules of Chan, the Abbot leads the assembly to their seats, while the seat to the left is prepared for the guest master.

The Holder of the Seat (chih-wei) stands in the right-hand row below the ritual documents (shu-tieh). After the officiant has descended from the seat, the newly appointed incumbent steps forward, bows in greeting before the Abbot, and is presented with the Dharma robe.

There are specific words for receiving the robe, and there are also words for handling the ritual documents and presenting the kōan; whether these are performed or not is not strictly fixed, though they are practiced according to the conduct of the practitioners.

The funds for the ritual gifts and the meal provisions shall be personally delivered by the special envoy to the treasury office, where they shall be deposited and used to prepare the feast.

At the entrance of the mountain gate, a position is established to host a specially prepared tea service, with the two ranks of officials, the elders, and the leading attendants serving as honored companions. The Head Seat shall oversee the proceedings.
Regarding the formal conduct for seeing off [a guest] at the mountain gate: if it concerns the West Hall or a subordinate head official (*shoushou*), they first pay their respects to the assembly.

Prior to departing, they join the special envoy in ascending to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to offer incense and formally take leave (performing three prostrations with the head touching the ground). Next, they visit the various administrative offices (*fangliao*) to take leave;

there, the head of the mountain gate presides over the serving of tea and soup, while the two ranks of attendants accompany them in performing the rites. The striking of the great bell to see them off follows the same protocol as the previous ceremonies.
The Ancient Method for the Abbot’s Entrance:

Carrying the bundle on one's head and wearing the rain hat, one arrives. If met by those coming to welcome him, he removes the hat and performs a formal greeting (*wenshen*). If he encounters officials or nobles, he sets down his bundle and merely bows.

Upon reaching the entrance of the mountain gate, he removes his bundle and hat and burns incense (for which there is a specific liturgical formula). Then, proceeding to the front of the Sangha Hall, he rests his bundle.
After washing one’s feet at the rack, one returns to the front of the Sangha Hall, takes up the robes, and puts them on.

Entering the hall, if there are attendants accompanying one, they enter together before the Holy Monk (Śākyamuni) and perform three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*dazhan*). They then circumambulate the hall once. The attendants exit first;

the *Vina* (Reverend of Affairs) escorts [the guest] back to the bowl-seat, where they exchange a bow (or, according to the Chan tradition, perform three prostrations). The special messenger should beforehand deliberate on this and submit a petition to grant an exemption from the labor of the assembly. The two classes of officials and the senior elders shall offer incense...

the lead officer inserts incense and performs three prostrations, saying: "On this day... (as appropriate), we now receive the honor of the Master presiding over the Dharma assembly; our humble hearts are filled with the utmost gratitude.

the elders each insert incense, followed by the local dignitaries, former associates, and dharma relatives who offer their congratulations in succession.
