The person designated to read the documents first presents them for inspection; according to precedent, the *weina* reads the opening petition of the mountain gate (*shanmen shu*), the *shouzuo* reads the remaining petitions, and the head officers (*tou shou*) read those of the treasury office (*kusong*).
Incense is prepared and sent to the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to pre-invite the various masters of the mountains.

At the seat of the mallet-beater (*baichui*), officials are seated in rows facing one another. Incense is offered and candles are held by attendants. First, the attendant is informed, and subsequently, the abbot is informed.
The abbot strikes the drum to assemble the assembly; the rites are the same as the standard procedure. The attendant, together with the special messenger, enters to invite the abbot.
The ritual assistant strikes the gong, and flowered banners and raised lamps lead the way as they proceed to the position before the Dharma Hall.

If it is not the occasion of receiving the invitation, one should first utter the formal words and don the Dharma robe. Next, the special messenger offers incense and performs three prostrations, saying: (On this day...)

"I humbly receive the Master’s gracious presence at this Dharma assembly today; my inner feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. (Two prostrations and three bows according to the monastic regulations.
First, present the official document containing the Dharma words for the *Weina* to announce. Next, the attendant holds up the formal petition (*shu*).

Then, the petitions from the various monasteries, mountains, rivers, and lakes are presented one by one. The kōans are raised and read aloud. If there are petitions from incumbent officials, they are requested [to be presented].
The officials opening the hall must first personally present their memorial (shu). Next, the abbot presents the monastery’s memorial;
having received the instruction to point to the seat, he ascends the platform and offers incense to pray for the Emperor. He then offers incense to the local magistrates and officials.

If there is a great donor who has established the temple or donated land, that donor should also offer incense (the attendant offering it one by one). Only the incense for the Dharma heir is drawn from within the robe; once offered, the abbot himself inserts it into the burner.

The attendant ascends to the seat and burns incense; the two classes of officials descend from their seats and perform the ritual of inquiry (*wenshun*). Once this is concluded, the attendant ascends the seat, burns incense, and performs the ritual of inquiry;

these rites are the same as usual. The Right Seat official makes the formal announcement and strikes the gavel, saying: "In this Dharma assembly of dragons and elephants, you should contemplate the primary truth (*paramārtha*).

He then presents the outline of the discourse and offers thanks to the officials and the various mountain monasteries, saying: "To open the hall and pray for the longevity of the Sovereign, I dare not..."

[After] praising the virtues [of the guest], the special envoy, the two ranks of officials, the elders, and the assembly briefly offer words of thanks and conclude the session with the formal strike of the gavel, saying:

"Observe closely the Dharma-King’s Dharma; the Dharma-King’s Dharma is thus. [The master] descends from the seat. The abbots of various mountains and the visiting officials take one or two steps forward.
The administrators escort them to their guest seats. The attendants and the guest-head monk immediately advance with incense burners and candles, standing in a single file.

Before entering the hall for the formal greetings, the Master of Ceremonies, the Hall Attendant, and the Ritual Practitioner shall call out: "Greetings from the various mountains," followed by "Greetings from the West Hall" (at which point the incense offering and prostrations are waived).

Then, the officials of the administrative staff perform their greetings (three prostrations; according to the Zen regulations, two bows and three prostrations). Next, the Head Seat, the elders, and the assembly from all the monastic quarters each offer incense and perform their greetings (three prostrations).
Finally, the stewards, the storehouse keepers, those from the hermitages and pagodas, and the lay associates from one's hometown perform their greetings.

Upon first arriving, one performs prostrations together with the assembly, using the following general formula: "Humbly receiving the Master’s grace in presiding over this Dharma assembly, our humble hearts are filled with the utmost gratitude.
(According to the Chan regulations, one performs three prostrations. The response is: "Having the honor of presiding over this famous monastery, I am overcome with shame and trepidation.

One proceeds through the *guasizi* lattice to take one's seat. The attendant (*shizhe*) offers incense and performs nine full prostrations (*dazhan jiubai*). The junior disciples (*xiaoshi*) offer incense and perform [nine prostrations]. The master [of the hall]... [text continues].

The nine prostrations are performed without words. Next, the practitioners from the various halls, the practitioners from the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), the personal attendants, and the six administrative offices take their turn.

Then, the head of the assembly leads the group in offering incense and performing three prostrations. Following this, the sedan-chair carriers, the *zhijin* (direct supervisors), the village headmen, the workshop foremen, and the masters of the various quarters (*liáozhu*) lead their respective groups in taking their leave.
Finally, the Abbot proceeds to the Guest Seat (*kewei*) to express his gratitude to the visiting officials.
The assembly of monks from all the mountains [gathered] (to fulfill the rites).
The newly appointed official toured the various quarters;
incense was spread out, seats were arranged, and censers, candles, and incense were prepared. Each maintained their dignified demeanor as they waited in succession for the tour.
The attendants of the various quarters and the guest master go ahead to announce the arrival to the Abbot.

Upon reaching the various quarters, the head attendants first stand at the entrance with their hands lowered to welcome him in, inviting him to sit cross-legged. They offer incense, and the Abbot returns the incense, briefly exchanging pleasantries regarding the weather and expressing his gratitude before seeing them out.

He then listens to the call for the collection of incense, completes the circuit of the quarters in order, and returns to the Abbot’s quarters to attend to visiting officials and monks from other mountains.

**Special Tea Service for the Sangha Hall** If the Abbot wishes to simplify the procedure, he should issue a notice in advance exempting the service from tea and soup. The administrative office (Kusi) shall prepare an invitation letter along with a ceremonial cloth (*pao*), incense burner, and candles, and proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and perform the rites (according to the *Zen Regulations*:
two prostrations and three bows). The invitation is made as follows: "Upon the conclusion of the midday meal, we shall gather in the Cloud Hall to serve tea."

I specifically entreat you to show compassion and deign to attend. Having received the invitation, the *ketou* (guest master) is instructed to invite the two classes of senior monks (*qijiu*) to serve as honored companions.

The notice board is posted and the quarters notified; the seats for the abbot and the assembly are prepared in the Sangha Hall. When the long gong sounds at mealtime, incense is lit and prostrations are performed.
The hall is inspected, and tea is served. After the meal, the drum is struck to assemble the community; the head administrator bows to the abbot.
Holding [the incense], enter the hall and take your seats; bow as you sit and burn one stick of incense. Bow before the Abbot and inquire after his well-being while standing amidst the incense.
After the tea service is completed, the tea pitcher is brought out; go before the Abbot and bow for the tea, then withdraw to the right of the shrine and burn another stick of incense.

Perform three prostrations with opened sitting cloths (*kaihō*), exit the hall, and lead the entire assembly to the Abbot’s position to perform a ritual of thanks for the tea, using the standard wording for the day (as usual). Then escort [the Abbot] away.
Having exited, he returns to the hall, burns incense, and exchanges greetings with the elders and juniors of both the upper and lower sections.

He collects his bowl and withdraws from his seat. If there is a formal notice (a *bang*), it should first be placed in his quarters and presented to him. On the day of entering the monastery, the tea and soup service is hung before the Sangha Hall for both the upper and lower sections;

one simply burns incense and makes the request. After the second announcement, he says: "I request the Venerable Master’s soup. Once the soup has been served, he takes his seat for the medicinal food (*yao-shi*). (This Sangha Hall is specifically for the tea and soup service; in Vinaya monasteries, this is less common.)

The formal document:
By the monk [Name], the storehouse officer of this monastery.

The above [Name] respectfully submits that this day, following the conclusion of the midday meal, we shall proceed to the Cloud Hall to serve tea as a formal gesture of congratulation. We humbly entreat Your Reverence’s compassionate grace to deign to honor us with your presence.

Respectfully submitted. On the [Day] of the [Month] of the [Year], by the monk [Name], Treasurer of this Temple. [Seal] *Note: "Right" (右) indicates the end of the document. "Cai-tui" (齋退) refers to the conclusion of the vegetarian meal.
"Yun-tang" (雲堂) is the Cloud Hall, a communal space for monks. "Dian-cha" (點茶) means to serve tea. "Chen-he" (陳賀) signifies expressing congratulations.*
The format for the "Tang" (letter) is the same as before, with the exception that the character "Tang" is changed [to "Zhuang"].

(Omit the following: Format for the "Zhuang" (memorial): Respectfully submitted by the monk [Name], the steward of this monastery, To the newly appointed Head Monk of the Great Monastery (before his honored seat). Sealed respectfully.
The donor Li recited the sutras and established this temple, donating fields as a great patron.
The administrative office dispatched personnel to solemnly prepare the ancestral shrine and provide offerings of congee.

Once the preparations were complete, the assembly gathered and proceeded to the Sangha Hall; the administrators arrived first to burn incense, serve tea and hot soup, and present the offerings. When the Abbot arrived...
The incense sticks are offered and the assembly returns to their seats; the Rector (Vina) recites the sutra and performs the dedication of merit. The Water-Manager attends to the special envoy;

the administrative officers (Zhishi) present their preliminary report to the Abbot (Zhu-zhi). The special envoy is granted a generous donation; the person who proclaims the memorial and the placards is given offerings of robes and alms bowls; the various departments prepare the supplementary placards.

When the offerings of heavy and light gifts are properly arranged and the day arrives, the seating positions are prepared by nailing them up in the dormitory hall. Two groups of senior monks are invited to serve as honored companions.
A special seat is set out in the center for the Special Envoy, who is personally invited by the Guest Attendant; the others are invited by the Abbot and the Head of Guests.
The ritual protocol for these invitations is the same as that for the Special Envoy.
The Abbot requests the two classes of officials (the *bangban*) to remain.
The two classes wait until the reception of the special envoy is concluded; thereafter, they all proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to report their departure and withdraw.

(The Head Seat reports the assembly for the West Order; the Chief Administrator reports the assembly for the East Order. The Abbot treats them with courtesy and affection, escorting them out himself. The Attendant is ordered to prepare trays and cloths (*panfu*), and the Guest Master is instructed to set them in place.
The abbot, together with the attendant, shall visit each of the quarters one by one for the serving of hot soup.

The guest master first announces this to the quarters and meets the abbot outside the door on the right side. Upon entering the door, they take their seats, with the abbot occupying the seat of honor.

The attendant burns incense, serves the soup, and collects the bowls. Once the abbot has finished his detailed exhortations, he is escorted out of the door; the same procedure applies to all other quarters and the administrative offices.

If your term of office has expired and you have waited for a long time, you should also visit the various quarters to partake of the medicinal broth; this is an earnest effort to remain and fulfill the duties of hospitality.
Once the abbot has finished his midday meal, wait for a leisurely moment to submit your formal petition for leave, and then proceed with the proper sequence of taking your leave.
Upon departing and upon entering the monastery, before attending upon the local magistrates and their subordinates, one must first present a formal letter of introduction (*mensō*) for an audience.

Subsequently, one should visit the patrons (*dānapati*), visiting officials, nobles, and other monastic leaders, also using letters of introduction for all such places that require a formal visit; this shall be handled by the administrative officers (*chiji*) one by one.
After reporting to the Abbot and departing, the attendant shall transmit instructions to the Head Seat, the Rector, the various heads of departments, and the administrative officers, stating:
"You should proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to await his departure; the Treasury Office shall meanwhile ascertain when the Abbot returns.

Once this is known, the Hall Office shall post a notice to inform the assembly, and upon the Abbot’s arrival at the mountain, the bell before the Sangha Hall shall be struck to assemble the community to welcome him at the gate. When the Abbot emerges from his sedan chair, they shall bow in greeting.

[The abbot] says, "Do not trouble the assembly," and immediately proceeds to the Buddha Hall and the Local Deity Hall to burn incense. The Head Seat leads the assembly to the Abbot’s Quarters; once they have been received, the assembly withdraws.
The Guest Master bows and invites the two classes of officials and the senior monks to offer hot water; after a brief exchange of conversation, they withdraw.

The attendant of the Abbot’s Quarters then offers incense and prostrates. Next, the Head of the Assembly leads the group to prostrate before the Abbot, who must then visit each of the monastic quarters.
When returning from a visit to a nearby city or town where one enters and exits morning and evening without fail, it is not strictly necessary to perform the formal protocol.

However, upon returning from a distant journey, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) shall lead the assembly to welcome the Abbot. The Abbot shall convey a message excusing them from visiting the Abbot’s quarters. Alternatively, if he returns secretly to his seat in the meditation hall, he should join the assembly for the meal.
Once the bowls have been hung, the Guest Master (Ketu) shall announce: "The Abbot, the Venerable Master, is touring the hall to pay his respects."
The assembly from the lower ranks shall take one stick of incense, circumambulate the hall once, and exit. Upon exiting, they shall shout: "The Abbot has sent word;
there is no need for further inquiries. They shall then proceed to the Abbot’s quarters, or alternatively, return secretly to the quarters.

The two classes of officials and the senior elders must all go to the quarters to inquire after his well-being. They should burn incense, offer tea, and engage in detailed conversation before dispersing.
Kun: Handing over the household items;
the Abbot invites the two classes of officials and the senior elders for tea and discusses the affairs of the monastery in detail.

Next, they proceed to the tea reception at the Treasury Office (Kusi), where the overseers jointly inspect the imperial calligraphies, precious vessels, land deeds, and other assets; these are first presented to the Abbot and subsequently presented to the Head Officials and the elders.
The old accounts must be settled point-by-point through a formal handover, and the ledgers for grain and wealth must be clearly audited to determine exactly how much is currently held;

these shall be presented to the Abbot for reference against the *Xuzhi* (Necessary Regulations). The Abbot shall prepare a notice to be posted at all manors to inform the tenant farmers of the exchange of contracts.
It has been observed that in many places, when the Abbot exchanges contracts, the administrative officers engage in fraud by extorting money and goods from them. Subsequently—
This is no small matter; one must be careful. On this day, the various storehouses (kūshi) prepare *ten-shin* (refreshments).

At the Abbot’s quarters (*hōjō*), there is a small seating for the serving of hot tea (*tō*), and the Vinaya Hall (*rituin*) follows this same practice, though with slight differences. The Zen regulations state that in former times, ceremonies were performed on the four seasonal festivals. However—
Once during the summer retreat, the brothers relied on their strength and status to contend over seniority; consequently, the practice was discontinued.

That such an event has not been heard of in the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*) for some time is truly lamentable. According to the established regulations, there are three seats. The first seat is divided into two:

the East Hall and West Hall *shouzuo* (head seats), who serve as the primary companions. The second seat consists of four departures: one departure for the two classes of elders and heads, and two departures for the heads.
The Administrative Officer (Kaji) shall emerge from the West Hall; the Senior Monks (Kojū) shall emerge from the East Hall.

The Third Seat (Daisanzō) shall divide into six groups to attend to administrative affairs at the Head Temple and various branch temples. The Head Seat (Shuso) shall accompany them according to the rank of their respective offices, with those holding the same office following in order.

The Attendant (Jisha) shall prepare a preliminary diagram and present it to the Abbot (Hōjō) for deliberation and determination; should there be even slight discrepancies, each must [ensure accuracy].
On the day of the *Tōni* (Endurance/Retreat), write the names on the name-plates (*shōhaidai*) according to the register.

In the afternoon, prepare tables and cloths (*chaku-fuku*) for one, two, or three seats, arranging them in the lower section of the main hall (*shindan*), as well as in the east and west wings of the front hall. The Chief Administrator (*dōji*) and the Guest Attendant (*jissha*) shall each go to their respective quarters to invite [the guests], saying:
"The Abbot invites you this evening to the main hall for a special offering of hot water (*kentō*). This applies to the remaining head officers and the various quarters.
The Chief Attendant (fangzhang) and the Guest Attendant (ketou) invite [the Abbot] to the Hall of Rest (qintang). They nail up the name tablets (weipai), light candles, and burn incense.
Once this is finished, the Guest Attendant informs the Assistant Attendant (shizhe), who in turn informs the Abbot; the drum is then struck. The first seat (dizhuo) and the assembly of guests gather.

The Assistant Attendant welcomes them with a bow, and the Abbot receives them, exchanging greetings regarding their welfare. They enter their respective positions and stand still. The Assistant Attendant specifically bows before each person as he makes his circuit.

Sitting, one performs the inquiry after sitting (*wèn-xùn*). Having finished sitting, one returns to the center and burns a single stick of incense. Going before the person specially honored, one bows, offers the incense, and performs the inquiry.

Returning to stand in the center, the wooden board is struck twice. Next, the hot water is served; again, one goes before the person specially honored, bows, offers the water, and performs the inquiry.
Returning to the center, one burns incense for the assembly. The wooden board is struck once to collect the bowls, and the drum is struck three times to conclude the session. Second.

When the guests have arrived, they are ushered in to their seats. Two attendants stand facing each other, one above and one below, taking turns to inquire after them with bows and inviting them to be seated.

A single stick of incense is burned; as it passes through the various sections, they bow for the incense and bow for the hot water. When the incense has finished burning and the bowls are collected, the drum is struck three times, and they withdraw from their seats.

They unfold their sitting cloths to express thanks for the hot water; if this is waived, the ceremony stops there. Third, when the guests have assembled, they are received and escorted to their places.

The ritual procedures are identical to those previously described. As for these seating arrangements, they are generally divided by the head of the assembly (zhuōtóu), who must inquire after each person in turn; it is essential that the order be maintained so that the proceedings remain dignified.

(According to the rules of monastic discipline, on the fourteenth day prior to the commencement of the retreat on the fifteenth day of the fourth month, a small seat is prepared before the morning assembly, and the ritual for serving hot soup is performed.)

Sword: To prepare the morning tea for the Abbot.

If a Dharma heir arrives at the temple, he is presented with tea; the attendant is then instructed to lead him to the administrative office (Kusi) to consult on the preparation of food, calculate the expenses, and arrange for their delivery.
On the evening before, the attendant first reports to the Attendant Office (Sisi) to request permission to announce the arrival to the Abbot, who then assumes his majestic demeanor.
Proceeding to the Abbot’s quarters, insert incense, perform prostrations, and request as follows: "On the coming day, we shall offer a modest meal in the Cloud Hall;
we humbly beseech your compassionate grace to deign to honor us with your presence. Your disciples are moved by the utmost gratitude.

Instruct the Attendant to allow the two classes of officials to request their invitations individually, and have the single-celled quarters post notices to inform the assembly. On the appointed day, prepare the seating for the Abbot’s bowl.
At the *zhuofu* (the communal meal), when the time for serving tea and refreshments arrives, the signal board (*huopan*) is struck and the assembly proceeds to the hall.

The person serving tea and refreshments follows the Abbot into the hall, bows to take their seat, and burns one stick of incense in the center. After performing a formal greeting (*wensun*) before the Abbot and circumambulating the shrine (*kang*), they exit.

The Abbot extends his hand to greet the server, who then takes their seat. The Hall Attendant (*tangsi*) and the Ritual Assistant (*xingzhe*) chant: "I request the assembly to set down their bowls. [The meal begins.]

The person serving the *jiandian* (refreshments) burns incense, distributes alms (*qin*), and pays respects to the Abbot. He bows and returns to his position, instructing others to distribute the alms-food.

When the meal is finished and the bowls have been packed away, he withdraws. The Abbot places the *jiandian* tray on the stand; the person serving the refreshments burns one stick of incense, pays respects before the Abbot, exits behind the shrine-casket, and pays respects before the incense burner.
The bell is struck to signal the serving of tea; the attendant goes to each person, including the Abbot, to offer tea, and then returns to the shrine-casket.

The attendant steps forward from behind to lead the way, and the abbot performs three prostrations with the head to the ground, saying: "On this day... [as appropriate]... This humble offering is but a trifling intrusion;

that you have condescended to honor us with your presence is a source of profound gratitude beyond measure. (According to Zen regulations, there are two prostrations and three bows. The abbot exits the hall and is escorted out.
The person serving tea and refreshments returns to the hall, burns one stick of incense, and bows in greeting between the upper and lower sections to express thanks for the light.
The attendants again inquire after his well-being, ring the bell, and collect the bowls; they then proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to express thanks for his gracious descent.

The Abbot follows them to the guest seat (keli) to offer his own thanks. If the various mountain monasteries have prepared tea and offerings (jian-dian), the Abbot proceeds to the hall to bow to the Abbot [of that monastery], who shall then decline further formalities.
After bowing to the tea servers and returning to their seats, once everyone is seated, he rises to burn a single incense stick and approaches the Abbot.

After the initial inquiry after health, the distribution of alms (*dakṣiṇā*) is performed for the assembly; one offers a single incense stick of *guangban* (burning-light companion) incense and returns to one’s seat.

The formalities for serving food and tea are not discussed. When the tea session concludes, everyone proceeds together to the Abbot’s quarters (*upādhyāya-śālā*). The Abbot must first go to the guest seat (*ātithya-pīṭha*) to express his thanks.

Title: *Ryōban Shindō Tenjinteki* (The Tea Service for the Two Ranks in the Quarters) On the day of the tea service, the *shuso*, the administrative officers (*chiji*), and the elders (*kiju*) proceed to the abbot’s quarters (*hōjō*) to offer incense and formally invite the *jūji* (abbot).

Following this, they invite the attendant (*shijō*) and the junior disciples (*shishō*). The two ranks and the elders take their seats as usual; however, among the junior disciples, [the designated ones] sit within the inner hall.
When the time for the meal arrives, the Head Seat (Śraddhādeśaka) requests the Abbot to emerge from his quarters; they bow to one another and perform the formal salutations.

If the Abbot declines the formal salutations, he exits from the right side of the incense burner and burns a single stick of incense. He then steps forward to inquire after the well-being of the assembly and immediately distributes alms-food (dakṣiṇā). The Head Seat and the three preceding monks likewise inquire after the well-being of the assembly and return to their seats to eat.
When the meal is finished, the Head Seat rises, burns incense, declines further formal salutations, and takes his seat to offer tea.

In the Great Hall (Gyo), during the tea service in the Abbot’s Quarters (Sintō), the seats are arranged as usual. The person serving the tea proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and invite the Abbot;

next, the guest master (Kakutō) is instructed to invite the two classes of elders, the attendants, and the junior disciples to serve as companions. When the time arrives, they are invited to enter the Quarters.
Before the incense burner, briefly exchange greetings regarding the weather; the abbot waives formal salutations, so there is no bowing as they take their seats.

Once everyone is seated, burn one stick of incense and offer the *dakṣiṇā*. The abbot rises and bows to the person serving the tea and refreshments. When the meal is finished and the tea has been served, express gratitude before the burner for the honor of the visit.
The abbot escorts the two classes of officials a few steps and then proceeds to the lodging to offer thanks and discuss the matters at hand.
A junior disciple of a Dharma relative prepares the tea and visits the Abbot’s quarters on the following day to request the ceremony;

the same applies to the two classes of senior officials, retired elders, and Dharma relatives who have business to attend to. For other guests, the seating arrangements in the dormitory follow the usual custom. Junior disciples sit in the inner section;
they are invited to take their seats, and the ritual for serving tea is identical to the protocol for serving tea in the Sangha Hall. If it is a senior Dharma relative who prepares the tea...
Omit the remaining rites and dispense with them, performing only the burning of incense and the distribution of monetary offerings (*dakṣiṇā*).

If a venerable elder visits the monastery, the abbot’s office shall investigate their arrival and notify the *karmadāna* in advance; the *karmadāna* shall then post a notice to welcome them. Upon arrival, the guest’s formal letter of introduction must first be presented at the gate.
Upon arriving at the abbot’s quarters, the great bell is struck and the assembly welcomes him at the gate. If he declines formal greetings, he may enter the temple incognito;

once inside, he shall submit his credentials at the main gate. In the meditation hall, incense is prepared and candles are lit. If the visitor is a venerable kinsman of the Dharma, the monks’ hall bell is struck as he proceeds to the abbot’s quarters for formal greetings;
he then offers incense, which the abbot declines. Before the rest of the assembly arrives, the attendant invites him to be seated.

When the assembly has arrived for the tea service following the incense offering and prostrations, the Chief Seat (Shouzuo) and the administrative officers (Zhishi) perform the incense offering and formal greetings.
Only then does the Attendant (Shizhe) offer incense and prostrate. The Guest Master (Ketou) then bows and invites the two classes of officials and the elders to accompany them for tea.

When the tea is finished, the attendant accompanying the guests offers incense and prostrates; next, the attendants of the sedan chair follow to pay their respects at the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang), where the attendants perform their prostrations.

The visiting head bows; the assembly performs prostrations; the sedan-chair carriers bow in succession. After the guests have finished their prostrations, the attendant burns incense, offers hot water, and escorts them to their seats.
The host sits on the right and leads them inside to offer incense. The guests decline the formalities, briefly exchange pleasantries regarding the weather, and depart.

Each member of the two classes of officials offers incense and pays their respects; the attendants see them off separately before they are settled. The guest master orders the sedan-chairs to be prepared for the abbot.
The attendant who leads the inspection of the quarters follows along, while the guest-head provides advance notice to all the various lodgings.
Once the inspection is complete, the Abbot enters the Abbot’s Quarters together with them to converse, as one would exchange greetings with old acquaintances in one's home village.

Upon returning to the reception hall, the attendant in charge of guests prepares a formal document to invite the Abbot specifically for the serving of medicinal soup. He proceeds to the guest seat, incenses the burner, and bows, saying: "The Abbot invites the Venerable Master."
"Tonight, in the *shindō* (sleeping hall), we specially offer *nōtan* (hot water); we pray that you will look upon us with compassion and deign to attend.

Having presented this formal petition, the *kattō* (guest master) replies, "We request the *hōshi* to partake of the *nōtan*, after which he shall take his seat for the *yaku-seki* (medicinal food). In the *shindō*, the *shōjō-hai* (tablet of illumination) is hung and the special guest-companion seats (*kōban-i*) are arranged.
The guests are urged to perform the rites; once the *nōtan* and *yaku-seki* are concluded, they are escorted out, following the same protocol as the previous special offering.

The guest master proceeds to the guest seats and makes the invitation, saying: "The Abbot invites the Honored Master for tonight’s soup and fruit. He then invites the two classes of officials to serve as companions.

The following morning, he invites the attendants for the morning soup; the incense-burner attendant and the prostration-practitioner inquire after his well-being, while the servants respond with a formal acknowledgment.

After the invitation for the morning gruel, tea, the midday meal, and the afternoon refreshments, the guest master’s attendant prepares a formal document to invite those specially designated for the reception, and the temple kitchen prepares the food.

When preparing the offerings of robes and bowls, or when providing supplementary offerings such as burning incense, the attendant performing the rites should follow the same protocol as the two classes of officials and their companions.

If the recipient is a younger brother, a nephew, or a dharma-grandson of ordinary standing or lower, one should not be overly diligent in the ritual observances, lest one invite derision from those who know the proper conduct.
Statement of Petition The Abbot of this Temple, Bhikṣu [Name], respectfully submits:

The Vinaya-piṭaka, the treasury of precepts, is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma, maintained and transmitted by successive patriarchs to extend and magnify the teachings, contemplation, and models of conduct.

It rescues beings from the three realms and delivers those in the four modes of birth, clarifying supramundane matters and turning the Great Wheel of Dharma. Through the simultaneous cultivation of understanding and practice, it ensures that name and reality correspond;

acting according to what is taught, its lineage of masters has a firm basis. It awakens those of superior faculties, guides and entices those of middling and superior capacities, and serves as a supreme condition for accomplishment.
