Whether partaking of gruel and rice or attending tea services, he looked back to the past and forward to the present to instruct his brothers. His conduct served as a model of discipline, conforming to the standard and the square; he delivered formal lectures and provided exhortations.

There are established regulations for everything: the distribution of coarse or refined rice gruel and meals is entrusted to the attendants; the funeral affairs of deceased monks are inspected and carried out by the master;
and when one fails to attend the assembly, a message is sent. If there are lapses in communal recitation or study, detailed instructions must be provided.
How could this matter not be considered of great importance for the continuity of the lineage through a hundred generations? Those who hold these offices ought not to be lax or negligent.

The Dàn Hòutáng (Dàn Rear Hall) occupies the rear board; he assists in promoting the patriarchal style, lectures on ritual protocols, and sets an example for juniors. He manages affairs within the monastic community and reprimands his brothers;
thus, he belongs to the Qiántáng (Front Hall). If the position of the Qiántáng Zhùchí (Front Hall Abbot) is vacant, the [Dàn] Hòutáng shall preside over the lecture and discourse on another day.
Then, turning back to the front board, the assembly is served tea as a courtesy to see them off back to the Front Hall quarters.

Once they have bowed to the Front Hall, the remaining matters—such as opening the lecture to instruct the disciples—are handled in the same manner (if there is a recitation of the Buddha’s name or sutras in a Vinaya temple, it is appropriate for the Head Seat to lead the chanting with detailed slowness and rhythmic precision).
Regarding the *rin* (monastic register): the Chief Administrator (*duganshi*, now called the *dutō*) is responsible for the affairs of the mountain gate;

the Head Priest (*tōji*) is responsible for managing both public and private matters. The Head Priest must be diligent day and night in the incense and lamps, and examine the annual accounts in the ledgers.
He shall attend upon officials, offer congratulations and thanks to donors, and manage all receipts and disbursements according to the regulations.

In providing the assembly with meals and congee, one should always maintain a superior mind when dealing with others and must not act with negligence. Should a servant commit an offense, one should measure the transgression before proceeding;

punishment should not be severe. One should sincerely appeal for forgiveness, and in managing the duties of the storehouse and treasury, one should select and appoint those with public-mindedness, honoring the worthy and being inclusive of the masses so that a harmonious atmosphere pervades.
Regarding the deficiencies of the assembly, one should exert every effort in planning and scheming, ensuring that all matters of repair and construction are fully accomplished.
Cultivate a mind of harmonious cooperation; promote talent and virtue while keeping matters of conduct and private affairs confidential.

Should there be grave transgressions that might bring disgrace upon the mountain gate, conceal them from the abbot so that the pure assembly hears nothing, and manage the situation through skillful means so that you do not fail in this one matter.

Attend the hall during the two formal periods of the day, setting aside all busyness; when speaking of major affairs, distinguish between public and private matters with the utmost precision, down to the smallest detail.

He cherished and protected [this teaching] so that it remains eternally present; when he encounters the right conditions in the future, he will surely become a model for all gods and humans, his magnificent radiance beyond measure.
[Seal] Qian, the Confessional Leader.

The Commentary states: "Since the principle requires that the seeds of offenses once formed must be expiated through repentance, so that one's form may be pure and the mind clear, one should follow the monastic rules.
Therefore, the Sarvāstivāda-vinaya says: 'There is no dharma more swift than the mind; one must not discard it forever because of a temporary evil.
Thus, one must perform repentance. Now, we wish to establish its fundamental framework and standardize the categories of the mind and its objects, so that right and wrong may be reflected therein."

If one clarifies the capacities and functions of the ears and eyes regarding gain and loss, what worry need there be that deluded karma will not be eliminated or that the deluded mind will have no place to rest?

One must know that the two types of repentance—those of phenomena and principle—encompass both the monastic and the secular; the signs of transgression are difficult to discern, and the responsibility of the leader of repentance is no small matter.
If one’s efforts are merely aimed at seeking fame, what is the purpose of such an office?
The Vinaya-master (Vīnā): In Sanskrit, *vīnā*;
in Chinese, "one who delights the assembly" (*yuezhong*). One must carry out every rule of the monastic forest (*saṃghārāma*) according to its regulations.

This office is ranked among the western classes. One must master the minor sections of the scriptures; one's duties include seeing off and welcoming guests, and one’s conduct must be diligent. When a monk is seriously ill, one must ensure that his recovery is properly managed.
Brothers, you must exercise careful and thorough care in matters of reception and assignment to quarters. Upon returning to the hall, inspect the ordination certificates (*du-ndie*).

In the Sangha Hall, draw the curtains, fan [the assembly], close the doors, and plaster the windows; always take account of the cold and heat. Regarding the belongings of deceased monks, ensure that the distribution is fair and transparent;

practice drawing lots (*nian-jou*) rather than following private bias. Recite the *Bai-fo* (Praise of the Buddha) and the sutras with detailed slowness and rhythmic precision. Attend the formal procedures for the tea ceremony.

Do not fail to provide instruction when requested; you should encourage those who come to study. If there are other circumstances, the registers of seniority and the registers of temporary leave should be sent to the Office of Guests.
All matters, both great and small, shall be set forth in detailed regulations.
It is fitting that you oversee every matter concerning the community of monks, acting with a heart of universal care for the assembly.

The Attendant (Xiang) informs the Guest Master (Zhike), the officials, the noble donors, the venerable elders, and the subordinates of the various mountain monasteries; they are then notified to proceed to the gate to welcome [the guest].

Once the report has been made to the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang) and the Storehouse Office (Kusi), the Guest Master shall lead them in for an audience. The degree of courtesy in the reception should be adjusted according to the circumstances as the occasion demands. After they have been settled in their lodgings...

When leading visitors on a tour of the mountain and reviewing the halls, one must not speak of vulgar matters; when receiving incoming brothers, provide tea and refreshments according to the prescribed rites.

When a patron enters the mountain, they must be received and guided in advance by the Head of the Lineage (*zongzu*). Furthermore, one must pay close attention to the chanting and recitation of liturgy, ensuring it is dignified and worthy of observation;
the language used must be classical and authoritative so as not to mislead those who have come to study. This is the duty of the Rector (*weina*).

When one goes out on temporary leave, the affairs of the monastic community (saṃghārāma) must be handled as one; whether acting for oneself or due to other circumstances, one must report [one's departure] to the *vina* (steward) and the attendant (*śrāmaṇera*), and the procedure is the same.
Before the Sangha Hall, one inspects the distribution of benefits for guests, supervises the serving of porridge and rice, and prepares the midday meal.

Upon encountering the death of a monk, one assists the attendant in managing the funeral affairs and temporarily assumes the role of the presiding mourner. During the summer retreat, one practices the recitation of scriptures and the serving of tea and soup.
The ritual procedures for the bath are the same as those for the *vīna* (robe).
The bath attendant shall post a notice before the meal prior to every bath: in the cold months, there is one bath every five days; in the hot months, one bath daily to wash away perspiration.
After the congee has been served, the fire is lit, the bathhouse is prepared, hand towels are hung, face basins are set out, and shoes are neatly arranged with foot-cloths provided.

The head attendant dispatches the attendants to go directly to the bath. At mid-afternoon, the bath master covers his head; then the Head Seat, the Abbot’s quarters, and the Rector strike the drum three times.
The sacred bath-tubs are all filled with hot water. In succession, they patrol the corridors and strike the wooden board three times, signaling that the bath is open.
First, the entire monastic community; second, the head officers; third, those in charge of affairs and the laborers; fourth, the supervisors and enforcers.

Regarding the sequence for bathing, a notice is posted at the entrance. According to ancient precedent, the Abbot enters the bath at the third watch (the third drum) and uses a screen to shield the laborers.
Nowadays, the Abbot enters the bath between the second and third watches and pays respects at the small plaque.
"First the white powder, second the hot water, third the full bath; observe that there is a donor who provides the bathing, recite the sutra, and perform the dedication of merit.
If the preceding thought is ordinary and the succeeding thought is sacred, then the effort will not have been applied in vain."
The Master knows that the hall is solemn and pure, the desks and tables are always full of lamp oil, and the sacred images are dusted from time to time;

he provides offerings as appropriate and maintains the practice of not misappropriating the patrons' funds for incense or oil. He strictly commands his two attendants to diligently serve the incense and lamps, and whenever they encounter...
If wind arises, the furnace fire must be extinguished; when tying up the ends of the banners, do not let them come near the lapis lazuli.

During the new and full moon days or during holidays, open the palace gates so that officials and commoners may pass to and fro and gaze upon [the sacred objects] at their leisure. Do not collect fees for oil, as this will cause people to develop feelings of revulsion and instead bring about evil karmic results.

The Fire Attendant (Huoshi) performs the duty of burning incense while attending closely to the Master’s left and right, listening for instructions at dawn and dusk. He oversees the assembly of the Dharma path and promotes the elevation of worthy and capable individuals in accordance with public consensus.
He manages all matters of correspondence and protocol, ensuring that the conduct toward venerable elders and monastic leaders is respectful and harmonious during both arrivals and departures.

In every matter, consult those who possess prior knowledge so as not to invite derision from superiors and subordinates alike. When attending to the Abbot, serve him like a son serving his father; at other times, do not sit in the Abbot’s quarters in advance.

If a servant commits an error, admonish them constantly. The affairs of the *zhuchi* (abbot) are manifold; matters concerning the *weina* (rector) and *zhike* (guest master) are likewise shared with him when he is away.
The procedures for the *huanghua* (turning toward the west) and the raising of the *juhe* (the formal call) are identical. For deceased monks, the turn of duty (*lunba*) shall be maintained.

The various accounts regarding the visiting of the mountain temples (sangha) by the two classes of officials (yangban) involve the insertion of incense and prostrations. When officials arrive, they stand with joined palms to listen and respond.
The abbot, fearing there may be points of omission or forgetfulness, should speak on their behalf at that time.

The circumstances of the formal assembly (baekseok) and the opening of the lecture (kaegwang) are discussed orally and immediately recorded. Regarding the difficult passages in the ancestral texts (jowon), one should incessantly seek clarification, just as Ānanda served the Buddha.
"Gautama, you must not treat this with indifference!
The office of *shuzhuang* (secretary) stands out with exceptional brilliance, adorning the ancestral gate.

Handling the correspondence between officials and the mountain gate, composing ritual texts (*su*), drafting public notices (*bang*), and preparing detailed lists upon the issuance of orders from the abbot’s quarters to be submitted for approval—this is how one assists and supports the abbot."

Regarding the duties of the Guest Master (*qingke zhizhe*): he must be one who stands out from the crowd and excels among his peers, providing support to the monastic community (*conglín*). When high-ranking officials, honored elders, or masters from various mountains visit, he must receive them with full ceremony and hospitality.
He must provide special care for their tea and soup during the ritual periods of the lunar calendar. First, he shall prepare an invitation document (*qingzhuang*) inscribed with his own name;

the incense-burning attendant (*shizhe*), the person handling dedications (*huixiang*), the chant leader (*juchang*), and the manager of the hall (*bazhang*) shall all act together as his superior in these matters.
Upon arriving at the gate, if the abbot is unaware of the visitor's arrival, one should first go forward to receive him;

by consulting and inquiring with him morning and evening, the path of practice will be perfected, and from this point onward, one shall set forth on the journey that will lead to becoming a leader of the monastic community in the future.

The duties of the *kaṣāya* and *pātra* officers should be entrusted to those who are mature and experienced, having spent their lives within the monastic groves; this is the universal custom throughout all regions.

It is a grave error for juniors to assume these responsibilities due to a lack of virtue. One must recruit the worthy and virtuous to offer loyal counsel regarding faults and deficiencies, and engage with others according to circumstances without failing to act at the proper time.

Regarding all matters of etiquette for the Abbot’s quarters, one must apply the mind to provide guidance and supervision, ensuring that no administrative posts in the various halls and lodgings remain vacant.

Each individual must be guided and cared for according to the proper time; the advancement and retirement of the two orders of officials must be consulted in advance, as the priority lies in securing the right person so as to accord with public opinion.

The duty of the *zhirì* (daily supervisor) is generally assigned by rotation among those of junior seniority (*niànlà*) within the assembly; however, the *weina* (chief administrator) often appoints this person directly.

The *Ān-guī* (Rules of Conduct) states that the *Vaiyāvṛtyakara* (Karmadāna) and the *Pravrajyācārya* (Preceptor for Inquiry) must provide detailed instruction so that [the practitioners] become exemplary.

Regarding the rituals for receiving the precepts, the *poṣadha*, the *varṣā* (rain retreat), and the *pravāraṇā*, once the signals for entering and exiting the hall have been given, one must always remain six feet away from the *sthavira* (abbot) when passing through the door before him, lest one should step upon his shadow. This applies to the *saṃghārāma*.
At both [morning and evening] services, strike the mallet while waiting for the hall bell to ring; leave your position and enter the hall with the left hand first, offering one incense stick.

Step back two and a half paces to perform a formal greeting (*monshin*), join your palms, and enter. Stand by the side of the mallet and first observe the daily dedication (*ekō*) as indicated by the divine signs.
When the bell ceases, strike the mallet once and join your palms to dedicate the merit to the deities of that day, reciting: "The pure Dharma-body."
Standing with the left hand in the gesture of holding a canopy, one presses the side of the mallet against the sounding block;

with the right hand, one strikes the mallet no higher than five inches, lowering it only when the sound has ceased, ensuring the rhythm is neither too hurried nor too slow. When serving food, one faces the shrine, turns around, and retreats to stand at the head of the platform.

Once the meal is finished, one steps forward and strikes the mallet once more. Reciting the concluding verse, one joins the palms and exits the hall, turning around upon reaching the threshold of the door.

When facing the Honored Monk for inquiry, one should join the palms and return to the position of the alms bowl; all other ritual procedures should likewise be performed with detailed deliberation and rhythmic precision.
[End of Section] List of Staff Positions:

The office of the Vice-Abbot (Fu-si) is one where the responsibility is great despite the position being small; it is upon this role that the lifeblood of the community depends. The rice and flour must be fine and clean;
the gruel and cooked rice should be prepared with care for excellence and abundance. Soy sauce, yellow beans, and fermented soybeans (dou-ji) must be prepared in a timely manner;

salt, vinegar, ginger, and oil must be provided in full for the assembly. Should there be a deficiency, one must plan ahead. The Head (Shang-shou) must be strict and vigilant regarding those below, never succumbing to private favoritism or seeking personal gain.
In my own estimation, I have cherished these matters with the care one guards one's own eyes. The former masters divided duties and assigned responsibilities originally for the sake of the community;
yet today, people obscure their source and subject it to severe exploitation.
While those who bear the burden are ignorant of the truth, the reality lies in the faults of the abbot.
Regarding the office of the *dianzuo* (kitchen steward), those who lack a sincere heart for making offerings should not act on personal favoritism or make arbitrary requests.

One must consult with the head seat (*shouzuo*) of the front hall and select the candidate through the consensus of the assembly; in this way, there will be no failure out of ten thousand attempts. One should cultivate vegetables extensively and exert effort in weeding away weeds and filth.
Various plants should be sown according to the four seasons, and one must diligently tend the old gardeners; it should be understood that the gardeners must be treated as one's own kin.
Be considerate of the cold and heat; ensure that the soup and vegetables are seasoned with all five flavors.

Since the stockpiles of oil, sauce, ginger, and spices are limited, you must contribute from your own pockets and solicit donations from patrons to support the offerings for the Hall. Let each person cultivate their own mind.
It is frequently observed that those holding nominal titles or positions as supervisors and collectors usurp half of the garden lands to plant hemp and sow seeds.
Ramo (ramie) is used for gardeners' clothing; washing and mending are handed down through successive generations, forming a tradition. It is forbidden to discard any base items within the kitchen.
Those appointed to service must be diligent ascetics of mature experience. If a great vegetarian feast (*dazhai*) is prepared, the menu must be discussed with the head administrator (*zhishi*);
neither excessive portions nor arbitrary reductions are permitted. If practitioners are undisciplined, they will be admonished until they reach compliance.

Those who do not accept further instruction shall be reprimanded or punished. Benefits shall be shared equally, and rice gruel and meals shall be distributed from atop the buckets while incense is burned;
one must prostrate toward the Sangha Hall and always hold all others upon the crown of one's head. You will personally obtain blessings and merit; I do not deceive you.
The duties of the *zhisui* (year-steward) require that daily affairs not deviate from their proper timing;

he must protect the forests and mountains to preserve the geomantic "wind and water," tend to the fire-tenants and livestock, maintain the monastery buildings, sweep the corridors and courtyards, clear the drainage ditches, procure firewood, patrol against fire and theft, record leaks with ash, and prepare for repairs once the weather clears.
For all major construction projects, there are specific officers assigned to each task.
Maintain diligence and exert yourself forward to fulfill your duties; reflect upon the words of the ancients: "If one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day.
The duty of the *Jōshu* (Abbot) is to supervise agricultural affairs so that the seasons are not lost, to inspect the fields, and to care for the livestock.
Punish those tenant farmers who are obstinate and violent; provide preferential support for those who are poor or ill; and assign labor services to single men at appropriate times.

In the event of droughts, floods, or pestilence, perform recitations and offer prayers for protection, and do not permit licentious sacrifices that recklessly harm living beings. Should any tenant commit a grave offense, report it to the Mountain Gate (the monastery).
When visiting or passing through, provide them with hospitality regarding food and lodging. As for the time of guarding the estate fields... [end of fragment].
At that time, the Superintendent of Dikes was appointed to ensure the repairs were firm and solid, searching for leaks and incessantly building up and blocking them.
In spring, water was accumulated early to manage the rice seedlings; in autumn, there was defense against wind and tides, which was especially urgent during the night.

Winter plowing and summer sowing did not miss their proper seasons, and emergency provisions were always kept ready at the estate. Within the dikes, there were fresh-water sluices to prevent the entry of tidal water.
If, when entering the dark [of the night], one suddenly encounters a drought and a briny vapor is emitted, the rice will perish. Do not indulge in further exploitation;

exert all your strength in planning so that the fire-tillers may have cause for remembrance and the permanent residents may benefit from the leftovers of the broth—only then will it be truly excellent.

The duty of the *jiefang* (neighborhood alms-collector) is to solicit donors to provide supplementary support for the monastery (*changzhu*), never deviating by even a hair’s breadth from the donor’s intention.
If such requests become frequent, one must not repeatedly press the original benefactor, lest they develop feelings of weariness or contempt.

As the World-Honored One practiced begging without visiting more than seven households, and as Ānanda traveled through the neighborhoods, a poor woman offered him a tattered felt cloak; because she honored the Buddha, she was reborn with the thought that he was difficult to encounter.
Such thoughts are permissible. Regarding the duties of the Water Head:
every morning, he must boil water for the assembly to wash their faces; the hand towels must be kept clean; in the winter months, they must be kept warm by heating;

lamps and candles must be constantly prepared; tooth-cleansing medicine and incense must be ready; and when the time has not yet struck, the face basins must be laid out and awaited until the washing of faces is finished.
Cover the original spot and pick up the hand-towel to prevent further defilement. Leave one or two towels in the basin, including one old towel, to await those who come later.
Prepare firewood in advance, keeping virtuous intentions in mind.
Regarding the duties of the Charcoal Master: during the hot months, one should prepare charcoal lumps and manage the accumulation of white charcoal;

whether by soliciting donations from patrons or drawing from the storehouse, one must take care beforehand to ensure sufficient stock for use. In the winter months, these should be distributed evenly to the various quarters of the monastery;
it is appropriate to act with a heart of compassion toward all.

The duty of the *Matou* (Head of the Grinding Room) is to serve as the throat and collarbone for the pure assembly. Wheat must be washed and dried until it is uniformly warm; fine honeyed flour is prepared in the kitchen and divided into portions.
Rice is pounded until pristine white, and the chaff and broken grains are sifted out and removed at the proper time. These may be sent to the storehouse or distributed as communal benefits.
The priority must be public integrity and the efficient management of affairs for the sake of the assembly; furthermore, one should cultivate the path of practice outside of these duties.
The duties of the garden master are arduous; one must first irrigate the plots and plant the vegetable seedlings.

One should care for the gardeners without negligence morning or night, and when it comes to harvesting, sowing seeds, and planting according to the seasons, one may follow the ancient methods of fire-weeding and slash-and-burn cultivation, keeping these traditions in mind.
Regarding the duties of the Head of the Grove: the pine paths of the mountain gate are shrouded in shade, and the bamboo and trees must be protected and cherished so as to provide for future repairs.
One must constantly inspect them and plant replacements in a timely manner; the cause and effect of this is manifest, and its merit is not bestowed in vain.
Even if the pines wither due to a lack of personnel, it will not be too late to restore them later.

The duties of the *jingtou* (cleaning head) arise from their causes: every morning, sweep the floors, prepare incense, and at the proper times trim wicks, light candles, change tally-sticks (*zhouchi*), wash the latrines, remove buckets, and replace slippers and hand towels.
Ensure that clean water and ample ash are always available, and never allow things to become disheveled;
maintain diligent order. When gathering firewood and washing tally-sticks, show compassion for the laborers' strength and be clear about the boundaries of your duties.
The complete purification of the path of pure practice—how could it be anything less than a great contribution?
Regarding the "Hundred-Foot Rule" (Bǎizhàng guīshéng):
the Great Wisdom Chan Master Bǎizhàng, following the tradition of the Chan school from Shaoshi to Caoxi, mostly resided...
Although Vinaya temples are called "separate cloisters," they have not conformed to the proper standards regarding the preaching of the Dharma or the administration of the community;

thus, a separate set of five rules was established. While the Chan school has flourished, these five rules, though not derived from the Vinaya, constitute a clear regulation; one should understand that this is its prescribed method.
If clothing or other items are lost within the hall or the quarters, one must report the color, quantity, season, and location of the missing articles to the administrative officers.

Upon verification of their presence or absence, the truth or falsehood of the report shall be established. If the offense is deemed serious, the Hall Administrator shall be notified to assemble the community for a search of the hall and quarters.
The offender shall be publicly dealt with; if they act deceitfully, they shall be expelled from the community.

If among the noble assembly there are those who commit theft, indulge in wine or women, engage in quarrels and disputes, defile the community with clamor and disorder, or fail to observe the precepts, they shall all be assembled before the community and expelled from the monastery;
if they do not comply, the matter shall be reported to the authorities.

If there are those who assume false names or misappropriate the appearance [of a monk] to mingle among the pure assembly, or who cause other matters of disturbance and clamor, the Hall Administrator shall investigate and report them;
they shall be stripped of their registration, expelled from the monastery, and barred from the community to ensure its peace.
If there are those who repeatedly commit offenses and bring disgrace upon the monastic community and the monastery itself, the assembly must immediately gather to strike them with staves,
burn their ritual implements, and expel them through a side gate to demonstrate their humiliation.
If the pure assembly within the hall is not sufficient to manage the affairs of the mountain gate, they should merely join the general assembly for meals and formal invitations;
otherwise, each person should reflect upon themselves, maintain their station, accumulate virtue, and promote the Way to bring glory to the sacred seat.
It is impermissible, beyond these duties, to arbitrarily alter the management of monastic affairs, create disturbances, or stir up rumors and disputes that disturb the pure assembly.
To ensure tranquility, those who violate these regulations shall immediately comply with the monastery’s orders.

As the Holy Masters of the Southern Mountain (Nanshan) have said: "When propagating the teachings in a region and establishing rules, they must be comprehensive; when adjudicating disputes within the assembly, one must rely upon the Vinaya and the scriptures.
If the laws deviate from common sense and lack scriptural authority, then disciplinary penalties will resemble those of the vulgar, and the net of the teaching will [collapse]."

If one can only bestow [teachings] upon those who are heavy with worldly affairs and coarse, and who are stubbornly prone to much clamor and disorder, such actions will cause the various Dharmas to perish quickly;
they will not encounter the era of a Buddha and will be cast into hell like an arrow shot.

If there are those within this monastic community who know the Dharma, they must carry out the disciplinary punishments prescribed in the Vinaya—namely, the seven and nine types of penances—in order to accord with the Buddha’s regulations.

These are: censure, banishment, dependence, prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople, suspension for failure to acknowledge an offense, suspension for failure to repent, suspension for not relinquishing evil views, the treatment of a "bad horse," and silent exclusion (these are the nine methods;
those seeking them should consult the *Senggang pian*).
Official: Daily Regulations for Pure Conduct.
Now, the Vinaya is the precept, and Chan is meditative concentration. Without the precept, concentration does not arise; without the discipline of the Vinaya, Chan is not perfected.
In reality, these regulations are all one and the same. During the Jiading era of the Song dynasty, Chan Master Wuliangshou sat on the seat of honor at Fenze Temple.
At Guifeng, I observed that the daily regulations largely conformed to the rules and models;
I therefore ordered that those points which were identical be extracted to prepare for daily practice, so as to complete the ritual procedures of our school.
Among these, there may be those who are newly learning who find a point of entry, whereby the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices will become spontaneous.
When brothers first arrive, they must know the rules for entering the assembly: one should not sleep before others and should not rise after others.
Before the five-watch bell has sounded, rise early with a light body so as not to startle your fellow residents.

Shake off all lethargy, sit upright upon your bed, and contemplate the texts you recite that day—whether there are portions of the composition yet unfinished or passages of the reading not yet mastered. As the Patriarch said:

In a quiet place, contemplate the correct path of the subtle Way. Proceeding through the stages of transformation, descend from your seat, take a hand-towel, drape it over your left arm, and recite this verse of mindfulness:
"From dawn at the hour of Tiyin until evening, May all sentient beings be protected and guided.
If by my feet I have inadvertently harmed any form, I pray that you may immediately be reborn in the Pure Land. Oṃ yid ti luyi."
*Svāhā*). Gently open the door and go to the back shelf; do not step on the shoes, do not cough or make noise, and take the basin with light hands.
When washing your face, do not rinse your mouth excessively. You must lower your head when spitting out water, guiding it down with your hand.

When spitting water, straighten your waist; if you spit while leaning over, you may splash the neighbors' rafters. There are four things that, if used for washing the head, are disadvantageous to both oneself and others: (1) soiling the bucket; (2) ... [text fragment].
3. Oil rags; 4. Withered hair; 5. Impairing the eyes. One must not make noise within the nose; one must not spray water onto the face; one must not vomit loudly;
one must not soil the wash-tubs with mucus or spittle. An ancient saying states: "Boiling the face at the fifth watch was originally for the sake of cultivation;

yet vomiting into the basin creates clamor that disturbs the assembly. When burning incense and prostrating, one must don the *kāṣāya* robe first, join the palms, and place them upon the crown of the head while reciting.
It is said: "Excellent is this robe of liberation, the signless field of merit. I now receive it upon my head;
may I wear it constantly in every lifetime. Oṃ siddhāna svāhā."
When folding the *kāṣāya*, it must be done with precise alignment; place it on the clothing rack, perform a greeting (*praṇāma*), and then depart.

If you go to the hall first to prostrate, do not occupy the central position (reserved for the Abbot). Do not chant the Buddha’s name aloud, and do not pass by the heads of those performing prostrations.

When the signal board sounds in sequence and the assembly returns to the hall for the liturgical repentance (*pratikramaṇa*), each person must be sincerely devoted; once the repentance is completed, proceed.
When returning to one’s seat, turn clockwise toward the left shoulder and ascend the platform; one must not enter with one's back turned toward others.

When entering the hall door, one should enter from the southern side, never by the center or the northern side (this is for the sake of honoring the abbot). Upon returning to one’s seat, one should bow low and perform a formal greeting (*wensun*) to the senior, middle, and junior seats.
Even if one has already sat down when the senior, middle, and junior seats arrive, one must still join one’s palms. As the ancients said: "Not..."
Respectfully pay homage to the senior, middle, and junior seats; there is no distinction among the assembled Brahmins. The verse for ascending the platform says:

"Ascending this celestial bed of liberation, with the pure light of equal wisdom. Upon hearing the long board strike, lower the bowl, raise the body to stand upright, and only then turn the body (also from the left shoulder).
Joining the palms, recite the verse: "Holding the alms-bowl, one should [pour forth] for the assembly..."
Born, having accomplished the vessel of the Dharma, receiving offerings from devas and humans: take the bowl, supporting it with the left hand while unfastening the hook with the right;
turn the body to face straight ahead, squat down and place the bowl on the ground to avoid striking others with the waist or back;
do not sit down abruptly, nor climb onto the bed roughly; do not swing the arms left and right while taking the bowl; place the bowl before you and listen.

At the sound of the mallet, join the palms and recite this visualization: “The Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, Attained enlightenment in Magadha, Taught the Dharma in Vārāṇasī, And entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara.
The method for unfolding the bowl is first to join the palms and recite this verse:
“The Tathāgata’s vessel of measureless capacity, I now unfold and spread; May it be shared with all sentient beings, Equalizing the three wheels.”
Having [attained] emptiness and stillness, then untie the cloth bundle and spread out a clean towel to cover the knees. Fold the bundle into a triangle so that it does not hang down.
Next, spread out the bowl-cloth; with hands turned upward, take the bowl and place it upon it.

With the index fingers of both hands joined together, take the small scoop (xuanzi) and unfold the [bowl] from the inside out in sequence, ensuring that no clattering sound is made. Protecting the fourth and fifth [fingers] is for...
"Touch" refers to the bowl-wiping cloth. Fold it and place it across the front of the body. Place the spoon and chopsticks on top of the horizontal bag, and place the bowl-wiping cloth underneath.
When exiting [the dining hall], the spoon comes out first; when entering, the chopsticks come in first. The handle is the clean end; it must not point upward toward the shoulder.
The bowl-brush should be placed within the third joint-seam [of the staff], protruding about half an inch, to hold raw rice. The tips of the spoon and chopsticks must not protrude from the raw rice.

However, seven morsels are too few; this constitutes stinginess in eating. When the head monk raises the chant for the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name, everyone must join their palms without being out of alignment.
The hands should be level with the chest, positioned correctly, and one must not support the mouth with the hands. As the ancients said:
"Joining palms out of alignment and not at the chest, Ten fingers interlaced and thrust into the nose, Dragging sandals and pointing at the curtain—these are no subtle deeds."
Vomiting sounds and releasing gas to display one's "heroism. When receiving food with both hands holding the bowl, one should recite this verse:
"When receiving food, I vow that all sentient beings shall take the joy of meditation as their sustenance and be filled with the bliss of the Dharma.
If one sees the bowl full, one should recite this verse: "Seeing the bowl full, I vow that all sentient beings shall possess complete satiety and be fulfilled in all virtues."
Regarding the roots: when food is served, one should give rise to the mindfulness that restrains the hands. As the verse says: "This food, its color, fragrance, and taste... (as detailed below).
Upon hearing the signal for the meal, one should look at the upper and lower shoulders and face the food with the front of the face;

one must not face the food directly, but rather move the hands to both sides. (The verses for the five contemplations during small meals and main meals, as well as the verses for generating merit, are all as follows).
Regarding the method of eating: one must not bring the mouth to the food, nor bring the food to the mouth.
When receiving food, do not call out to request it. When placing the bowl down or picking up the spoon and chopsticks, there must be no noise. One must not cough, nor harbor nasal mucus;
if a sneeze occurs, one should cover the mouth with the sleeve of one's robe. One must not scratch the head, for fear of scattering dust and dandruff.
One must not pick at one's teeth with the alms bowl; one must not make noise while chewing rice or sipping soup;
one must not pick at the center of the bowl to eat; one must not take large mouthfuls of rice; one must not open the mouth and wait for the food to enter;
one must not drop grains of rice; and one must not scatter rice with the hand. If there are vegetable scraps, they may be placed in a secluded spot, or used to fan oneself.
Do not fan the shoulders of your neighbors; if you yourself fear the wind, sit outside the hall. You must not rest your elbows upon your knees.
Receive food according to your capacity and do not request extra portions; as the Vinaya says, "Eat according to the measure of your belly.
You are not permitted to put wet food into your head-bowl (*tō-hatsu*), nor may you use the broth from the bowl to rinse your rice, nor may you pick at the vegetables with your head-bowl.
When eating rice mixed with other foods from within the bowl, one must observe whether the shoulders are raised or lowered; the pace must be neither too slow nor too fast.
One must not rinse the bowl before being invited to do so again, nor should one make a slurping sound while rinsing. One must not become angry or demand food before it has been served.
As the ancients said: "Staring blankly in all directions, greed and anger arise; Mouth watering at the thought of food, frequent coughing."

Slopping soup and slurping broth, mouthfuls packed full; Unfolding the mat and spreading the bowl, the sound reaches all neighbors. As for the method of washing the bowls: place water in the head bowl;
it is not permitted to wash the spoons and chopsticks inside it. Wash the small bowls (*xunzi*) in sequence. One must not rinse the mouth nor spit water into the bowls.
Do not first fill the bowls with hot water to wash them; until the water has been drained, do not first put them away.
One must not use the knee-cloth to wipe sweat from the knees, nor drip water onto the ground; when pouring out the water, recite this verse:
"This water for washing my bowl, With a flavor like celestial nectar, I bestow upon you, all you ghosts and spirits, May it satisfy you all to fullness.
Oṃ maheśvara-svāhā. Having finished, collect the bowl, press it down with your fingers to secure it, and enter [the dwelling] in due order.

Fold the *fù* (cloth covering), join the palms, and recite the verse for after the meal (the verse for when the meal is finished, which follows below; this verse is traditionally recited by lay families): "The meal is finished, and my physical strength is restored. Once the meal is concluded, one must not rise first.
After the wooden mallet has been struck, the Abbot descends from his seat. In succession, the bowls are hung away; one must not step on the edge of the platform while descending.

Having exited the hall and ascended to the Dharma Hall to chant, each person returns to their own quarters to recite scriptures, prostrate before the Buddha, or recite texts as appropriate. Upon arrival...
When seeking instruction from the Master, whether reading the texts or reciting them back, each person must exert themselves and not lightly disregard the assembly.
When attending tea or soup services, one must not sit with robes trailing on the floor, nor speak or laugh in groups, nor greet others with both hands.
When reading sutras, one must not spread the paper too wide, nor let the sutra straps hang down, nor hold them [in a manner that obstructs the text].
When walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*) or reciting sutras, one must not raise the voice nor lean one's back against the headboard of the platform.

As the ancients said: "To chant aloud is to disturb the crowd; to lean the back against the headboard is to slight the assembly. When setting up the rear framework, the Vinaya regulations require that a bhikṣu wear his five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭhina*).
He should drape a hand-towel over his left hand; if he has no towel, he should untie his sash and tie it to the crossbar.
Fold the upper garment and undergarment neatly and secure them with a belt; hang each about one chi (尺) long to serve as a marker for identification.
Do not urge others from outside, nor engage in conversation or laughter with anyone. Holding water in the right hand, enter the latrine and change your shoes, ensuring they are not placed unevenly.
Place the clean bucket directly in front of you, snap your fingers three times to startle away the dung-eating demons, and squat with your body perfectly upright.

One must not force air through the nose to make a sound, nor may one converse with others across a wall. An ancient saying states: "The door must be closed securely; one should snap the fingers lightly.
When people are crowded together, how can one bear to make noise? Upon entering, use a tally to distinguish between the defiled and the pure areas;
When exiting, water is required, avoiding a haphazard crossing. One must not pour water over both sides [of the anus]; rather, wash thoroughly while protecting the thumb and the second finger.

Regarding the frequent use of counting sticks (shouzhi), the ancients said: "Use few counting sticks when bathing; refrain from picking them up. With dry hands, take your undergarments and enter the trouser-legs;
exit the room holding the bucket in your left hand and change your shoes. You must not touch the door panels or the door jambs with wet hands.
Return the clean bucket to its original place. With your right hand, first pick up the ash, then the soil; you must not handle the ash or soil with wet hands.
When one has vomited or defecated and must wash the hands with mud mixed with water, one must use soapwort (*Gleditsia sinensis*) to wash up to the elbows;
furthermore, when exiting or entering the latrine, one must recite the mantra for each instance.
Entering the toilet: (Oṃ haṃ rudāya svāhā). Cleansing: (Oṃ hana mṛtyuṃjaye svāhā).
Washing the hands: (Oṃ jukarāya svāhā).
Purifying the body: *Oṃ śrīye svāhā*. Removing impurities: *Oṃ vajra-nātha svāhā*.
If one has discharged urine or feces, one must likewise wash the hands with water.
Furthermore, it is not permitted to walk back and forth (*caṅkrama*) within a Buddha hall while wearing straw sandals while traveling in the mountains.
The ancients said: "When entering the latrine, one should wear a side-opening robe; when wandering the mountains in straw sandals, one must not tread upon the Dharma Hall.
One should yield to the elders as one walks through the corridors, moving slowly with shoulders lowered. It is not permitted to wear monastic shoes on one's feet, nor to walk while holding hands.
Discussing the right and wrong of worldly affairs—The ancients said: 'Having bid farewell to both parents and abandoned one’s own teacher, one goes forth to seek [the Way].'"
When seeking a teacher, what do you intend to do? You have never spoken of the matters of the Zen school;
that you have reached old age without achievement—whose fault is it? You must not lean against the balustrade before the hall, nor act with reckless haste.
As the ancients said: "In walking, one must take slow steps, emulating the majestic demeanor of Aśvajit; in speaking, one must lower the voice, following the model of Upāli. The Hall and the Pagoda.
Internally, one is not permitted to wander idly. As the ancients said: "No business, do not ascend the Buddha hall; In leisure, do not walk through the rafters.
Were it not for changing the water or adding incense, Even sands of Ganges’ merit would be exhausted. After the meal, washing clothes is not permitted while wearing a single-layered robe (*chā*).
One must not tip over the hot-water pitcher or the bamboo pole. Once used, they must be returned to their original places.
Newly arrived brothers must observe the rules with diligence. You should encourage one another with kind words and not give rise to feelings of resentment.

One must not walk along the ancestral corridors while wearing a sleeveless garment, nor may one fiddle with prayer beads while playing with toys. After the evening recitation (raṅ), you are not permitted to leave the mountain gate, nor enter the small quarters.
When opening the bathhouse, take the bathing implements with your right hand; according to the Vinaya regulations, you must wear the five-fold robe (pañcakaṣāya).
Entering through the door beneath the [main] gate, one bows in greeting while looking toward the empty space, then returns to one’s position and performs a formal bow (*e*).
Placing the *sashō* (upper robe) first upon the crossbar, followed by the *gojō* (five-strip robe), one spreads out the bath-cloth (*yoku-fuku*), takes up the bathing implements, and sets them aside.

One removes the upper garment, discards the lower garment, wraps the body with the foot-cloth (*kyaku-fu*), and fastens the bathing skirt (*yoku-jo*). Then, one folds the undergarments (*kin-kō*) inside the bath-cloth.
Hang the *zhiduò* (straight robe) and the five-strip robe together; put on clean garments, place them inside a cloth bundle, and enter the bath with slippers.
As the ancients said: "When the bath drum sounds three times and one enters the hall, One must distinguish between upper and lower robes for purity.
Loud laughter and speech are both forbidden; Do not let coarse conduct violate the dignified demeanor. Furthermore, one must not enter the bathhouse barefoot.
Those in the lower section must wait their turn for the bath in the empty space; those in the upper section must yield to the head monks and senior elders.
Do not allow the hot water to splash onto others or yourself. When drying off after bathing, do not soak your feet in the bucket.
Do not wash private parts while standing in the bucket. Do not prop your feet up on the bucket. Do not scrub your feet against the edge of the tub. Do not relieve yourself in the room.
One may speak and laugh, but must not scoop water with the mouth nor ladle it from the bucket to pour over oneself; one must protect the entire body and must not expose unseemly limbs.
One’s undergarment must not be removed from the body. If one has a foot ailment, one should not enter the tub.

Whether washing a sore from moxibustion or applying ointment for scabies, these should both be done after entering the bath. One must not use excessive amounts of hot water, nor should one [use it] to...
The master uses a hand-towel to wipe his face and exits the bath; he must bow to those above and below him and sit with his shoulders aligned.
He puts on the upper garment first, using the *zhiduò* (straight robe) to cover his body before donning the lower garment.

Having removed the skirt and shirt, he places the foot-cloth (*jiǎobù*) inside the skirt and shirt to prevent them from becoming damp. He must not drape the wet foot-cloth over his hands; furthermore, he bows again to those on his left and right.

Upon exiting the hall, if there is a donor who has provided a bath, one may recite sutras at will and perform the dedication of merit. When the evening bell tolls, join the palms and recite this verse:

*Hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions grow light;* *Awakening grows, and wisdom arises.* *Leaving hell behind, emerging from the fiery pit,* *May we attain Buddhahood and deliver all sentient beings.* When leaving the hall on ordinary occasions, the *zhidu* (straight robe) should be worn with the hem of the trousers exposed.

It is improper to wear a *kosode* under one's trousers; when sleeping at night, one should drape the five-strip robe (*gosō*) over the right side, as the right flank is considered honorable, while the garment covers the left shoulder.

Lying face up is the posture of a corpse, while lying face down is the posture of a lecherous sleep; therefore, such postures often result in evil dreams. When the brothers of the Dōbō lineage walk, stand, sit, or lie down, they do not transgress the prescribed rules.

It is precisely during the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night that one should apply oneself diligently to ritual propriety; if one is negligent in these matters, it will cause commotion among the assembly.
Be mindful as you attend to the various rules and regulations; each has its own statutes. In all your actions, look to those of superior character and conduct;

be cautious not to follow the vulgar and base. What the monastic community values most is order and solemnity. Not only should one examine oneself three times a day, but now, in compiling these daily practices, I have merely set forth the general outlines.
If you wish to avoid failure and deficiency at every turn, you must attend to each and every detail.
Only after practicing accordingly may one dare to say that, by following the teachings to establish and cultivate practice, one destroys delusions and manifests the principle,
transcends birth and death to attain nirvana, seeks the Buddha-way above and transforms all sentient beings below.
The *Ten Verses on the Ten Postures* were composed by Chan Master Xiaoweng as he practiced the ancient way.

Among them, the four verses concerning washing the face, spreading out the alms bowl, attending to the toilet, and bathing are entirely his own words; the remaining six chapters are adaptations [of earlier texts].
This is merely a restatement for the purpose of completing the "Changing the Bones" (Huan gu).
It is the same by day as it is by night. When sleeping, one should rise later; when waking, one should rise first.
For temple rituals and recitations, wait until the period of silence has ended. In all movements and postures, perform the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) toward the left shoulder. (1)
When washing your face at dawn, do not be reckless; When rinsing your mouth, keep your head bowed and use little water.
If your head itches, you must wait until after bathing; A clean hand-towel will not hinder you.
(2) Write characters or compose poems to dispel the demon of sleep; Do not treat this as mere idle chatter.
The teachings and contemplations of the Southern Mountain abound in profound principles; One should diligently apply effort to polish and refine them.
(3) When unfolding the alms bowl with body and mind in tranquility, One should take up the chopsticks first when exiting and the spoon first when entering.
The eating cloth must be folded and tucked away at the very end; In bowing to those on one’s left and right, let no ritual be neglected. (4)
After the congee is finished, bow in greeting; after the hall meal, serve tea. When reciting the *Shuowen* and practicing reading, do not be noisy or clamorous.
Leaving the hall and entering the quarters must accord with the pure regulations.
(V) To see that there are masters within the monastic groves, when assigning monks for the *shizi* (self-criticism) ceremony, they must naturally maintain dignified deportment according to the rules.
Lately, a certain class of people has no sense of shame, Wearing small-sleeved shirts beneath their monastic robes.
(6) When drawing lots for recitation, they act most unseemly; Do not let them disturb the silent Dharma Hall.
While it may be tolerable even if there are no rewards for excellence, A prostration of punishment before the monks is most difficult to endure. (7)
When putting on or taking off robes, value neatness and order; When closing the door, one must release it slowly and keep the latch secure.
Recite mantras with gravity and snap the fingers lightly; When reading scriptures, always hold the book with the right hand.
(8) When entering the bath, wear the robe with quiet dignity; When requesting hot water, strike the board with composed decorum.
One should not place foot-cloths upon the wooden trough; how could both feet be placed inside a bucket?
(9) Carrying a book-satchel to seek out teachers, one is called a student; that one’s craft becomes refined and fame achieved depends on diligence.
When the cool air arises in the autumn hall after the rain, who can understand the bright lamp illuminating the ancestors? (10)
