Compiled by the Bhikṣu Xingwu, Successor of the Patriarchs and Abbot of Yanzhong Lushi Temple in Siming.
The Imperial Successor, the incumbent Abbot Nianbo:
When the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, the patriarchs followed the sūtras for encoffining and interment, and the rituals were orderly.

Regarding the nourishing of life and the sending off of the dead, both Confucianism and Buddhism take these as their principles. For instance, at the Twin Trees, he was encoffined in a golden casket while the ten disciples wept, lamented, and repented.
In Vārāṇasī, Śakra, Brahmā, devas, and nāgas wailed and leaped about, their tears flowing like oil from an axle.
Kāśyapa returned from a foreign land, regretting that he had not beheld the true form of the World-Honored One;

the Buddha’s coffin was displayed with its two feet visible, and through the great sovereign samādhi, the golden coffin was brought into the vast void, where it circled the city of Kuśinagara three times before reaching the site of the cremation for the eight kingdoms.
Raising armies to contend over the division of the *śarīra* relics and each returning with their share to erect stupas—would this not be contrary to propriety?

Nevertheless, Baizhang’s regulations stipulated that all clothing and belongings of deceased monks were to be distributed and exhausted for funeral expenses; he memorialized the throne so that the decree might be entered into the imperial canon as a fixed standard.
During the time when the World-Honored One was dwelling in the world, there was an ancient Buddha named Upānanda who manifested the appearance of entering *parinirvāṇa*. When the World-Honored One...

The Imperial Decree commanded that the assembly be gathered to appraise the robes and alms bowl before the multitude, so as to cause the fourfold assembly to observe and be enlightened regarding the impermanence of this body;
those who thereby realized the second fruit of the path were beyond counting. This was intended to counteract external conditions by encouraging the cultivation of one's own practice.

When a predecessor passed away, his dharma robes—enclosed in a paper bag—were left behind specifically for the purpose of inviting the new abbot; it was not for any other matter. This served to manifest the nature of the world.
The Venerable entrusted his robe, intending for it to await Maitreya’s appearance in the world to preach the Dharma; he wished for future generations to clearly recognize its provenance.

Having first issued his final testament and letter, the Venerable Elder manifested illness, and as the time for his passing drew near, he requested the senior members of both assemblies to seal his belongings, leaving behind only—
Regarding the bathing, encoffining, and personal vestments: if the robes and bowl are not numerous, instruct the junior attendant (xiǎoshī) that they must not don hempen garments or wail in grief.
Request the Head Seat (shǒuzuò) to preside over the funeral; all other Buddhist rites are waived. The Head Seat shall join the assembly in reciting the Verse on Impermanence (*wúcháng jì*).
The assembly shall recite, with the Head Seat leading: "The Hall Master (Tángtóu) [Name] Venerable has entered *yuánjì* (perfect stillness). We now lift the coffin to proceed to the tea ceremony."

Everyone should look up with reverence and recite: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss. Recite this three times, then rise.
Once the enshrinement and cremation are completed, let everything be clear and manifest to verify the person's life.

If there is an abundance of robes and bowls, or if royalty and ministers have provided for the funeral, these must be handled according to the prescribed rites. As for the robes and bowls themselves, they shall remain only within the abbot’s quarters.

The administrative office shall dispatch impartial servants to guard the property; once the auction has concluded, they must be careful not to treat what exists as non-existent, thereby wasting the monastery's assets.
Furthermore, all bequests and letters of instruction from external patrons and venerable elders of other mountains must first be settled.

**Regulations for Entering the Shrine** Whenever the Master manifests illness, composes a verse, or enters extinction— regardless of the specific time— the attendant shall immediately instruct the guest-master acolyte to notify the two classes of officials and the assembly of all quarters,
saying: "The Abbot has sent word to the assembly that he is pressed by the 'wind and fire' [of life’s end]."
If one has not had the opportunity to personally bid farewell [to the deceased], the attendant of the Hall Office shall strike the bell before the Sangha Hall;

when the assembly has gathered, the Abbot shall go to the quarters to offer condolences (but must not yet raise the voice of lamentation). The Head Seat, together with the two classes of senior monks, shall deliberate on whom to appoint as the presiding mourner (*sangsang*).

One must select a person from a neighboring monastery who has already completed his funeral rites, or a venerable elder who is a Dharma relative (*hapkyun*); otherwise, one may simply appoint the Head Seat. If there is a specific final instruction from the deceased, it must be followed accordingly.
The filial son, the attendant, and the personal followers shall arrange for the bathing, dressing, and cleansing of the hair, and then place the body in the coffin.

A memorial verse is posted on the left side of the coffin. The *vinaya-dhara* (rector) and the filial son proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and request the *śrāmaṇera-prathama* (head seat) to perform the ritual for entering the coffin.

The coffin is then placed in the dormitory hall, where an incense burner, candles, and a table for offerings are set out for veneration. When the time arrives, the bell in front of the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community.
When the assembly has lifted [the remains] into the shrine and the Buddhist rites are completed, the Rector (Vina) recites the *Amitābha Sūtra* for the dedication of merit, saying:

"It is all because [of the Buddha’s] wondrous power that he universally manifests the traces of his transformation among humans and devas; yet his wondrous essence alone remains, giving rise to profound mechanisms within the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

We reverently contemplate the Abbot, the Head Monk: the moon of solitary, perfect wisdom suddenly withdraws the waves of the ten thousand waters, while his vast and great compassionate heart responds to the ten directions."
Now, feeling moved as I gaze upon his countenance, I find no ground for hesitation; my aspirations have found their refuge.

This collection is for the true disciples who recite with single-minded sincerity the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Buddha-spoken Amitābha Sūtra), one fascicle, and chant the great names of the Four Holy Ones.

May the merit thus accumulated be dedicated to the Hall Head Preceptor’s ground of non-arising, so that it may be wondrously adorned and perfected throughout the ten directions and three periods of time... [and so forth]. Once again, the sūtra is recited for the dedication of merit.
[Cloud] (The foregoing merit from chanting the sutras is dedicated to the Abbot, the Venerable Chongben, and to those of the ten directions and three periods of time, etc.
That night, the assembly gathers for the chanting of sutras and the dedication of merit: for the two periods of serving rice gruel and meals, and the three periods of serving tea and soup;
the assembly chants the sutras, and the incumbent *vinaya-dhara* (Ritual Master) performs the dedication of merit.
Text: Regarding the presiding mourner (*shūsō*).
One who presides over the mourning rites must be a mature and venerable elder of established virtue; how could anyone else be deemed fit for this request?

When the presiding mourner arrives, the great bell is struck, and the assembly welcomes him at the gate to the shrine. Upon offering incense before the shrine, the two ranks of the assembly exchange formal greetings, after which the assembly disperses.

The two classes of officials and the elders escort the guests to their seats; the two classes of officials insert incense and perform the rites of courtesy, at which point they should decline the honors.
The presiding mourner takes his place at the head seat; the head seat rises and burns one stick of incense while remaining in his position, then offers tea.

The filial son immediately steps forward, bows in greeting, inserts incense, and performs three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*dazhan*). Next, the attendants of the abbot perform their prostrations, followed by the head of the assembly (*candou*).

The assembly offers incense and performs three prostrations; thereafter, the attendants of the Abbot pay their respects. Following this, they present hot water and escort the two classes of officials out.
The storehouse prepares refreshments for the midday meal, and the two classes of officials accompany one another as they proceed in order to visit the various quarters.

**Title:** *Jūbusshi Junryō* (The Funeral Rites for the Buddha’s Affairs) After the two ranks of senior monks and the filial sons have visited the various quarters, they proceed to the guest seat (*kakui*) to present the inventory of robes and bowls (*ihatsu-bu*), posthumous writings, and other items.

The presiding mourner (*sōshō*) attends to the dressing of the deceased and the tea ceremony, while the procedures for requesting the funeral rites (*busshi-shiki*) are set forth below, followed by the request for the personnel of the funeral office (*sōshi*).

First, it was deliberated that the cloth for the mourning garments should be measured and distributed as follows: If the presiding mourner is far away and has not arrived within three days, the next head official is requested to oversee the relocation of the shrine and the associated Buddhist rites.
Upon the arrival of the presiding mourner, he must privately calculate the number of robes and bowls and divide them into three portions:

one portion to be distributed among the assembly for their expenses and offerings; one portion for the funeral funds and the meal expenses; and one portion to be given to the staff of the funeral office as a token of gratitude.
Regarding the Buddhist rites for mourning: the administrator of the funeral shall daily provide one portion of funds to perform memorial services (*zhāi*) and recite scriptures during the procession.
The Chief Seat (*shouzuo*) must share responsibility for these matters. The presiding mourner may only express grief before the spirit tablet.

Monks accompanying the funeral procession must not interfere with the performance of duties or the Buddhist rites. If the offerings of robes and bowls are abundant, it shall be discussed whether to invite monks from neighboring regions.
The retired abbot (*laocheng*), the senior monks of this temple, the West Hall Chief Seat (*xítáng shǒuzuò*), and the daily stipend recipients shall recite scriptures and offer tea and soup.
This shall not be restricted to the two classes of officials; rather, each group of senior monks shall appoint one person to manage the finances in order to eliminate idle gossip.

For the funeral rites, they shall also invite the Senior Funeral Director (*shīsāng*), the Secretary (*sīshūjì*), the Rector (*wéinà*), and the Guest Master (*zhīkè*) according to public consensus to jointly appoint an Attendant (*shìzhě*) to oversee the accounts.
The officials of the funeral administration shall dispatch the treasury clerk, the guest master, the tea master, and their attendants to manage affairs;

they shall further invite the incumbent *vinaya* master and the guest master to deliberate on the Buddhist rites. The incumbent guest master shall receive external guests at the gate, while the funeral administration staff and servants shall arrange the seating order, post the notification, transfer the reliquary casket, and offer wailing.
Then, three days after the *kaṅkha* (relic casket) has been moved into the back of the shrine, the shrine door is closed. The administrative office (*kōji*) prepares the ceremonial rites;

within the Dharma Hall (*hōdō*), curtains of various colors are hung, beds and couches are solemnly arranged, and implements for use are displayed on racks to the left and right. Sandalwood vessels and other ritual utensils are set out upon the tables.
In the section for writing implements, inkstones, and ritual vessels, one prepares the incense burner, vases, offering bowls, hot-water flasks, braziers, and tea-service utensils;

attendants are stationed to guard the central area where a grand sacrificial banquet is laid out, with raw silk curtains and canopies erected and a Dharma seat prepared, upon which the portrait is hung.
For the upper section of the sacrifice, a shrine bed is placed in the lower section, draped with curtains and canopies; the memorial tablet is installed on its stand, preceded by a low table.
With offerings of plain flowers at both morning and evening services, tea, congee, and rice are served; the recitation of sutras, incense, and candles proceed without interruption.

Lamps are arranged and lit, and the *nengbo* gongs and flower banners are displayed. The bell is struck to assemble the community for the performance of Buddhist rites. Once these are completed, the shrine is moved down to the Dharma Hall (according to the Zen regulations, this is the "Ceremony for Requesting the Locking of the Shrine").
Donning the mourning attire, hang the portrait, express grief, and present the offerings of tea and soup.
Once the shrine has been moved, the portrait is hung in the Dharma Hall; the attendant then presents the final testament to the Head Seat (the presiding mourner) and the assembly, saying:
"The final words of the Abbot, presented to the Head Seat and the Assembly" (the title of the letter). The Head Seat [reads it].
The funeral party presents the letter to the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera). The Head Seat incenses the letter over the incense burner and hands it to the Rector (Karmadāna), who reads it aloud.
Once finished, the funeral attendant pastes the notice upon the upper-left corner of the curtain at the center of the Dharma Hall. The presiding mourner says: "The Abbot has passed away;

it is fitting that we observe the rites of mourning. Having performed the Buddhist service, he wails three times, and the assembly breaks into lamentation as the sons of the deceased take their places.
Those beneath the mourning curtain weep in grief; the presiding mourner burns incense and requests the ritual of offering tea.

After the presiding mourner presents the sacrifice and the guest master (zhikè) recites the memorial text, the ritual of offering tea is requested once more. The filial sons prostrate before the sacred image and then return to the mourning curtain.

The presiding mourner again burns incense and pays respects to the image, to which all the filial sons respond with bows. The presiding mourner then enters the mourning curtain to offer condolences to the filial sons.

Perform three prostrations in accordance with the ritual; then, the words of consolation for the two ranks of the assembly are as follows: "It is a misfortune for the Dharma Gate that the Abbot, the Master of Transformation, has passed away.

We venture to hope that the Great Assembly will graciously assist in completing his final affairs. The words of the Head Seat are: "We rely upon the Master to graciously assist in completing his final affairs.
The words of consolation for the filial son from the two ranks of the assembly are: "It is a misfortune for this mountain gate that the Master has returned [to the Pure Land]."
[The family] sincerely requests that you restrain your grief to complete the great task [of the funeral].

**Ritual Order for Hanging the Portrait:** Once the portrait has been hung according to the sequence of the offerings, the Ritual Director shall prepare a list of items and arrange the order of the offerings, which shall be posted upon the lower curtain of the Dharma Hall. (Protocol)
Upon seeing the deceased, one should perform the memorial service once or twice daily by chanting sutras; this does not apply to offerings presented by lay patrons from various mountains.

If a dharma relative or successor comes to offer a memorial service wearing mourning attire, the guest prefect (zhikè) shall receive them at the gate and immediately notify the funeral director, who will then deliver the mourning attire before the service begins.
Any ritual items used for the funeral that remain after the expenses have been settled shall be returned.
The temple property must remain intact; otherwise, the mountain palanquins and attendants will all cause disturbance to the monastery’s assets.

The funeral director shall assemble the two classes of officials and the senior elders to inventory the robes and bowls according to their actual count. Following public deliberation, items other than the final bequests shall be set aside.
The funeral director shall then calculate the number of new and old items, as well as their respective lengths and monetary values, so that they may be readily available when the time comes.
Evening Vigil Facing the Spirit: Arranging the Offerings of Tea and Soup (In the Chan regulations, this is called "Facing the Spirit for Brief Consultation and Recitation").

Once the portrait has been hung, the Venerable Director of Affairs (Vina), together with the filial sons, goes to the guest seat to bow and invite the presiding mourner to attend the vigil at night (to attend the vigil at night means to stay overnight).

In the Dharma Hall, facing the portrait, a seat is prepared to face the spirit for the "Arranging the Offerings" ceremony (explaining the causes and conditions of the Pure Land). When the evening bell tolls, the drum is struck to assemble the assembly.

The two classes of officials (nobleman and scholar-official) take their positions as usual, without their personal attendants. The attendant burns incense, and after the Dharma talk is concluded, the filial son prostrates and presents the offerings.

The Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) then leads [the procession] to the front of the coffin and ascends the incense altar. The Rector (Karmadāna) recites the *Amitābha Sūtra* and performs the dedication of merit (the ritual for which follows).
The two classes of officials present tea and soup offerings and present their own sacrifices. Next, the individual spirits are honored, followed by the filial son presenting his sacrifice.
When the assembly disperses after the chanting of scriptures, the head of the assembly leads the group in calling for the session, prostrating, and chanting scriptures;

they perform the ritual of bowing and acknowledging the presence of the lower quarters, chant the scriptures, and the attendants of the Abbot’s quarters, the head of the assembly, the general public, and the laborers join in the vigil.

Regarding the rites for the funeral procession, the hanging of the portrait (*zhēn*), the offering of tea and soup, and the ceremonial escort of the deceased, these must be performed in accordance with proper measure. One should calculate the quantity of robes and alms bowls and consider the heat or cold of the weather;

whether it takes ten days or half a month depends on the completion of the necessary tasks. The administrative officer (*zhīshì*) and the director of funeral affairs (*sāngsī*) shall oversee and regulate the funeral ceremonies and incense offerings.
The ceremonial pavilion is set up with banners, streamers, and musical instruments; the ten great disciples are arrayed in their niches, wailing before them.

Canopies, chairs, book-caskets, incense burners, rows of lamps, fly-whisks, and incense containers are arranged alongside the dharma robes. The filial sons follow the bier, sounding the tower bell, wooden fish, drums, and clappers as they escort the funeral procession to the entrance of the mountain gate.
The painted pavilion displays the true likeness [of the deceased], and Buddhist rites are performed while tea is offered.

When the funeral procession for the Buddha-service begins and the two classes of officials and the assembly stand in rows at the gate awaiting the emergence of the reliquary shrine (*stūpa*), the *karmadāna* of the mountain gate stands facing inward beneath the canopy with palms joined.
He leads the recitation of the mantra for rebirth in the Pure Land or the four sacred names.

The presiding mourner leads the assembly in a clear and orderly procession to escort the funeral; those on the left and right hold willow branches and purple twigs, ensuring they do not crowd one another or converse, each maintaining a solemn demeanor.

In deep sorrow, the Director of Funerals (Sangsi), the Rector (Vinaya-master), the Official in Charge of the Funeral (Ap-sang), the Guest Master (Jikgak), and the Attendant (Sije) distribute the funeral insignia. [The following are] the positions:
Holding the Ruler (Bing-gu), Hanging the Portrait (Gwa-jin), Reaching the Nirvana Altar (Sang-ji-neomnae-tae).
The Director of Funerals and the Rector wait until the Abbot (Duse) has finished offering incense; they then step forward to burn incense and make the request.

The Abbot conducts the Buddhist rites; once the rites are completed, he performs the recitation of the *Śūraṅgama-mantra*. The Director of Funerals and the Guest Prefect lead the assembly in a uniform recitation for the dedication of merit (the formula is shown below).

Next, the laypeople perform the recitation of the sutra for the dedication of merit, which the entire assembly must chant together. Once finished, the Head Seat leads the assembly back to the monastery.

The laypeople, dharma relatives, and the filial son accompany the burning of the shrine and the collection of the bones. When the meal is finished, the Head Seat gathers the assembly to prepare for the subsequent proceedings.

With formal ceremony, the remains are welcomed back to the dormitory hall, where a portrait is hung for offerings and sutras are chanted. At two times of the day, rice gruel and meals are served; at three times, tea and soup are offered.
This continues for ten days or half a month until the assembly arrives to chant sutras, at which point the remains are enshrined in the stupa and the chanting is concluded.

On the day the remains are enshrined in the stupa, prepare the full ceremonial protocol and assemble the congregation for the ritual of exhuming the bones. Escort the bones to the site of the stupa; upon their entry into the stupa, perform the relevant rites.

Once the recitation of sutras is completed, welcome the sacred image back to the shrine hall. Hang the portrait there and make offerings. The presiding mourner burns incense and pays homage to the portrait.

Next, the assembly of the two classes of officials and the filial sons complete the ritual of paying respects to the portrait. The filial sons insert incense and perform three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*tae-jin sam-bye*) to thank the presiding mourner.
The assembly of the two classes of officials then speaks these words of thanks to the presiding mourner: "The mountain gate has met with misfortune as our late Head Monk passed away;
we are deeply grateful that you have taken charge of the subsequent affairs. The presiding mourner replies: "I am deeply grateful for your support, which has enabled me to avoid dereliction."

Upon the conclusion of the funeral rites, the presiding mourner and the entire staff of the mourning office shall tour the quarters to offer their thanks. Next, the filial son (the deceased’s heir) shall tour the quarters to pay his respects.
The *weina* (rector) shall escort the incumbent officials and the attendants observing the mourning period back to their rooms.

Daily, tea and soup shall be served at the three periods of the day at the mountain gate, and the assembly shall gather to chant sutras; however, this is suspended for the memorial tablets (*paivi*) in the Patriarchs’ Hall. Alternatively, one may wait until the new abbot has arrived before entering the Patriarchs’ Hall.
The State: The entire body is placed within the stupa;

the funeral rites are as previously described, with only the division of the *xueliu* (willow branches) for entry into the stupa and the chanting of recitations (the form is shown below), the incantation of the stupa, the recitation of sutras, and the dedication of merit (the forms are provided below).
The spirit-tablet is welcomed back to the resting hall for offerings.
When there is a distribution of robes and bowls, having first marked the new and old items and their respective values, one lists the quantities on a register.

Seats are arranged within the Dharma Hall, and outside, a long signboard is placed horizontally with a brush, inkstone, and large chime. The bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the assembly.
The presiding mourner and the head seat (shouzuo) divide the assembly into two groups and sit with their hands hanging down; the rest of the assembly sits in succession.

The ritual director (sangsi), the rector (weina), and the guest prefect (zhike) face the presiding mourner’s position for the chanting (the format is shown below). First, the storage chest is opened and the robes and bowls are removed, arranged on the mats according to their numbers.
The "Ceremony of Requesting the Robes" (qitiyi foshi) is performed; as soon as the words conclude, the rector immediately says: "As for the method of chanting the robes..."
Generally speaking, the standard is that when loud, it does not exceed seven or eight *chāng* (measures), and when low, it does not go below one or two *chāng*.
Furthermore, tell me: how do you deliberate on the state of being neither noble nor base? [The Master] lifts his robe and says: "One *chāng* and five hundred.
If there is no formal request for a ritual service (*fóshì*), he simply lifts his robe and says: "The Tathāgata’s True Dharma Eye; the golden robe of the monk."
Unfolding, he pervades and transforms the great trichiliocosm; gathering in, not even a hair’s breadth separates them.

His body of a thousand cubits is not too long to cover the sixteen-foot form, nor is it too short. Although he is hidden within Mount Kukkutapāda, how can he avoid being here today as he demonstrates his passing?
(Master [Name]), having completed your journey for the sake of Dharma, you now cast off your hands and depart.
Taking up the robe with his hand, he addresses the assembly for appraisal, holding up the garment and saying, "One bid: five hundred.

If there are many Dharma robes, they are all left as a legacy to be presented in succession. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) receives them and bids the price; the funeral director and relevant officials must act with impartiality.
The presiding *vinaya-dhara* examines the items personally with his own eyes and hands, determines the value, strikes the *kangling* (wooden clapper), and the treasury office records it.

The procedure for announcing the names and designating the items is as follows: The *shangdan* (upper single) attendant, relying on the single list, announces the items by calling out their names; the *jiadan* (lower single) attendant, relying on the single list, announces the number of bundles and the amount of cash;
the presiding mourner (*zhusang*) relies on the single list to hand over the cash and receive the robes, not acting according to personal preference or allowing reductions;

the presiding mourner takes primary responsibility for these matters. In recent times, various formal methods have fallen into disuse; the method of chanting has ceased, and instead, items are first determined by drawing lots (*jiunian*), after which the value of the robes is fixed according to the current market price.
The names of the sites and so forth are written on slips of paper and distributed one to each member of the assembly present. Two slips are written for each site;
they are cut in half, and each person rolls one portion into a ball and places it into a common bowl. Each person retains the other half as a witness.
Then, one person takes up a robe and presents it to the assembly for their knowledge, while another novice monk is instructed to scramble the slips within the common bowl.
Trusting one's hand, he picks up a phrase and chants it for an individual, asking, "Under which number of 'Heaven' (Tian) does it appear?

Then, the assembly draws forth the remaining half of the divination slips marked with the "Heaven" numbers that were previously set aside; when these are combined, the Director of Funerals immediately issues a "piercing slip" (piao jiu) according to that name and casts it into the water basin.
If no one responds after three such chants, he then takes the slip marked with the specific "Heaven" number [of the respondent].
Furthermore, cast [the remaining items] into a water basin and draw one more lot; then draw them out in succession, ensuring there is no partiality.

If the deceased monk’s robes and bowl are abundant, rather than using personal funds for the funeral procession, distribute the robes and bowl among the monks present according to the aforementioned method of drawing lots.
In this way, there will be no favoritism, which accords precisely with the Vinaya regulations.

The *yu* (host) shall provide hospitality in advance during the registration of the deceased, determining that three parts of the provisions be set aside for the preparation of the farewell letter (*yishu*) to be entered into the Patriarchs’ Hall (*zutang*).

The *yu* shall also provide hospitality for all officials of the funeral office (*sangsi*), ensuring that the distribution of monetary offerings (*qinli*) is equitable to settle all disputes. Subsequently, the mountain gate (*shansan*) shall provide hospitality for the presiding mourner (*zhusang*).
The procession shall include two attendants as offerings, accompanied by two elders as usual; the protocol for their reception shall be identical.
Tao Xiao, the attendant junior disciple (wearing a hempen robe), the two head officials (wearing linen robes), the presiding mourner, and close kinsmen of the Dharma.
The Abbot (wears a long robe of raw silk *chángshēng jiù zhíjiǔ*); next, the Dharma relatives, teachers, disciples, those who have settled matters, and local residents (wear raw silk waistbands);

the donors (wear raw silk head-cloths and waistbands); the attendants of the Abbot’s quarters (wear hempen head-cloths and monastic robes); the servants of the Abbot’s quarters (wear hempen garments and head-cloths);
the various attendants (wear head-cloths of ramie cloth); the foremen, fire-keepers, and farm laborers (wear hempen head-cloths); and the work supervisors (wear hempen garments and head-cloths).
Tang Dynasty: Lament for the Passing of the Abbot.
His traces of transformation benefited both the manifest and the hidden realms of the Imperial Tang; his divine spirit wandered through the inner court, and his grief moved the forests and springs.
Although by Dharma there is neither coming nor going, we respectfully offer this memorial service to express our condolences. We pray that the tuft of hair between his brows [shall remain eternal].
With the light of every buddha-field radiating from his tongue, like wind and thunder, he proclaims the predictions of enlightenment for every mote of dust.
[This is] the order of the offerings for the memorial service:
the administrative officers, the head monks, the presiding mourner, the western hall monks, the elders, and the various department heads.
Former attendants; fellow villagers; dharma relatives; farmhands; hermitages and stupas; junior disciples and grand-disciples;
the abbot’s quarters staff; the six administrative bureaus;
the hall attendants; those on call for the abbot; the abbot’s sedan-chair bearers; the senior laborers; the village headmen; and the fire-attendants.
For the construction project (including the various ritual offerings for the head mason),
the people performed recitations and various rites throughout the night,
dedicating the merit for the sake of the Abbot, who has entered Parinirvāṇa; now, having assembled the great assembly, we solemnly [proceed].
Approaching the shrine, we chant the sūtras and extol the holy name; may the merit thus accumulated be dedicated toward the exaltation of the station of the Abbot, the Master who has entered Nirvāṇa.

May he never forget his vow of power to once again manifest the *tánhuā* (rare flower) and launch the boat of compassion across the surging waves of birth and death, ferrying the multitudes of deluded beings to the other shore of Bodhi.
Once more, I entreat the great assembly to recite [the names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions...]
As the world speaks thus (and so forth).
○ When the coffin was raised, the golden casket lifted itself up and circumambulated the great city of Kuśinagara;

banners and streamers swayed in the void as it proceeded to the grand rite of cremation (at the funeral, say "Nanda"). We now rely upon the Great Assembly to recite the Great Name, thereby expressing our grief at parting. Above—
Auspicious Invocation for the Path of Awakening (The Ten Buddhas of the Pure Dharma Body have already completed their realization; now they arise in action).
The Head Monk of the Transformation Hall has finished his rounds for offerings and suddenly returns to True Suchness.
His sacred coffin is encircled by the city of Kuśinagara, and the fire of nature spontaneously consumes it this day. We now rely upon the assembly to assist his awakened spirit: *Namo*.
In the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, to Amitābha Buddha of Great Compassion and Great Kindness—(after the tenth recitation, say:

The sacred name has been extolled above and the transformative rites have been reverently performed. His essential form follows the ancient patriarchs; his spiritual capacity is so sublime it admits neither Buddhas nor patriarchs.
To open the way for future students, he employs a heart of compassion that still gathers in devas and humans. Now, may these hundred members of this illusory body enter the fire.
With the *Tejo-dhātu-samādhi*, I offer three libations of tea and incense from a single burner to escort you upon your journey to the clouds. I pay homage to the assembly of noble ones.

Regarding the enshrinement of the entire body in the stupa: it is essential that the wheel-mark on the feet demonstrates the legacy of Vulture Peak, while the stupa emitting the light of precepts manifests the transformative influence of the *Zhizhu Yuan* (the Garden of Mushrooms).
The full capacity of the Great Function is revealed and concealed; we look up with reverence to the beginning and end of the Dharma, relying entirely upon the great assembly.

Offering for the Awakening Spirits: *Namo* to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*as recited ten times previously*). We only pray that the mirror of wisdom may radiate its brilliance and the clouds of compassion spread far and wide;

within the realms of the four modes of birth, you shall reveal the cause of non-arising and non-extinction, and amidst the paths of the six destinies, you shall discourse upon the Dharma of no-self and no-person. [Three libations are offered] (as detailed previously).

Your Dharma heir, deeply moved by your kindness that surpassed that of a nursing mother and your righteousness that exceeded the legacy of gold, has yet to fulfill his heart’s desire for the Phoenix Hall, when the *huashu* tree has already withered like a flying bat.
Since the principle of existence and cessation is ultimately resolved, filial piety must mourn this solemn transformation.

We have prepared these meager offerings to cultivate merit, merely to express our profound longing. We humbly pray that your power of meditative concentration may rise as high as mountains piercing the earth and touching the clouds, so that your blessings may flourish.

The Dharma-ocean increases, its waves surging to the heavens and drenching the sun; its abyss becomes ever more vast. Once again, I entreat the great assembly to recite [the names of] the Ten Directions and Three Periods of Time, and so forth.

My junior disciple would rather grind his bones and shatter his body than have even slightly repaid the grace of your guidance. Yet, like a falling star or a sudden flash of lightning, you have suddenly passed away.

Having entered the gateway of death, how distant are the instructions received in the courtyard; the solemnity of the grave and its surrounding trees grows ever more remote. Gazing upward toward the Grove of Enlightenment, I am overcome with sorrow.
I humbly pray that your compassionate heart may be moved, sending forth the waters of wisdom to moisten this withered forest;

that for the destitute son who has no refuge, the sun of brilliant wisdom may shine to open the path for those lost in the wilderness. Once again, I beseech the Great Assembly to take thought [for us] throughout the ten directions and three periods of time.
[Thus it is said.
Entering the stupa and chanting sutras to dedicate the merit of the preceding recitations, this empowerment of the precious stupa has achieved great merit.
Even the kalpa-stone may be worn away, yet its majestic power increases and vibrates; auspicious light shines everywhere, suddenly illuminating the dark recesses and causing all to be clearly seen.
How much more so for those who linger [in the world], all of whom shall ascend the shore of Bodhi (the ten directions and three periods of time, etc.).

Obituary Notice:
The Bhikṣu [Name], Director of Funerary Affairs at [Name] Temple, respectfully seals and dispatches this letter from the late Great Master Abbot of [Name] Place.
Posthumous Letter.

When the funeral rites are completed, the presiding mourner requests attendants and those who have assisted with the affairs to serve as special envoys; they shall travel by different routes to deliver the offerings to the various monasteries.

Only for fellow practitioners, lay patrons, and officials of noble rank does one write a formal letter of greeting for the venerable elders, selecting capable individuals to serve as these special envoys.

Upon arrival at the guest quarters, the guest master (zhīkè) shall first receive them and conduct the formal greetings; he will then lead them to the administrative office (shìsī), where preparations have been made in advance.

The attendant, carrying the books and items in a carrying cloth, goes to the Abbot’s quarters to announce his arrival. The Abbot shall immediately receive him and instruct that the two classes of officials be invited.

The special messenger steps forward, bows in greeting, and says, "Please, Venerable Master, sit in the lotus position. He offers incense and performs the formal guest etiquette by unfolding his ritual implements;
the Abbot declines this. Once seated, they drink tea. After rising before the brazier to express thanks for the tea, he offers large sticks of incense.
One prostration, three bows, and says: (On this day... [as appropriate]... I, so-and-so, have had the honor of beholding your venerable countenance;
my humble feelings are filled with the utmost joy and gratitude. Having completed the ritual, he says: (The Master of such-and-such place passed away on the [day] of the [month].

His final letter and personal effects are sent by me for your acceptance. He then presents the letter and items to the Abbot, who says: (The Dharma-gate is in decline; I cannot bear the grief and sorrow.)

The attendant of the abbot’s quarters receives [the letter]. The two groups of officials assemble and perform a formal inquiry (*monshin*). The head seat takes his place at the side. The special envoy and the abbot sit facing each other;
the envoy withdraws one seat back and sits. They drink tea. Rising, the abbot says:

"It is a misfortune for the Dharma that the Venerable Master of [Place Name] has passed away; our grief is beyond measure. The attendant prepares a writing tablet, cuts it, and presents the written materials to the abbot.
The attendant takes the letter; the abbot receives the letter, incenses it over the incense burner, and hands it back to the attendant to deliver to the *karmadāna* (rector).

The attendant and the *śrāmaṇera* (novice) pass it to the messenger, who opens the seal and reads it aloud. Once this is done, the attendant bows to the special messenger, who takes a seat facing the abbot.

The abbot serves hot water according to the usual protocol and escorts the messenger back to his assigned quarters. First, the abbot performs the formal greetings (*puruṣa-kriyā*), followed by the two attendants.

The administrative staff (banren) shall take cognizance of this, and the Guest Master (lizhu) shall lead the tour of the quarters (*xunliao*), first visiting the Treasury Office (*kusī*) and then the quarters of the Head Monks (*tóushou*) and the individual monks (*dānliao*).

This is because offerings are made to each of them. That evening, the Attendant (*shìzhě*) shall request a special serving of hot tonic (*tàng*) and medicinal gruel (*yàoshí*). By nightfall, the hot tonic and fruit have been served;

the Great Square (*dàfāng*) has sent a letter of invitation, and the two classes of officers (*liǎngbān*) shall act as companions. As for the second [invitation], the two classes of officers—the Head Monks and the Rectors (*wéinà*)—shall act as companions.

The attendant shall request a person skilled in composition to discuss the origins [of the deceased] in person and draft the memorial text. For the memorial of the Abbot, the Abbot himself usually composes it;
for the memorial of a Dharma relative from the Lake or River [lineages], the administrators shall all prepare the offerings and incense. The attendant must oversee each of these details.

Early the next morning, the Abbot shall invite [the assembly] to drink soup and eat congee, followed by tea. Then, at the lower section of the Dharma Hall, the ritual space shall be prepared with nails and hangings, and the memorial service shall be performed.

The abbot covers the *fangzhang* (abbot’s quarters), strikes the gong to assemble the assembly in the Dharma Hall, and proceeds to the altar to offer incense, light the soup, present the offerings, and serve tea.

The abbot and the two classes of officers perform prostrations; the special envoy sits to the right and returns the prostrations. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) recites the memorial text, whereupon the abbot again performs prostrations and the special envoy returns them.
The sutra is chanted and the merit is dedicated, following the same procedure as for the anniversaries of the patriarchs. The two classes of officers [perform the same].
Once the local people have completed their offerings at the site of the incident, the Abbot leads the assembly in dedicating the merit to the Dharma relatives and junior disciples.

Those below the rank of the official in charge of the funeral affairs do not return the bow; they simply perform three prostrations before the altar to thank the Abbot. Next, they visit the various quarters to express their gratitude.

Upon returning to the mountain gate, the Abbot provides hospitality for the official envoy and his two attendants. The senior and junior Dharma relatives of the mountain gate are also invited to join the gathering.
The prostrations must be performed with proper rhythm and in the correct order. There are no offerings for the mountains, rivers, or lakes.

When the posthumous letter from Master Shang-si arrives at the Abbot’s quarters, the two classes of officials shall first offer condolences to the Abbot. An altar is then established in the center of the Dharma Hall; before the offering is made, the incense is picked up.
When the incense has been offered, the words for raising the lamentation are recited three times, and the Sūtra is chanted. The Head Seat leads the assembly in circumambulation;

once the dedication of merit is complete, they perform three prostrations before the offering table, followed by three prostrations for the hot water offering. After the food has been presented, the drum is struck, and a special tea service is held for which three prostrations are performed. The ritual implements are then withdrawn.

Those who offer the final three prostrations include the two classes of officials, fellow practitioners from various regions, local laypeople, Dharma relatives, and junior disciples; all having completed their offerings, the ceremony concludes.
The manner of offering condolences before the Abbot who leads the assembly is the same as described previously.
Format for a Final Letter: [I], a mountain-dweller who has failed to contribute to the Teachings and the Community, am unable to rise due to a slight illness.

Having failed my duties toward the Monastery, I am now suddenly tormented by a confluence of wind and fire. Gazing upon the clouds and mountains, my compassion increases; yet, as we are separated by face-to-face absence, I can only offer these words of deep respect. Thus ends the letter.
Prayer.
○ This Dharma-relative, having unworthily occupied this mountain, feels ashamed before his fellow disciples. As he grows old and infirm, he will remain here for the rest of his life;

thus, he respectfully presents this handwritten letter as a token of parting in person. I hope that you, the direct successor who has heard the teachings intimately, will exert yourself [to uphold the Dharma].
I have been entrusted with this by my late teacher and am departing in haste; I humbly pray that you will take care of yourself.
○ As a mountain-dweller living on a neighboring border, I have been of no benefit; I constantly rely upon the light emanating from your neighbor’s wall.

Since the realm of dreams is fundamentally empty, I am fortunate to have escaped the illusions of worldly conditions. Though we cannot agree upon a face-to-face parting, my heart yearns for you most earnestly. I pray that on the day of the Buddha, your radiance may increase.
The lineage of our school is further revitalized; as I am pressed for time and lack leisure, I venture to offer these humble words.

I pray you will cherish yourself. I, your former disciple, have long had the honor of following in your footsteps. Yet, subject as we are to the laws of separation and union, I was unexpectedly summoned by others and compelled to labor under meager conditions.

Like lightning and dew, all things are suddenly empty; like clouds and mountains, the distance grows ever more vast. I dare to entreat your protection so that this tradition of our culture may endure.
This prayer is offered with incomplete formalities.
○ On the flap at the top, write: "Respectfully Submitted" (拜覆). Sealed by the Abbot (堂頭大和尚) of [Name] Temple, the Bhikṣu [Name] who presides over [Name] Temple. Respectfully sealed.
Regarding the succession of the abbot’s final affairs:

when the two classes of officials assemble the great assembly for a council, they must select one who is fully endowed with both learning and wisdom, possesses eminent virtue, is advanced in years, and whose conduct is pure and white, such that he is worthy of the community's trust.
The assembly must submit a formal petition supported by the signatures of the members, ensuring that the candidate accords with the standards of all the monastic communities throughout the world.

Only through public selection can one be known by public opinion; let the elders and former officials not act on private favoritism. If the monastic community obtains worthy individuals, the Dharma will abide for a long time.
If, however, one relies on wealth and power to seek livelihoods, forms alliances, or advances with false pretenses, this Way will perish.
How can name and position be entrusted lightly?
Seated [in meditation]:

When a sick monk passes away and his condition is grave, the fellow practitioners shall go directly to the patient’s quarters. Lay associates and old friends from the local community shall arrange incense, candles, and Buddhist icons at the bedside;
they must invoke the Buddhas and devas with sincere prayer. Should the illness reach its final stage, one shall inform the *vina* (steward) and request that the body be sealed.
The Hall Attendant, the Treasury Officer, the Head Seat, the Administrative Officers, and the Attendants shall go together before the patient to record his oral instructions.

Once the patient has passed away, they shall, together with the public officials, pack the clothing trunk and personal effects, seal them securely, and leave them for the purpose of dressing the deceased;
or, if there is no time to do so, the Rector and the Head Seat must also take the lead in preparing the number of monastic robes required.

The pearl-fragrance box, foot-binding cord, sitting mat, shoes, socks, hair-cleansing cloth, bone-receiving cloth, cotton wadding, and other necessary items shall be combined into one bundle and placed together with the patient's meal for safekeeping.
For those who have no belongings, the full monastic protocol shall be observed;
the Abbot and Head Seat shall take primary responsibility for seeing them off. Once the luggage has been sealed, the key and seal shall be signed and returned.

The head seat’s robes and bowl, as well as those belonging to various quarters, shall be carried back to the Hall Office by the laborers. If they belong to a private cell, they must remain in that room;

one must appoint someone to guard them. Since a deceased monk who has no relatives cannot leave a written will, his belongings must not be handled arbitrarily, as this would inevitably lead to disputes.

In the morning, when a deceased monk who was free from illness passes away, his fellow practitioners report it to the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina), who then instructs the attendants of the Hall Office to announce it and prepare the hot water.

The Head Seat, the Guest Prefect, and the Attendants are notified, and the administrative office dispatches personnel to carry the bier and arrange the bathing boat for the deceased. The *vinaya-dhara* then tests the temperature of the water.
Upon completing the cold and hot baths, wipe the deceased with a bath towel and robe, then provide a clean hair-drying towel.

Entrust the attendant and the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) to supervise the dressing and placement in the coffin. Place the coffin within the central space beneath the Amida Buddha image (either in the main hall or the bathhouse).
Set up chairs, tables, a name tablet, incense, and lamps for offerings. As the monks present chant sutras, perform the dedication of merit, and light a perpetual lamp throughout the night.

The attendants of the Hall Office (Dangsi) prepare the snow-pine (sae-ryu) for the great monastery; since the shrine-cabinet (gum-guk) has already been constructed, those required [materials] must be carried there.
In small and medium-sized monasteries, who has the leisure for such matters? One should observe the condition of the sick;
if their state is critical, one must prepare timber in advance and assemble it so as not to cause errors or neglect the outward appearance at the last moment.
The spirit tablet reads: "Spirit of the newly deceased (Name) Dharma Master" (or, for a West Hall Abbot: "Spirit of the Former Abbot of [Name] Temple, [Name] West Hall Great Monk").
If the person performing the service holds an office, their title and name shall be used accordingly.

Question: Regarding the daily recitation of sutras, the serving of congee and rice by the ritual attendants (*jikō*), the offering of tea and soup at the three periods of the day, and the presentation of incense:

after the morning congee has been served, the attendant on duty strikes the *inkyō* (leading chime). The Head Seat (*shuso*) leads the assembly to the front of the shrine (*kō*). The ritual attendant first offers tea and presents the incense.

The Incense Custodian takes up the incense; the Rector recites the *Amitābha Sūtra* for the dedication of merit. Next, the village elders recite the sūtra, and the village head burns one stick of incense.
Every day at the three periods [of morning, noon, and evening], they assemble together until the third day after the funeral procession, at which point the recitation of the sūtra ceases.

Dedication Verse: (The merit from the foregoing recitation of the sutra is respectfully dedicated for the sake of the newly deceased [Name] Dharma Master, to adorn his ground of retribution throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time...
When referring to public figures, use only their single-character name.
The path: Divide the space and set up the niches.

The *vina*, *zhike*, and *shizhe*, together with the attendants of the Hall Office and the various *shouzuo*, shall prepare the tally-stamps and seals, record the current count, and seal them to be kept at the *shouzuo*'s quarters.
Either in the morning or at noon, the *zhike* and *shizhe* shall proceed to the *bowei* (bowls' positions).

The eye is shared equally; when the assembly of monks arrives for a temporary visit, they share together with [the resident monks] according to the number of coverings. The *karmadāna* and the *sthavira* (senior monk) determine the count.
Other items are distributed as damaged goods. Robes and bowls are distributed abundantly. When distributing the items, one should recite the ritual procedures during the funeral rites.
[The Venerable] requests the performance of the Buddha-service (butsuji).
The Office of Administration shall inspect the previous list and arrange the Buddha-service in due order, preparing the cloth coverings, incense burner, candles, and incense box.

The *kanna* (ritual leader), accompanied by an attendant, shall proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*hōjō*) to request the Master to perform the rite. [The attendant] shall insert incense and announce: "I, [Name], [the Dharma Master], having passed away [X days/years] ago..."
On the day of the cremation, request the Abbot to hold the torch. The invitations for the various quarters shall be identical.

Furthermore, notify the two classes of officials to assemble at the Hall Office (*dangsi*) to conduct a census of the deceased monk’s effects. One must invite the senior monks (*qijiu*) to gather and present the sealed casket containing the belongings;

these are then arranged upon the mats. The attendant of the Hall Office shall present each item individually before the eyes of the public officials, and together they shall calculate the total value.
When a guest ascends, the attendant shall post their name—using characters such as "Tian" (Heaven), "Di" (Earth), "Xuan" (Mysterious), or "Huang" (Yellow)—on the single row of racks.
If the garment is half-new, it is labeled "Old"; if half-old, it is labeled "Tattered. The value must be appraised secretly so that the crowd does not hear it.

Books, Buddha images, sutra scrolls, and playthings are for the purpose of establishing karmic connections; they are drawn by lot and moved about. As for miscellaneous items, those required for communal boundaries, quarters, or deficiencies in use are recorded upon the ledger.

At the time of the formal handover (*jiāo*), the patient’s junior attendant or any capable person with the strength of mind and body should labor diligently (there will be a list of items and refreshments).
[The family] shall chant scriptures and perform the sacrificial offering.
When the funeral procession arrives at the hall tonight, the *xingxing* (attendant) of the Hall Office shall report to the Abbot and the Head Seat to post the notification boards;

he shall also notify all the various quarters in advance. The Storehouse Office shall prepare the sacrificial food. The Storehouse Office shall dispatch personnel to set up the sacrificial tables. When local guests or Dharma relatives arrive at the Storehouse Office, they shall pay money for the return-sacrifice, and a memorial text shall be composed.
Each person shall prepare a small piece of incense. This applies even if the West Hall or a senior *qishi* (venerable elder) is present.
Regarding the ritual offerings made by the two classes of attendants at the former abbot’s quarters: the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) shall proclaim the liturgy.

At evening, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community before the reliquary (*kaṅ*). The *karmadāna* first offers food, tea, and soup; once this is finished, the Abbot burns incense. (According to the Chan Regulations:

the *vinaya-dhara* steps forward from the ranks to burn one stick of incense, then requests the person who will lock the reliquary to step forward from their position to burn one stick of incense. He then bows in respect to the right side, proceeds to bow before the Abbot, and thereafter the *karmadānas* proceed in order until the end of the row, followed by the monks of the western class until the end of the row.)

The assembly exchanges general greetings and enters the shrine from the end of the western order, standing to the right. The hall attendant (táng-sī xíng-zhě) prepares the incense and locks the shrine, performing the ritual service; once the attendant has locked the shrine, they return to their original position.

If the incumbent is present, he enters from his own position in the assembly to perform the service. The rector (wéi-ná) recites the sutra and performs the dedication of merit. The abbot stands before the chief administrative official (zhí-shì shàng-shǒu), while the person offering the sacrifice stands to the right.

They exit to offer incense and exchange greetings, then enter the shrine from the end of the western order. After the tea and water offerings have been presented by the attendants, they exit and insert the incense sticks before the burner.

After the incense has been extinguished, the presiding officer inquires after the health [of the deceased] and performs prostrations to the right of the shrine. Once the recitation of the ritual text is completed, the scripture is lifted for the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).
Next, the head of the assembly leads the group in chanting the scripture; the monks of the monastery chant the scripture, while the lay associates of the deceased chant the scripture alongside them.

On the day of the funeral, prior to the departure of the coffin, the Supervising Official (Jianzuo) is instructed to prepare the cremation wood and the accompanying funeral pyre branches. He shall also allocate manpower to carry the shrine (kan), hold the banners and canopies, and arrange the incense tables, drums, music, and all other funeral rites so that they are fully prepared.
On the eve of the funeral, he shall cover the Dharma Hall and post notices for the two classes of attendants to inform all parties.

**The Funeral Procession (Chan Rules)** In the Zhudang, the official strikes the mallet and announces: "After the morning gruel, upon hearing the bell, all shall assemble for the funeral procession, with the exception of those on duty in their quarters; everyone else shall rise together. This is respectfully announced. Once the morning gruel has ended, the funeral rites are prepared.
An attendant of the Hall Office strikes the gong to signal the striking of the bell before the Sangha Hall to gather the assembly.

They proceed to the front of the shrine where the Venerable Director of Rituals recites the liturgy (the form is shown below). When the ritual for raising the shrine is completed, the hand-bell is struck, and the shrine is carried out to the head of the mountain gate.
When the offerings of hot water, tea, and refreshments have been placed before the face of the shrine, the Head Seat (Śraddhācārya) leads the assembly, standing in two rows facing inward.
The Rector (Karmadāna) stands beneath the canopy facing inward with palms joined. He intones the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-mantra* or the names of the Four Holy Ones of the West.

As the Head Seat leads the assembly in reciting the mantra, the pallbearers line up facing the shrine, palms joined and heads bowed, waiting for the formal salutation; once the monks have all passed by, they follow behind.
The Head Monk (*duwei*) and Attendant (*shizhe*) escort the deceased; the Ritual Master (*weina*) follows the coffin.
Chapter on Cremation:

When the remains arrive at the Nirvana Platform, the Abbot offers incense, the administrative officers (*zhishi*) offer hot water and tea, and the Ritual Master offers incense and requests the Abbot to lead the assembly.
The torch-bearer stands holding the torch while burning incense and bows to the assembly. He steps forward and stands; an attendant holds an umbrella.

The *zhizai* (administrative head) performs an inquiry. The torch is passed to the torch-bearer. Once the torch-bearing is complete, the *weina* (rector) performs the "Mountain Peak" ritual service (*shan-tou fo-shi*). The senior administrative official (*shang-shou zhi-shi*) serves tea and offers incense.

The guest master recites the *Lengyan Zhou* (Śūraṅgama Mantra) for the dedication of merit. The lay associates (*xiang-ren*) recite the sutra and offer greetings to the elders. The lay associates accompany one another.

The *huawang* (funeral director) and the *weina* (monastic administrator) go back and forth to inspect; the attendants of the Hall Office escort the deceased’s remains, collect the bones, and welcome them back to the original hall for offerings, where they recite sutras for three days.
Regarding the Chanting for Robes (*cai yi*):

according to the ancient rules of the monastic forest (*conglin*), the chanting for robes takes place on the day after the bones have been returned to the temple. Lately, however, the chanting for robes is held on the same day as the funeral rites, and the deceased's belongings are collected while their remains are being gathered.

Who can witness such a practice? It is fitting that this be carefully examined. As for the chanting for robes following the conclusion of the midday meal, it is the duty of the hall attendants (*tangsi xingzhe*).
After the morning gruel is finished, the two attendants of the Abbot’s quarters cover the robe-signboard and announce it to all the monastic quarters.
The attendants then arrange a corded bed-platform in front of the Sangha Hall. The Abbot and the Head Seat take their seats on opposite sides, facing each other.

Inside the door, a long mat is laid crosswise, upon which brushes, inkstones, and counting-slips are set out. Mats are spread upon the floor, and laborers from the various quarters are assigned to carry the robe-caskets and arrange the seating.

The Hall Attendant (Shangtang) reports to the Abbot’s quarters; the two classes of *vinaya* masters (*weina*) and the attendants (*shizhe*) ring the bell before the Sangha Hall to assemble the community.
The *vinaya* master, the guest prefect (*zhike*), and the attendants enter the hall together with the assembly, perform a formal greeting (*wensun*), and take their seats.

The attendants stand in a single file to perform a greeting, then carry the incense casket (*langlong*) forward to present it before the two classes of officials. After the seals have been inspected, they remove the lock, open the casket, and return it to the hall.
The attendant takes the robes and belongings out and arranges them on the seats according to their labels. The empty baskets are opened and placed on the ground.

The *weina* strikes the *qing* and recites (the ritual form is shown below). Upon completion, he says: "As for the method of chanting for the distribution of robes, it follows established regulations;

one should take care of the new and old, the long and short. Money must be used as common currency and shall not be mixed with worn-out or damaged coins. After the sound of the *qing* ceases, [no further discussion is permitted]."

[The officiant] expresses regret and respectfully announces: Holding up the ordination certificate (*duòdié*), he says: "One ordination certificate for the deceased monk is now torn before the assembly and submitted to the authorities.
He makes three horizontal cuts across the place where the name was written, passes his finger through the perforation to show the assembly, strikes the *qing* once, and says:
"The tearing is finished. In order, according to the number, the robes are presented; the *weina* (chant master) takes up the robe and announces: "Heaven..."

When the name is called once for one set of alms bowls, the chant is "Five hundred wen. The attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi Xingzhe) receives it accordingly, chanting from "five hundred" up to "one guan," and from "one guan" up to "ten guan" as the rule.
Once the price has been called in sequence and the chime is struck, the attendant chants the determined name and reports it to the Guest Master (Kezhi), who registers it on the guest list.
The Attendant (Shizhe) then matches the list to issue the robes and requisites, and the relevant number of cash notes is written out and affixed.

The Hall Steward (Tangkusī) shall deliver the inventory list (*piāo*) to the person chanting for the distribution of robes (*chàngyī rén*). The robes are placed in a basket, and the inventory list is exchanged for the robes; no refunds or reductions are permitted.

Once the chanting is finished and the merit has been dedicated, the assembly disperses. The Head Seat (*zhǒuzuò*) signs off on the list, the Rector (*wéinà*) collects the inventory list, and the Attendant for Robes (*yìshì zhě*) takes charge of the robes.
The inventory list must be returned within three days; those who fail to do so shall be reported and urged until the full amount is recovered. Upon completion, the record is established.

The distribution of funds for various scriptures shall be determined according to the three-tiered ledger system as the standard format. All fields, lands, gold, and grain belonging to the senior monks shall be returned to the permanent property (*sāṃghika-vastu*).
Long-standing debts shall be liquidated according to circumstances; when collecting on new debts, the permanent property shall take a commission:

ten *kuan* from every hundred *kuan*, with no commission taken if the amount is less than one hundred *kuan*. The two classes of officials and all the monastic quarters shall submit detailed lists and distribute [the funds] accordingly.

Regarding the funds for the communal recitation (jingqian): even if only half a coin arrives temporarily, it must not be withheld from the deceased; this is not to be included in the formal accounting ledger.

The funds for the communal recitation shall be two hundred cash, while the funds for the Buddhist service (foshi) shall be one string (one thousand cash). The funds for the abbot’s Buddhist service shall be double that amount.

As for the portion deducted by the Hall Administration (tangsi) attendants, it shall be based on a standard of three parts per string of the communal recitation funds for the assembly of monks. It is not permitted to arbitrarily establish charges for construction or other such purposes.
Regarding the matter of the head monk’s name being struck from the register and the resulting dispute, the Abbot personally took charge of the affair.

Once the funeral rites for the deceased were completed and the memorial tablets had been inscribed, the attendant of the Hall Office presented the document to the Abbot; it was then signed by both classes of officials, either after the morning gruel or the midday meal.
Before the Sangha Hall, spread out the seating charts and prepare brushes, inkstones, and counting sticks, instructing the assembly to review them and correct any errors.
Once the charts are finalized, the Hall Attendant (Dangsi) and the Ritual Attendant (Haengja) report this to the Abbot’s quarters; the two ranks of officials post a notice to inform the assembly.

Ash is prepared, incense and lamps are readied, and the ritual master strikes the bell before the Sangha Hall. When the assembly has gathered at the site for the bone-relics ceremony, the administrative officers burn incense, and the Abbot offers a lighted stick.

The Incense Venerable (xiāng wéinà) requests the rite for raising the remains (qǐgǔ fóshì), which is the same as the funeral procession; this is announced in advance to the stupa site. Incense and brooms are prepared, and the remains are brought to the stupa.
The administrative officer (zhīshì) offers incense and tea, while the Abbot (zhǔchí) burns incense. The Incense Venerable requests the rite for entering the stupa (rùtǎ fóshì).
The scripture is recited for the dedication of merit (huíxiàng); laypeople may also recite the scripture for the dedication of merit (the recitation of mantras is not mandatory).

On the Posthumous Affairs of Deceased Monks: Since one exists within heaven and earth, who can escape death? Regarding the abundance or frugality of robes and bowls, the funeral rites should accord with established regulations, and all Buddhist services must be performed. Frugal conduct creates the conditions for merit and is a source of beauty; thus, the three grades of memorial tablets shall be made a permanent rule for all. *Li: On the Posthumous Affairs of Deceased Monks* Indeed, as long as one has a body within heaven and earth, who can avoid death?

As for the abundance or frugality of robes and alms-bowls, the rites for sending off the deceased should conform to the rules, and all Buddhist ceremonies must be carried out. Frugality creates the conditions for karmic connection and results in excellence; therefore, the three grades of memorial tablets shall be established as a permanent standard for all.

The oral instructions for deceased monks, as well as their robes and bedding, shall be retained by the Hall Office for handover; the *xiuqi* (seven-day or five-seven day memorial services) shall be held in advance.

Sutra lists shall be issued for all quarters, and prefaces (*shu*) shall be prepared. Whether a ritual seat is established or the rite is performed at the head of the wooden mallet, the repentance rites must be solemnly conducted to honor the deceased’s karmic retribution, for the efficacy of such merit is no small matter.
Within the public community, it is improper to treat these matters with negligence or contempt. Baizhang founded the monastic groves (*conglin*) of the Chan school for the sake of the aged.
How should one regard a sick person? First, the Ritual for Recitation:
The Buddha-body of healing pervades the Dharma-realm. (At the conclusion of the four-line verse: Praise the Triple Gem and respectfully invoke them.
To certify that at this present hour, there is a sick bhikṣu (so-and-so) who, wishing to release the enmities of many lifetimes and repent for the transgressions of accumulated kalpas,
has specially mobilized his sincere resolve to assemble the pure assembly (to perform repentance or recite scriptures). By means of these gathered merits, he offers prayers to the divine spirits,
beseeching that [the person concerned] may attain single-minded purity, physical ease and tranquility, and long life together with wisdom.

May their life-span be extended and both the physical body and the Dharma-body be made firm; once again, I ask the assembly to recite [the verse beginning with] "The ten directions and three periods of time... etc.

If the illness is grave, we humbly pray that as long as their karmic conditions are not yet exhausted, they may soon attain ease; if their great life-force cannot escape its end, may they be reborn directly [in the Pure Land].
May the Great Virtuous One again deign to turn his thoughts toward the Peaceful Nurturing Land (the ten directions and three periods of time, etc.).

At the first watch of the night, as life and death alternate and cold and heat shift in succession—wherein its coming is like lightning flashing across the vast sky and its passing is like waves settling upon the great ocean—on this day, there has been a new one who has entered perfect nirvana: the Vinaya Master [Name].

The conditions having been exhausted, his great life has suddenly passed away; realizing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and that nirvana is bliss, we respectfully assemble the great multitude to solemnly proceed to the funerary shrine.
We recite the sublime names of the various holy ones to dedicate this pure spirit to the Pure Land.
We rely upon the assembly to recite [the Ten Buddha Names of the Pure Dharma Body]. Having finished the recitation, the scripture is now concluded. Thus ends the foregoing recitation.

In commemoration of the meritorious recitation of the sutras for the newly deceased (Name) Vinaya Master, we pray that his spirit may transcend to the Pure Realm and his karma be extinguished from the toil of the mundane world;

that he may bloom with the flowers of the highest grade and receive from the Buddha the prophecy of one more birth before Buddhahood. We again entreat the great assembly to recite [the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, etc.].
Raising the Shrine: As we prepare to lift the sacred shrine for the grand ceremony of cremation, we rely upon the venerable assembly to recite the great names of the various sages.
This serves to express our grief at parting and to provide spiritual sustenance for the path to awakening. [Recite the Ten Epithets of the Pure Dharma Body, then proceed.]
On this day of cremation for the newly deceased Vinaya Master [Name], who has passed away in accordance with conditions, we now perform the cremation according to the Dharma.
We burn the body that spent a hundred years propagating the Way, entering the path of the single road of Nirvana. We look up in reverence...
Relying upon the support of the venerable assembly for the awakening of the spirit:
*Namu* to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One (Chorus). (Recite ten times.

Having thus extolled the holy name to assist in rebirth, we pray that the mirror of wisdom may radiate its brilliance and the true wind may scatter its colors, so that awakening may blossom within the Garden of Bodhi.

Within the ocean of the Dharma-nature of the mind’s flowers, I wash away the defilements of the dusty heart. With three offerings of tea and one incense burner burning, I respectfully escort you upon your journey through the clouds.
Homage to the assembly of Noble Ones! Having completed the recitation of the sutra (the "Liao" verse says):
"The merit of this recitation and chanting of the sutra is dedicated for the sake of the newly deceased [Name] Vinaya Master, to adorn his retribution body at the time of cremation."
[The earth] (the ten directions, etc.).
○ Chanting the distribution of robes: like drifting clouds dispersing so that no shadow remains, and like a waning candle whose light naturally extinguishes;

now this chanting is performed to manifest impermanence. We rely upon the Great Assembly to recite [the ten titles of the Pure Dharma Body]. (After the ten titles of the Pure Dharma Body are finished), chant.

Having finished the distribution of robes, recite: "The merit of the chanting and recitation above is dedicated for [Name] the Vinaya Master to adorn the ground of retribution" (and so forth for the ten directions).

For large-scale accounting ledgers (*banzhàng*), the standard format shall be set at one thousand or two thousand *kuan*. Lands, gold, and grain belonging to the elders (*qijiu*) shall be returned to the permanent endowment (*changzhu*).

Proceeds from the auction of robes (*changyi*) shall not be subject to a deduction; apart from those items accounted for in the ledger according to the standard, the funds for the distribution to the monastic community, the funds for scriptural recitations, and the funds for Buddhist services shall be distributed as follows:

the head officiant (*toushou*) presiding over the recitation of scriptures shall receive twenty *kuan* as the standard for the primary offering (*zhengchōn*). If the total amount reaches three thousand or five thousand *kuan*, the same principle shall apply.
The above amounts shall be increased to assist the *kankan* (relic-shrine) office and the *dianzuo* (steward) in providing offerings; the remainder must not be misappropriated.

For every ten *guan* withdrawn from the distribution, one *guan* shall be added to the funds for Buddhist services (*foshi*), and two *guan* shall be added to the funds for the shrine, with one *guan* being added to the former.

For medium-scale accounts of four hundred or five hundred *guan*, the withdrawal for distribution among the assembly shall follow the same procedure as for the Buddhist services. For small-scale accounts of two hundred [units], [the same applies].

For those whose funeral expenses amount to one hundred, twenty, or even ten strings of cash, excluding the costs for the coffin, the bier, and miscellaneous expenditures, all matters concerning the establishment of karmic connections shall be presided over by the Abbot and the Head Seat, prepared by the administrative office (Kusi), and supported with compassion by the assembly.
They must see the deceased through the funeral rites with full courtesy; for who among us is exempt from death?
