*Rules for Monastic Affairs in the Garden of Vinaya*, Scroll Fourteen, Compiled and Narrated by the Bhikṣu Xingwu, Successor of the Patriarchs and Abbot of Mingyan Zhonglusi. Section:
Prohibitions on Visiting and Viewing.
When the visiting monks arrive at the Abbot’s quarters after the morning gruel and before the formal sitting, they proceed to the Attendants’ Office (*shisi*).
The attendant receives them, offers them seats, and serves tea and soup. They briefly recount their reasons for coming and then rise. Before the incense burner, they thank him for the tea and report:

"We, [Name] and others, have come at this time to pay our respects to the Master; we trouble the High Attendant to announce us. The attendant replies: "Please sit a moment," and then inquires in detail about their origins.

When meeting with former associates of the Abbot, or those who are Dharma relatives or fellow countrymen coming on business (after sitting for a short while and allowing [the guest] to announce himself), one should immediately inform the Abbot.

Whether it be an official guest or if there is some urgency, one must receive them promptly; otherwise, they may be received at a slightly later time. The Attendant shall prepare incense, hold a candle, and prepare tea, then report the arrival of the newcomer.
The Abbot shall emerge from the *shentang* (sleeping hall), and the Attendant shall lead the guest forward to meet him before the incense burner. The Abbot proceeds forward... [newcomer].

Upon arrival, [the guest] says, "Please, Venerable, sit in the lotus posture. If the host declines, the guest offers incense and spreads his sitting mat (*zaju*). If the host declines again, the guest exchanges greetings regarding health and well-being (as detailed in the ritual manuals).
Once seated, the attendant burns incense and serves tea; they engage in conversation and then rise.

At the brazier, the guest thanks the host for the tea, escorts him to the guest seat, returns the incense, and performs the formal bows. This constitutes the complete etiquette between host and guest; it is also necessary to spread the sitting mat so that both may show mutual respect.

When respectfully visiting the administrative office (shì-sī) to offer thanks, one says: "I have recently troubled your divine efforts; I come specifically to express my gratitude. The official replies:

"In accordance with the rites of the moment, why do you trouble yourself to honor me with such a visit? One then returns to one's lodgings. The guest-master (kètóu) is requested to provide a half-meal and refreshments.

Before the morning assembly (cān), tea is served; after the tea, medicinal food (yàoshí) is provided. At dawn, after the morning gruel (zhōuzháo) is finished, one is invited to offer tea. On another day, a formal meal is arranged.
Regarding the ancient protocols for hosting guests and receiving the incense offering, these must not be neglected.
Lately, when brothers from various quarters arrive on business, traveling and sightseeing and lodging wherever they may be, the abbot should also deign to visit them to fulfill his duty as host.
Recently, the West Hall Head Seat (Xitáng Shǒuzuò) of Dàfāng, a person of great virtue and renown, arrived for temporary lodging.
While discussing his intention to remain as a permanent resident, he revealed his meaning. The Abbot (Zhùzhí) earnestly urged him to stay.

The following day, after the tea ceremony was concluded, [the Head Seat] submitted this request: "I have not yet clarified the teachings and contemplations; I have come specifically to rely upon the Venerable Master for shelter."

[May you kindly accept this request. The Abbot replies: "If you do not reject me, we shall be able to maintain this together. On another day, or immediately following, a tea service is held for the two classes of officials.
The Abbot rises personally to burn a single stick of incense, then returns to his original position and stands, saying:
"The West Hall Head Seat from [Place Name] has not abandoned us and has come here to maintain our solitude together; I trouble the two classes of officials to escort him back. They then see him off.
The person who has come to offer their residence steps forward and says: "I have come specifically to seek refuge; I am deeply grateful for your compassionate acceptance.

The Abbot and the two classes of officials escort them back to the quarters. The Abbot occupies the seat of honor and says: "On this day, I respectfully wish that the Head Monk (Dharmasvāmin) may enjoy abundant blessings in his daily life.
It is a great fortune from past lives to look up to you and be accepted under your care. The Abbot then says: "The mountain gate [is fortunate]..."

"Fortunate to share this tranquil seclusion. [The guest] escorts the abbot out to see him off; the host bows to the attendants as they enter to offer congratulations, escorts them out, and bows to the two classes of officials (the *sangha* and the laity) as they enter to offer congratulations and are escorted out.
Immediately, [the guest] carries incense and proceeds to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*) to thank him for the bedding.

The Hall Attendant and the Treasury Assistant lead him to the Treasury Office (*kusī*), where he pays his respects to the various heads of departments (*śreṣṭhin*), the elders (*vṛddha*), and the various quarters. Tea is served in each instance, and the procedure is identical throughout.
Regarding the old precedents for the reception of visiting monks (*guādá*) from various regions who seek lodging to pay their respects:

after the tea ceremony has concluded, one should report, saying: "The guest quarters of [Name] Temple have long been closed. (1) *Jiùlì* (Old Precedents). One. Various renowned and excellent temples. Reception of visiting monks. When those seeking lodging arrive, after the tea ceremony is finished, they should report, saying: "[Name] Temple’s guest quarters have long been closed by custom..."
[The petitioner] says: "My contemplation is not yet clear; I have come specifically to seek refuge with the Venerable Master. I humbly hope that you will accept me. The Abbot replies:
"I am deeply grateful for your not being discarded; let us together gather in this silence. He then invites the Head Seat, the Chief Administrator, and the Rector to drink tea.

The Abbot rises personally to burn a single stick of incense and, as before, articulates his intent to convey his meaning. The recipient steps forward and says: "We, [Name] and others, have once again been graced by the Venerable Master’s acceptance."

The recorder shall then follow the assembly to hear the *jingce* (exhortation). The response is: "The monastery officials should extend an invitation to escort you. He is then escorted back to his quarters.
The abbot, residing as the presiding lecturer, sees him out the door and receives the attendant’s congratulations.

After the two classes of officials have performed their greetings, the person being escorted carries incense and proceeds to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*) to thank him for the bedding arrangement. A novice from the Hall Administration (*tangsi*) leads the way.
This concludes the matters regarding the various administrative offices and quarters.
Regarding the procedures for a Dharma relative arriving to register as a resident:

once they have arrived and before they have formally entered the hall, they should first visit the attendant (shizhe) and explain their background in detail, requesting that he report this to the abbot for an interview, during which they shall offer incense.

When performing the rites, if they are dharma-relatives such as younger brothers or nephews who have previously served [the deceased], they shall all receive the bow, the incense, the offering of tea, and the return-bow at the guest seat;
or they may be sent to the refectory, where the proceedings for the rising of the rite are the same as before.
When newly arrived monks first register at a Vinaya monastery, they should stay briefly for now.
Upon their arrival, the newly arrived brothers report first to the Guest Office (*keshi*). An experienced member of the monastic community is appointed as the leader (*chantou*) to head the group.
They assume a formal posture and stand to the right of the gate, saying: "We have come temporarily to pay our respects. The Guest Master (*zhike*) shall then receive them.
The entry into the hall says: "On this day, I respectfully wish that the Venerable Preceptor, the Guest Master, may enjoy abundant blessings in your daily life.
Having long admired your reputation for the Way, I am now honored to have the opportunity to behold you; my humble feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. The response says:

"The mountain gate is fortunate to receive your visit from so far away. He bows and takes his seat. Incense is burned and tea is served. He inquires about the guest's background, whereupon he rises to thank him for the tea. (If there is no such formal exchange, he simply remains seated.)
Upon arriving at their lodgings, they shall rest in the guest office (*keshi*) or by the brazier (*weilu*).
The guest master (*zhike*) shall escort them back, and the head of the assembly (*candou*) shall receive them, with everyone performing a general bow (*wenshen*). The guest master says:

"I respectfully wish that all you venerable fellow monks (*xiangzhang lushi*) are enjoying much well-being in your stay. We are deeply honored by your visit today and offer our sincere thanks; we are moved beyond words."
The reply says: "It is fitting to pay respects; how could you trouble yourself to descend so far to honor us? The head of the assembly personally escorts them out the door.
Next, they go to the attendant’s office (*shisō*) to meet and perform the rites as before. Standing there, he reports: "We have come specifically to pay our respects to the Abbot;

we venture to trouble the attendant to announce this. The attendant inquires about their background and reports it to the Abbot. If permission is granted, he informs them that they may have an audience, either immediately or at a later time.
After the congee ceremony, the abbot’s quarters and the meditation hall are connected; the head of the assembly (sanzhu) steps forward and requests him to sit cross-legged.
He turns, places incense in his hands, withdraws, and together with the assembly performs three prostrations. They take their seats. The attendant burns incense, and there is tea;

the etiquette for thanking for the tea is identical to that of the previous "mutual inspection" (xiangkan), though the wording differs slightly. The abbot escorts the head of the assembly out, saying, "The Master is most honorable," and they proceed together to the attendant's quarters.

The attendant offers thanks, saying: "We have troubled you with our service; we hereby prostrate ourselves to express our gratitude. They return to their quarters and stand in a single file outside the door, waiting for the abbot to return the courtesy.
When he returns the greeting, they bow together and lead him inside, saying: "We humbly wish that the Abbot, our Head of the Hall, has been well during this interval and enjoys much prosperity.
Our previous visit was not intended as a formal prostration, yet we were honored by your gracious descent to receive us; we are deeply moved by your kindness."

[The Head of the Monastery] says: "I am deeply grateful for your visit. As it is inconvenient for you to stay here, I hope you will be patient with me. The assembly escorts the head of the visiting group out; he then turns toward the upper hand, bows to the attendant, enters, and together with the assembly, performs a formal greeting, saying: "It has been some time since we last met. I trust that the Reverend High Attendant Dharma Master is enjoying good health and abundant blessings. It was my duty to come to your quarters to pay my respects, yet I have instead troubled you by descending to meet me; I am deeply moved by your courtesy. The attendant replies: "Please do not be concerned. The visitor then returns to his seat. The assembly follows suit and takes their seats. The attendant rises and bows once more. The visitor rises and bows in return. The attendant then leads the way back to the abbot’s quarters. The assembly follows. Upon entering, they perform a formal greeting. The attendant says: "We have just returned from the abbot’s quarters. We trust the Reverend High Attendant Dharma Master is well. [The Abbot says: "The Mountain Gate is most fortunate to have been graced by your visit from afar. We apologize for the delay in our expressions of gratitude and feel deeply humbled.
[The guest replies: "A light snack at midday and a special soup served this evening; please take your seats. A *yàoshí* (medicinal food) attendant burns a stick of *yàoshí* incense.

Alternatively, the head officers may accompany the meal. After the meal, the abbot escorts the guest out. On the following day, after the morning congee, he invites the guest for tea. During the tea ceremony, the guest offers thanks for the tea. Etc.
The ritual procedures are all as usual. After the tea, the newly arrived monk goes to the Attendant’s Office and requests the Attendant to report to the Abbot that he wishes to return to the Hall.
Once permission has been granted, the Attendant issues a notice for the Hall Office, and tea is immediately served.
The Rector receives the guest, burns incense, and after the tea is finished, reports: "We, [Name] and others, have received the Master’s command to attend upon the left and right."

"I humbly hope you will grant me your consideration. The response is: "It is a great fortune for this mountain gate that we may gather here in this secluded place. The *duòdié* (ordination certificate) is taken and given to the *wéinà* (rector).
Once the *jièlà bù* (register of ordination seniority) has been updated, the *wéinà* returns the *duòdié* to the head of the assembly (*cāntóu*), who receives it.

The *wéinà* then goes together with the newcomers to their assigned quarters to offer greetings. The guest says: "It is a great fortune to have come here, and I am deeply honored by your warm hospitality; my humble heart is overwhelmed with gratitude."

[Expressing] the utmost gratitude, he replies: "The quarters are inconvenient; I beg you to grant me a more spacious place. The head of the assembly (sanchō) escorts the rector (wina) out to exchange greetings and then disperses.
Next, the attendant of the Hall Office (dōshi gyōja) writes the notice header and hands the incense money to the attendant-in-charge (shijō).

The attendant-in-charge returns the incense, whether it be a single large piece or several smaller pieces, to the attendant, who then gives it to the head of the assembly. Finally, he reports that the hanging of the notice has been completed.
On the day designated for the *shūmon jōjō* (the formal presentation of the inquiry), the incense table, burner, and candles are solemnly set out in the *shindō* (sleeping hall).

The *sanzu* (lead practitioners) lead the assembly in a formal line; three persons form one group, with one person acting as the *shō-sanzu* (junior lead practitioner) who carefully records the words and the ritual gestures of advancing and retreating.
These must be practiced together in advance so that they may be performed fluently when the time comes. At that time, the *shidoshi* (attendant) joins the *sanzu*.
The *tōnyū* (head of the assembly) enters and invites the Abbot to emerge from his quarters and stand at the temple’s central position.

The *sanyū* (assembly leader) returns to his place, and after the entire assembly has performed a mutual greeting (*monjun*), he steps forward and says, "Please, Venerable Master, sit in the lotus posture" (*jūsoku*). He turns from the incense burner back to his own position, performs a mutual greeting with the assembly, and [does so] again.

He steps before the incense burner, takes incense from his robe, inserts it into his left hand, and returns to his position. The three individuals led by him perform a mutual greeting together and then unfold their sitting cloths (*shakuju*).
After three prostrations, the head participant steps forward and says: "On this day... [insert name] and the others have been fortunate throughout our past lives to receive your guidance and shelter;
our hearts are filled with the utmost honor and joy. They all perform a single inquiry and pass to the right, waiting until the end of the line.
Then, in groups of three, they advance and perform the ritual speech as before. Once each person has completed their individual prostrations, they all perform a collective inquiry and withdraw.

(Next, proceed to the attendant’s office, the head seat’s quarters, the treasury office, and the various monastic lodgings; after completing the formal greetings along the corridors, return to the assembly hall to await the return greeting).
Format for the Announcement Board: (Respectfully following the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, two monks [Name] and [Name] are being enrolled as attendants.
Attendant [Name], Vinaya Master, on the [Day] of this month, reports from the Attendants’ Office.)
○ Small Notice for Incense (The Head Seat’s name for admission is listed; he shall lead in the collection of one hundred coins to purchase incense.
The attendant of the Hall Office [Name] reports this.
○ Format for a Memorial to the Abbot’s Quarters (Fangzhang)
(Young bhikṣu so-and-so of such-and-such temple in such-and-such prefecture on such-and-such road) (The above,
so-and-so respectfully approaches) (the presence of the Master [with sleeves folded]).
(Prostrations) (The Grand Abbot of So-and-so Temple respectfully awaits) (Your Compassionate Instructions).
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], [Name], a minor bhikṣu of [Temple Name] in [Road Name],
respectfully submits this petition:

Regarding the formal return of greetings from the Abbot upon the completion of the registration ceremony (*guādá*), the newly registered person’s *rèngshǒu* (host) shall lead the assembly to a single location for the purpose of returning greetings to the Abbot.
Outside the hall, the attendants stand in a row on the lower side, waiting to escort the Abbot into the refectory. Upon arrival, they inquire after his well-being, saying:

"We respectfully wish that the Venerable Abbot has been in good health for some time and is enjoying much merit. It was fitting that we should pay our respects, yet we have instead received your gracious visit; we are overwhelmed with gratitude.
The assembly escorts the Abbot out and follows him into the refectory, where they turn to the upper side and stand. The head of the assembly (the *candana*) then receives and attends to him.

The petitioner enters and says: "We, [Name et al.], having been permitted to rely upon your presence, now receive this mark of your profound favor; our humble hearts are filled with the utmost gratitude.

The response is: "I thank you for your visit; my humble heart is filled with the utmost gratitude. The *santō* (head of the petitioners) escorts them out. The two ranks of monks enter, and the words of their petition are the same as before.
When this is concluded, the group of newly enrolled monks turns down to the lower section, with the *fusan* (deputy head) at the head.
The head of the assembly (sanchou) bows in greeting and the assembly disperses.
Upon returning, he thanks those who have been granted formal registration (guada).

The attendant (shizhe) prepares tea according to the seniority of the precepts (jielao). Those who have completed their registration are addressed by their full names (e.g., "Master So-and-so"), while the guest prefect (fangzhang ke) is addressed by his courtesy title.

The head monk goes to each [monk] to invite them, saying: "This morning, after the midday meal, the Abbot has requested that you attend the Tea Ceremony specifically for this occasion in the Quarters Hall.

If there are West Hall or Head Seat monks, they are also written in according to the order of their precepts. Next, the guest master is ordered to have them stand in line to invite the Head Seat to serve as the guest of honor.
If there are eminent West Hall or Head Seat monks, they take seats opposite the Abbot, with the Senior Attendant (Sanchou) next.
One must yield to one another and avoid clamor or noise that would constitute a breach of decorum. Once the meal is finished, the drum is struck to assemble the assembly.

Incense is burned, and the attendant bows to invite the Abbot to enter. The Abbot receives him with greetings of welcome. Next, the attendants of the guest are received, and they exchange inquiries after their health in the usual manner.

Tea is served to all according to the seating chart; each enters their assigned position as indicated on the chart. Having pre-announced this to the Abbot, the two attendants wait for his confirmation before performing the formal rites.

This is identical to the ritual for the small session of tea at the commencement of the retreat (in the *Changuī*, the tea invitations are written out with each person signing their name according to the command). If following the standard *Changuī* procedure, on the following day, the storehouse office (*kūsī*) serves the tea for the newly enrolled monks;

seats are arranged in the storehouse office, and once the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and his attendants have all taken their places, the head official (*zhishi*) strikes the board in front of the storehouse hall, and he and the members of his class perform the same rites as before.
Furthermore, on the next day, the hall office (*tángsī*) serves the tea for the newly enrolled monks.

When the Head Administrative Officer (Chashangshou) presides over the tea ceremony, he accompanies the abbot to the front of the monks' quarters (Mingliao) where the board is struck; a group of four or six officers stands in formation and performs a formal greeting.
If the Guest Master (Zhike) presides, after the incense has been offered and the seats have been arranged, the tea service proceeds for three days.

This is the ancient method. For tea served by the Abbot, the drum is struck; for tea served by the administrative officers or head teachers, the board is struck—each acting as both host and guest in turn.

When the abbot serves tea, the assembly rises to express their thanks; the administrative officers (*zhishi*) and head monks (*tou-shou*) also rise, while only the head of the retreat (*can-tou*) leaves his seat to thank him.
This ritual should likewise be observed.
[The King] enters the hall.
When newly ordained monks (xin guādá) wish to enter the hall for the first time, they should visit the Hall Office (táng-sī) on the evening of the day before.

They must invite the *weina* to the Abbot’s quarters (*fāngwǎng*) to request the Master’s presence, saying: "Brothers who have newly been admitted wish to enter the hall tomorrow morning; we humbly pray that the Venerable Master will compassionately deign to descend.
Having made this request, they return to the hall. On the following morning at the morning gruel, these brothers shall all spread their bowls outside the hall for a brief period.

When the morning gruel is nearly finished, it is left on the meditation platform, and one person is pre-selected to serve as the *sanchou* (head of the assembly). One waits for the gruel to be served throughout the inner hall;

once the attendant has exited the hall, the *sanchou* leads the assembly through the front gate into the hall. First, they step with the left foot; they stand in a line in front of the Holy Monk (*shengseng*).

The *sanchou* burns incense and returns to his position, where he performs three full prostrations (*dazhan sanbai*) with the assembly. After putting away their ritual implements and performing a formal greeting (*wenxun*), the *sanchou* is the first to depart.

The abbot stands in the front row; everyone bows in unison to inquire after his well-being, then lowers their heads and joins their palms while circumambulating the hall once, proceeding from the upper hall to the lower hall.
Upon exiting the outer hall, they first descend through the lower section and then the upper section.
Re-entering the hall, they stand in the central aisle to bow, then exit the hall and return to their respective bowl-positions to eat.
Form for Requesting the Relocation of the *zhāi* (Fasting Rite):
The junior bhikṣu [Name], right-hand side, now wishes to relocate the [Name] *zhāi* to the lower hall;
as he has not yet dared to act on his own authority regarding the removal and donning of robes, he respectfully submits this formal document.
Presented to the Abbot and Great Master upon whom this disciple relies for instruction: I humbly entreat your compassionate judgment to grant me the certification.
This is respectfully submitted on this [day], [month], and [year]. From the junior bhikṣu [Name], subordinate to the Dharma-preacher. Submitted.
For the use of the Hall Attendant Bhikṣu [Name]: Prepared by the Abbot on the third day of the first month. (Abbot’s Seal). [The Abbot’s Seal].
[Regarding the fact that although there is a formal meal for the Tathāgata, it is said one wishes to move the meal to a lower hall; as this has not yet received your compassionate permission:
Ring the bell. Requesting instruction and paying respects to the Master.

To request instruction by expressing one's sincere intent, first go to the *shisi* (attendant’s office) and report the matter in detail to the *shizhe* (attendant). The *shizhe* shall consult with the *zhuchi* (abbot), saying:

"The Vinaya Master [Name] wishes to visit the *fangzhang* (abbot’s quarters) tomorrow morning to seek instruction. If this request is granted, he will come to the *shisi* after the morning gruel is finished to await you.
The attendant shall then direct that candles be lit and incense prepared at the abbot’s seat, escort the visitor in, receive his inquiries, and have him offer incense.

Spreading out one’s sitting cloth, performing nine prostrations, and withdrawing the equipment, he steps forward to inquire: “I, [Name], have long been obstructed in my mind and the path of meaning has not yet opened.

I humbly entreat the Venerable Master to compassionately provide instruction through skillful means. With a reverent bow, standing to the side, he lowers his hands and listens attentively to the Dharma teachings.
When asked about his background, he answers truthfully from beginning to end. Having finished, he steps forward to inquire once more and then withdraws. Next, he proceeds to...
The attendants offer thanks, or the head officers and West Hall monks perform the rites of requesting instruction together in the corridor.
Feng [the Abbot] opens the lecture;
opening the lecture to instruct disciples is the natural duty of a monastic community. The lecturer provides instruction without weariness, and the listeners...
If one applies oneself with single-minded resolve, what concern is there that one’s undertakings will not succeed?

On the day of the formal lecture (*kai-kō*), the attendant of the Hall Office (*tōshi gyōja*) shall announce to the Abbot after the morning gruel has been served and the second lecture concluded: "Today the Master is giving a lecture" (*kyōju wa dōkō o uchi-masu*).

Then, after the bell for descending from the hall (*gedō no kane*) has ceased, he shall strike the bell for silence (*jōshō no kane*) three times (if the Head Seat [Shuso] is giving the lecture, this occurs after the midday meal; the procedure for striking the bell for silence is the same as above). This is followed by...
Hang the plaque for the commencement of the lecture on the east and west pillars of the Dharma Hall. The Rector (Vina), the Hall Attendant, and the ritual attendants shall prepare the lecture dais.
When the meal service reaches the half-meal point, they report to the Abbot;

if the Abbot has other business, he strikes the "lecture-bell" twice (this bell is struck when welcoming or seeing off guests, during general lectures, or when escorting the deceased). If the lecture is to begin, first walk along the corridors while striking the small hand-cymbals, and then strike the Sangha Hall bell.
When the front bell rings and the assembly gathers at the Dharma Hall, one may prostrate as desired before the incense burner without regard for formal order.
When the hall bell ceases its striking, the *dagu* drum is first beaten three times; as the upper pivot turns and the signal is given, the person on duty sounds two strikes of the "leader" (*yin*).

The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) then raises the *Saptabuddha-saṃkṣipta-śikṣā-sūtra*; when it reaches the words "one should train," he sounds two more strikes of the "leader. The person on duty then [proceeds].
At dawn, taking one’s sitting mat, go to the corridor (east or west) and wait at the head of the Dharma Hall for the lecturer to arrive.

When the signal bell is struck twice, inquire after the assembly; upon hearing the signal, everyone shall lift their mats and stand up. As the signal bell rings intermittently, proceed to the incense burner in the Dharma Hall and stand to the west.
When the lecturer burns incense and performs three prostrations, before he has finished bowing, the attendant on duty strikes the signal bell twice and returns.

The lecturer bows to the assembly; the assembly all respond with a bow. Rising, they collect their implements and perform the inquiry of well-being (*praśna*). [The lecturer] ascends the seat from the east or west end.
Upon the seat, incense is burned and the introductory signal is struck twice. The lecturer and the assembly bow together, set aside their implements, and sit.

The lecturer strikes the *shichang* (ruler) three times and raises it to perform the prostration to all Buddhas (*sarva-buddha-namaskāra*), saying [the liturgy] up to "I pray for the hidden grace of the Holy One regarding the adornment of the Omniscient Wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*)."

At the conclusion of the introductory recitation, the lecturer raises the *shichang* (wooden sounding block) once and says: "Namo to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha" (three times, with the *nanshan da zhi* [Southern Mountain Great Wisdom] chant).
Then, lowering the *shichang* once, they open the scroll and begin the lecture, extending or abbreviating the discourse as appropriate. Upon finishing the lecture, they close the scroll;

the lecturer strikes the *shichang* once and says: "The aforementioned merit of listening—may it be offered to the Dharma-protecting devas and dedicated to repaying the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence."

The monastery’s true guardians protect the Teaching and bring peace to the Sangha; may all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm together perfect the All-Knowing Wisdom. [Ten Directions, Three Times...
(In the midst of the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the measure is one chi and one cun). The assembly rises; the lecturer descends from the seat and proceeds directly before the incense burner.

The attendant on duty strikes the signal bell twice. The lecturer and the assembly do not perform the mutual bowing (*wèn-xùn*), but instead disperse. (The Abbot takes the eastern path; the Head Seat takes the western path).

When the Abbot presides over a lecture on the *Sangwan* (General Lectures), those who have not yet heard it are required by principle to attend and perform the ritual of *ch'an* (visitation). If abbots from other mountains arrive, they likewise perform the ritual of *ch'an*.
Even when the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) lectures, the Abbot also performs *ch'an*, out of respect for the Dharma. This applies to all visitors coming from outside to attend the lectures.

Wait for the bell to ring, then proceed to the side of the seat in the Dharma Hall and take your place according to rank. Wait until the assembly has chanted the name of the Great Wisdom Preceptor (*Mahāprajñāvinaya-dhara*);
at that moment, rise and stand before the incense burner. The head of the assembly burns incense, then steps back and performs a mutual inquiry (*wenshen*).

He then spreads his ritual implements and performs three prostrations. If there are four or more people, they should not perform these prostrations together, as the assembly does not pay homage to individuals. If one says "Master" (*shi*), [the following applies].
Regarding prostrations, there is no fixed rule; however, if one discusses the light of humility, both parties should not receive prostrations.

For those participating in the lecture, their seats are established first at the head of the hall with their heads facing west. When it is time for the lecturer to rise, they should instruct an attendant to convey a message excusing themselves from receiving prostrations and requesting them to be seated.

After the lecturer has finished rolling up the scroll, they should compose words of thanks (either in four-character or six-character parallel prose, or in free verse, as appropriate). The lecturer then descends.
Having seated oneself before the incense burner, one briefly expresses thanks for the lecture; next, one proceeds to one's quarters carrying incense to offer further thanks.
The protocols for serving tea, soup, medicine, and prepared snacks have already been clarified as before.
The Tree: Morning Worship.
Every morning, as soon as the temple’s long wooden board sounds, the assembly leaves the various halls and enters the main hall to burn incense and perform prostrations at will.

If the number of people is very large, they may not prostrate; instead, the abbot waits until the wooden fish resonates, after which they leave the various halls and enter [the main hall] to burn incense.

The Head of Incense (Xiang Toudou) shall stand outside the hall together with the Abbot (Zhuji) to burn incense until it is nearly finished; then the Head of Incense enters the hall. The attendants (Zhuren) strike the hall board (Tangban).
The Abbot ascends the hall, and the Great Bell (Daping) is struck three times. The Rector (Weina) intones the scripture.

The Abbot burns incense, circumambulates the hall, and returns to his position on the central meditation cushion (Puantun). The ritual attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi Xingzhe) has already prepared the "Plaque for Intoning Rituals" (Juli Pai).

Place the ritual implements before the person performing the prostrations. Upon the conclusion of the sutra recitation, the person performing the prostrations recites "All with Utmost Reverence" (as in the morning liturgy).
Having completed the Three Refuges, they withdraw the implements. The Abbot recites the Amitābha Praise and chants the Buddha’s name one hundred times;

the Bodhisattvas each chant three times (the remainder follows the usual procedure). Upon reaching "The Ten Directions and Three Periods of Time" (etc.), the Rector intones the *Xiāozāi Zhòu* (Spell for Dispelling Calamities) and takes his seat.
Leading the assembly, proceed to the hall.
Announce: "To the donors:

Namo to the Buddhas of the Ten Directions" (recite the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha three times). Through the empowerment of the divine mantra, may these pure foods and drinks be universally bestowed upon beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
May all spirits and deities be fully satisfied; may they abandon their stingy minds, immediately escape the dark realms, and be reborn in the good paths.

Taking refuge in the Triple Gem, may they study Bodhicitta and ultimately attain unsurpassed enlightenment. May their boundless merit extend to the end of the future, and may all sentient beings together partake of this Dharma-food. *Mantra.*
Namo sarvatathāgatapūjite oṃ sambhara sambhara hūṃ.
(Recite seven times; sprinkle the food with pure water. Next, recite the Amṛtoda mantra.)
Namo surūpāya tathāgatāya tadyathā oṃ suru suru prasu ru prasuru svāhā (Recite three times;
then recite the names of the four Tathāgatas).
Homage to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. Homage to the Tathāgata Suvimalavarṇaśarīra. Homage to the Tathāgata Vipulaśarīra.
Homage to the Tathāgata Vigatabhaya. (Recite this three times. Then recite the prayer for receiving food.)

This food, supreme in color, fragrance, and flavor, is offered to the Buddhas of the ten directions, presented to the various worthies and sages, and distributed downward to the classes of beings within the six paths;
bestowed without distinction, it satisfies all according to their needs, causing all donors to attain immeasurable pāramitās.
(Next, the verse for the arising [of merit] follows:)
"You hosts of ghosts and spirits, I now offer this sustenance to you. May this food pervade the ten directions and be shared by all ghosts and spirits.
By this merit... (and so forth, up to "the ten directions and the three periods of time," etc.).

The Universal Dedication of Merit from the Recitation of Scriptures and the Holding of Mantras (Kū): May this merit be offered to the various devas who protect the Dharma, and may it repay the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence.

May the true masters of the monastery protect the teachings and bring peace to the Sangha, so that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm may together perfect the seed-wisdom. Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time... (and so forth).

The assembly dedicates the merit of reciting this sutra and mindfulness of the Buddha to offer to the various devas who protect the Dharma, to repay the four debts of gratitude, and to benefit the three classes of beings, bringing peace and joy to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.

We bhikṣus repent of our roots of transgression and vow to adorn the Pure Land; may we, when this present life ends and we cast off our lives, rely upon these roots of goodness to ensure our certain rebirth there.
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, may they behold the Buddha, hear the Dharma, swiftly realize Bodhi, and extensively deliver all sentient beings, performing great Buddha-works.
Regarding the seasonal offerings at the Earth Deity Hall (*dìtǔ táng*):
for the four seasons, one should reverently arrange offerings at the Earth Deity Hall during winter and perform the recitation of sutras and dedication of merit, saying:

As the summer retreat begins, when the warm breeze fans the wilds and the Fire Emperor (Yan Di) presides over the season, it is the time for the Dharma King to observe the *śīla* of foot-restraint and the day for the Śākyaputrīyas to protect living beings.
We beg for your protective grace so that we may successfully complete our *varṣa*.

Respectfully gathering the great assembly, we shall proceed to the spirit shrine to recite the *Cīvarasaṃskāra-vidhi*, the *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Majestic Virtue for Eliminating Calamities*, and the secret chapters of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, while chanting the sacred name of the Great Mother of Buddhas (*Mahābuddhamātṛ*). [End of Collection]

By virtue of these meritorious deeds performed through the transformation of the horse’s wealth, we specifically offer this tribute to the local mountain deities (all ranks), the presiding masters of the entire hall, and all other spirits.
We pray that your divine radiance will provide mutual support, manifesting deeds of benefit;
may the monastic gardens flourish and the impartial grace of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time be eternally bestowed. (And so forth.)
The summer retreat has concluded as the golden wind fans the wilds and the White Emperor presides over the quarter;

this is the moment when the Buddha, the King of Dharma, releases his regulations and the day when the year of the Dharma reaches its full cycle. Having spent ninety days without difficulty while the entire assembly remained in peace, we employ these secret verses to repay his vast virtue.
At the juncture of the seasons, as the year turns and the time of the winter solstice arrives when the clouds record its coming,
it is the moment when the first Yang returns and the beginning of the emergence of the myriad species.
On this eve of the year, as the transformative power of the Dao operates in secret and the cycle of the year comes to a close, all rejoice in the peace of the four seasons.
To inaugurate the auspicious celebration of the Three Baths.
[The *Lengyan* Universal Dedication:
This is the ancient method composed by Chan Master Zhenxie himself, to be performed after the formal meal (fàngcān), when the assembly is summoned to gather in the Great Hall.

**Verses on Daily Life:** Generally speaking, one who has left the household life differs from the laity in both mind and form. Rising at the crowing of the cock, if one seeks profit and strives for fame, there is no manifest conduct whatsoever.

What efficacy could there be in esoteric practices? Nevertheless, regarding the activities performed throughout the twelve periods of the day, the Buddhist scriptures contain admonitions that must be followed and put into practice;
these are recorded below with care.
When falling asleep,
one should wish that all sentient beings may be entirely secure and attain great mastery. When rising, one should likewise wish this.
Upon first awakening from sleep, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the awakening of omniscience and survey the ten directions.
When using the latrine for either small or large relief, one should wish that all sentient beings cast away greed, hatred, and delusion, and eliminate all defilements and impurities.
Having finished washing one's hands and approaching the water, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings swiftly proceed toward the supramundane Dharma.
[Then] wash the face.
When washing the face with water, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the gateway to the pure Dharma and be forever free from defilement.
When ascending the hall and seeing the Buddha, one should wish that all sentient beings attain unobstructed eyes and behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Ascending the Pavilion and Mounting the Stupa: May all sentient beings ascend the pavilion of the True Dharma and see clearly all things. Beholding the Stupa: May all sentient beings ascend the pavilion of the True Dharma and see clearly all things.
Upon seeing a Buddha stūpa, one should wish that all beings be honored like a stūpa and receive offerings from devas and humans.
Prostrating at the summit of a stūpa, one should wish that no deva or human among all beings be able to see the crown of their head.
When washing the feet,
one should wish that all sentient beings be endowed with spiritual power and that their various activities be unimpeded. When bathing, one should likewise make this aspiration.
When bathing the body, one should wish that all beings be free from defilement in body and mind, pure and radiant within and without.
When receiving food,
at the time of receiving food, one should wish that all beings fully accomplish and perfect all aspects of bodhi.
When eating porridge or a light meal,
one should wish that all sentient beings take the joy of meditation as their food and be filled with the delight of the Dharma.
When the meal is finished:
(When eating a small meal: Having finished eating, may all sentient beings have their tasks accomplished and be endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
(When receiving flavors:
When receiving flavors, may all sentient beings obtain the supreme flavor of the Buddhas and be fully satisfied by the nectar of immortality.
○ The distribution of gruel brings ten benefits: it benefits practitioners; its karmic retribution is boundless; and it leads ultimately to eternal bliss.
Furthermore, there is a verse:
Pure in the observance of precepts and honored by all people, One who respectfully offers rice gruel at the proper time gains ten benefits for the practitioner:
Physical beauty, strength, longevity, and happiness; eloquence and clarity of speech;
The removal of undigested food and wind disorders, and the alleviation of hunger and thirst. These are called medicines, as taught by the Buddha.
If you wish to obtain the long life and happiness of humans and devas, you should offer congee to the assembly of monks.
By offering this meal of three virtues and six flavors to the Buddha, the Sangha, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, you universally provide for them all with equal offerings.

The three qualities are: first, lightness and softness; second, purity and cleanliness; third, conformity to the Dharma. The six flavors are: first, sweet; second, bitter; third, pungent; fourth, sour; fifth, salty; sixth, bland.
Furthermore, after the meal was finished, the verse said:
"The physical strength and vitality are now fully restored; His majestic power shakes the ten directions and the three periods of time.
A hero among the great, he turns causes back into fruits without a thought; All sentient beings shall attain supernatural powers."
The Five Contemplations: 1.
Calculate the amount of labor expended and measure the distance from whence it was brought. 2. Reflect upon whether your own virtue is complete or deficient to determine if you deserve this offering.

3. Guard the mind against transgressions, making the elimination of greed and other afflictions the primary objective. 4. Properly regard the food as excellent medicine for treating the withered body.
Fifth, for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path, one should accept this food.
The nature of the one who bows and the object of the bow are empty and quiescent; the mutual resonance of cause and response is inconceivable.
This my place of enlightenment is like a celestial jewel, within which the reflections of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear;
my own reflection appears before [the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas], and with head touching their feet, I take refuge and pay homage.
[Verse of] Homage and Praise to Śākyamuni.
Your countenance is most wondrous, Your radiance illuminates the ten directions.

I have made offerings to you in the past, And now I come again to behold you in person. O Holy Lord, King of Gods, With a voice like the kalaviṅka bird, You who have compassion for all sentient beings— We now pay homage and offer praise.
Praise of Amitābha Buddha:
Amitābha Buddha’s body is of true golden hue; His marks and signs are majestic and peerless.
The white tuft between his brows curls like five Mount Sumerus; His deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.
Within the light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear, along with boundless billions of assemblies of transformation Bodhisattvas;
through the Forty-Eight Vows, they deliver sentient beings, causing those of all nine grades to ascend to the other shore.
Furthermore, a verse says:
I prostrate to Amitābha, the Great Compassionate Father who saves the world, To the profound and true Dharma-treasury, and the Sangha of the worthy and holy ones of the Three Vehicles.
With a heart of sincerity, I seek birth in the Buddha’s Pure Land;
May all your original great vows universally employ unconditional compassion, Responding to thoughts and reaching those with whom you have a karmic affinity.
It is like the moon reflected in water.
Furthermore, from the *Amitābha-stotra* (composed by Dazhi Lushi):
"The eighty-four thousand wondrous marks are none other than the Amitābha of one's own fundamental nature; throughout the billions of lands in the ten directions..."
Though distant lands may differ in purity or defilement, they do not transcend the mind; though Buddhas and sentient beings appear distinct, they never deviate from one's own nature.
The substance of the mind is vast and empty, unimpeded by coming or going; its nature is inherently all-encompassing, so how could it be obstructed by grasping or rejecting?
Therefore, with a single thought, one ascends to the Jewel Realm and returns to the source of the earth.

In my homeland, with a mere snap of the fingers, I gaze up at Your compassionate countenance; truly, we are fathers and sons by nature, yet for many lifetimes I have failed You and suffered in the depths of samsara.
Today, as I cast myself in sincere devotion, I shall surely receive Your salvation.
With the three minds fully awakened and my single resolve directed westward, I shall rely upon You until the end of time and offer praise throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
Verses in Praise of the Bodhisattva:
The Bodhisattva is like the cool moon, Wandering through the ultimate void; When the water of sentient beings' minds is pure, The reflection of Bodhi appears within.
Praise to Avalokiteśvara, who manifests a thousand, ten thousand, and a billion bodies of purple-golden hue; To the one of wondrous white-robed form with thirty-two marks,
the Honored One of Perfect Penetration and Sovereignty— Throughout all lands, all praise your wisdom of great compassion.
Verse for Opening the Sutra:
The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma Is difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas;
Now that I have seen, heard, received, and upheld it, I pray that I may understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning.
The Verses on Returning to the Treasury:
Returning to the Treasure Abode via the Path, The definitive meaning is truly inconceivable;
May all sentient beings together enter the ocean of *sambodhi*.
Having completed [this], the long-term sufferings of the three miserable realms are forever stilled; The six destinies cease following the causes of drowning in samsara.
May all sentient beings realize True Suchness, And may every living being ascend to the other shore.
○ Third, the Three Refuges: I, [Name],
from this present body until the attainment of Buddhahood, in the interval between them, take refuge in the Buddhas, Dharmas,
and Sanghas of the ten directions, who abide eternally.
The six recollections of the transformative teaching:
Recollection of the Buddha, the Great Compassionate Father who saves the world; Recollection of the Dharma, the gateway to renunciation and liberation;
Recollection of the Sangha, the excellent field of merit for all beings; Recollection of the Precepts, the foundation of unsurpassed bodhi.
Mindfulness of the perfection of giving, mindfulness of the heavens, and protecting the Dharma to remain apart from worldly beings;
The Four Great Vows:
Sentient beings are boundless, yet I vow to deliver them all; afflictions are innumerable, yet I vow to sever them all.
I vow to study the immeasurable Dharma gates; I vow to attain the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
Verse of Repentance:
All the evil karma I have created in the past Arises entirely from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
Whatever has arisen from my body, speech, and mind, I now confess it all.
Verse for Rebirth:
When I am on the verge of death, May I completely eliminate all obstacles.
Beholding that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, one immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Once I have attained rebirth in that land, I shall manifest before me the fulfillment of this great vow."
All perfections were complete without exception; he brought benefit and happiness to the entire realm of sentient beings.
That Buddha’s assembly was entirely pure, and at that time, I personally beheld the Tathāgata of Infinite Light, who appeared before me and bestowed upon me the prophecy of awakening.
Having received the prophecy from that Tathāgata, He manifests countless hundreds of koṭis of transformation bodies;
With vast power of wisdom pervading the ten directions, He universally benefits all realms of sentient beings,
Until the exhaustion of empty space and the worlds, And until the end of sentient beings, karma, and afflictions.
When all these things are thus inexhaustible, may my vows likewise remain eternally inexhaustible to the ultimate end.
From the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance):
"This day has passed, and life accordingly diminishes; like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be in this?"
One should exert diligent effort as if extinguishing a fire on one's head; mindful only of impermanence, take care not to be negligent.

Regarding the ritual formats for prayers at various temples during the New Year and the Lantern Festival, they differ: some perform repentance rites such as the *Prabhāsa-avalokiteśvara-sūtra* or others.
Whether reciting the sūtras or merely chanting mantras, it is none other than a means of repenting for past transgressions and praying to gather future blessings;
as for the Vinaya according to various regions, it is difficult to establish a fixed standard.
Green Grass and Young Seedlings: Prayers for Ten-Thousand-Year Endurance.
The perpetual existence of the monastery relies entirely upon field rents and autumn grain; if these do not ripen, how can the monks be at peace?

It is only right that one should pray with great diligence to seek divine assistance. The regulations in various places differ: some merely perform offerings to the Buddhas and devas within the temple itself.

Whether reciting sutras and mantras or traveling around the fields at a manor estate, one should always follow the established precedents; since these have already been practiced for generations, they must not be transgressed.
As those who serve as abbots or administrators, can you not apply yourselves with diligent care?

I humbly pray that the five desires may flourish and that rain and dew may fall in due season; that all matters be brought to fulfillment, relying entirely upon the secret protection of the divine spirits.
Accordingly, I have maintained the established custom and prepared auspicious conditions:

monks have been assembled at the temple to circumambulate the fields and perform rites, chanting sutras and mantras, while the horses and wealth are consecrated through ritual refinement (as detailed). I earnestly hope for bountiful harvests in every field and lush growth in every plot.

Truly, there shall be no further anxiety regarding the destruction caused by locusts, grasshoppers, moths, or pests; instead, there will be the celebration of abundant surpluses of millet, sacrificial grain, rice, and fine grain.
