The Rituals for the Refectory (Xingtang) Regarding the serving of tea in the refectory and the concluding rites of the *jie-la* (end-of-year retreat): After the assembly of monks has finished their tea, the Chief Attendant (*shizhe*) of the Abbot’s quarters, together with the Guest Master (*ketou*), proceeds to the refectory to serve tea.
The Guest Master first notifies the Head of the Assembly (*cantou*), who then posts a notice to inform the community. Hot water is prepared, and the tea bowls are brought out.
The Chief Cook (Dianzuo) is requested to accompany the Abbot’s attendant to the administrative office (Kusi) to deliver the tea in advance. The attendant enters, and the Chief Cook receives him.
The Hall Master leads the assembly to welcome them at the gate; the attendant takes the seat of honor, acting on behalf of the Abbot. The Chief Cook sits to his right.

The attendant steps forward before the incense burner to offer a single stick of incense, then returns to his position and bows with his hands to the assembly as they take their seats. Once the tea has been served, the Chief Cook... [the text ends].
The head of the assembly (san-tou) is escorted out by the Hall Master; as soon as they reach the Abbot’s quarters (fang-chang), they proceed to offer thanks for the tea.

Once the Abbot has finished serving the tea, the administrative officers (chi-shih) go to the Hall to serve tea. The administrative officers occupy the position of honor, while the Head Cook (tien-tso) acts as their companion.

The protocol for serving tea is identical to that of the Abbot. As they are escorted out the door, he calls out: "The head of the assembly and the great assembly shall proceed to the Storehouse Office (ku-si)."
[The guest] bows to decline the tea. The attendant reports: "The administrative officers have transmitted the understanding that the tea-offering is waived.

The head official (Doushou) directs the preparation of tea for the hall. The hall office acolyte reports to the Head of the Assembly (Cantou) to post the notice board and report to the assembly to prepare the hot water and serve the cups.

He invites the Chief Cook (Diansuo) to accompany the head officials; the head officials sit on the right as a mark of courtesy, which is the same as before. [The guest] chants the formula for declining the tea.
Again, the shout for exemption.

○ Regarding the instruction of novice practitioners (*tonghang*): during the first month and a half, one should instruct the novices (according to the Chan regulations, this should be done after the five sessions of formal inquiry and the conclusion of the morning assembly).

The *santou* (head attendant) orders the *keshaku* (resting-food) attendants to notify the various duty-holding attendants (*gyoku-mu gyōja*). The attendants of the *gyōdō* (practice hall) hang a notice board in front of the hall to inform the assembly.

When the evening bell (*konshō*) tolls, the attendants of the *gyōdō* strike the wooden clapper three times to gather the assembly. The attendants enter the *shindō* (sleeping hall) and stand in formation.

The *santou* enters the *hōjō* (abbot’s quarters) to invite the *chūji* (abbot) to come forth and take his seat. The *santou* steps forward, offers incense, and announces the conclusion of the *keshaku* (resting-food) period.

Having likewise exchanged greetings and performed nine prostrations, he steps forward, holds his breath, and bows with joined palms to listen to the instructions. Having done so, he again prostrates three times with the assembly, bids them "farewell" (*zhēnzhòng*), and withdraws.
He has previously ordered the dormitory hall to be prepared with incense and lit candles, with an attendant assigned to oversee these arrangements.

When the *Xingtang* (Hall of Practice) is to deliver a general discourse (*pushe*), the head of the assembly (*cantou*) shall first go to the *Shisong* (Attendant’s Office), offer incense, and prostrate.

He then reports to the *Shouzhe* (Attendant), who conveys the request to the Abbot. If the Abbot grants the request, the *Cantou* shall strike the wooden board to assemble the community, who stand in formation in the *Qindingtang* (Sleeping Hall).
The *Cantou*, following the *Shouzhe*, enters to invite the Abbot to take his seat. The *Cantou* and the assembly perform a mutual greeting (*wenshun*), then step forward to offer incense.
When the meal is finished, the practitioners shout, "Not knowing [the answer]? (fuxin). They perform nine prostrations together with the assembly and inquire after the head of the retreat.

The head of the retreat steps forward and says, "We have long contemplated the Master’s instructions; we humbly pray that you will compassionately reveal the causal conditions. He then withdraws, performs an inquiry, and the group disperses.

On the following day, the hall attendant hangs the sign for a General Discourse (pushe) to notify the assembly. Inside the hall, a seat, an incense table, and candle stands are set up for the discourse. The participants attend.

The Head of the Assembly (Toubao) requests the two ranks of officers to take their places; the Vice-Head (Lifan) and the assembly of Gatekeepers (Zongmen) welcome the two orders of officers into the hall.

The Head of the Assembly and the Hall Master (Dangzhu) go to the Attendant’s Office (Shisishi) together to invite the Abbot to descend to the center of the hall. The assembly of fellow monks receives them as they enter and take their seats.

A group of Attendants (Shizhe) performs a formal greeting (wenxun) and stands to one side. The two ranks of officers, as usual, come forward from their positions to perform a greeting; once finished, the Attendants burn incense.

With one incense stick for inquiry, the abbot requests the Dharma as in a regular assembly. The head of the assembly leads the group in a single file, inserts incense, and calls for the assembly to prostrate three times.

They then withdraw and stand in a single file behind their respective east and west sections, listening attentively. Once the instructions and expositions are concluded, the head of the assembly leads the group back to their original position at the front, prostrates three times, and immediately exits the hall.
Standing to the right outside, they bow to escort the abbot and the two classes of officials.
Proceeding to the sleeping hall, insert a large piece of incense and perform nine prostrations before withdrawing. Next, go to the attendants' office, insert incense, and perform three prostrations.
The head attendant and the assistant attendant shall go together before the two classes of officials to offer individual bows of thanks; the offering of incense in this instance shall be waived.
And the Ritual Implements for Alerting the Assembly (Appendix: Monthly [Head] Knowledge).
Now, the bell, fish-shaped gong, drum, and wooden clapper are the ritual implements for summoning the monastic community. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"Ānanda, when you ascend the lecture hall and strike the *ghanṭā*, this is the Tathāgata’s drum of confidence" (*ghaṇṭā* refers to striking it to produce sound; according to the sūtras and śāstras...).

The term *gandi* (often translated as "wooden mallet") is glossed here as *zhì* (pronounced *jù hán* in reverse; this refers to the sound of bells and chimes). The *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "The meaning of *saṃgha* is 'harmony.

If they do not assemble together, there will be discord and separation; thus, governing the Dharma lacks the merit of decisive accomplishment, and when attending to affairs, one must occupy the position of non-transgression.
The text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says: "One should spread out the seats and strike the *gandi* so that everyone gathers in one place. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* says: [same].
When the bhikṣus gathered for the poṣadha at improper times, it hindered their practice of the Path. The Buddha said: "One should announce that the time has arrived;
one may strike the *ghanṭī*, beat a drum, or blow a conch. These should be struck by resident *śrāmaṇeras* or lay attendants (*karmadāna*).

They must not be too many; they should be struck three times. The same applies to blowing the conch. With the exception of trees containing lacquer or poison, it is permitted to use any other wood, copper, iron, or anything that makes a sound."

It is said that even śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus may strike the chao; furthermore, it is stated that one should use it according to the number of monks and the urgency of the matter, weighing the timing accordingly.

Regarding the method for striking the bell, the *Chaoji* cites the *Sānqiānwēiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners), as well as the *Guǐdù tújīng* (Diagram Sutra on Ritual Standards) compiled by the Patriarch, and various sūtras and śāstras, stating that "three strikes" refers to three downward blows. The *Tujing* (Diagram Sutra) further explains this as "gathering the three."

The number of strikes for the *cheng* (the mounting signal) is not fixed; however, when preaching the various teachings (*dharmas*), it is appropriate to take forty strikes as the standard, which generally hits the mark.
The *Tujing* states: "Grasp the mallet and settle the mind; strike ten times lightly. The *Niyao chao* states: "One must not strike loudly to disturb the minds of the assembly.
Gradually thin out the strokes and gradually increase them until the sound fades away; then strike three final blows, which is called the 'Threefold Strike' (*santong*)."
As for the method of the long striking: first, forty strokes as before; then two sets of forty, totaling one hundred and twenty.
For the second set of forty, divide it into two sections: the first eighteen strokes are performed as in the previous "arising" section;

the middle four strokes consist of nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, and twenty-two, with the sound ending just before the final strike. This rescues one from the suffering of the four evil realms (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras).
After the twenty-third strike, the subsequent eighteen strikes gradually become closer together and smaller. The third section consists of forty strikes;

the manner of their arising is the same as before, though there are slight differences toward the end. From the thirty-sixth strike, one strikes three times, which is called the "Triple End" (*sānti-mukha*).
The final two strikes are called the "Ceasing Mallet. The *Tujing* states: "Mindfulness of the Triple Gem and the preservation of the Five Assemblies; each assembly has eight [members]."

Because there are four pairs [of the four fruits and four stages of approach], forty is used as the unit of difference; when this is multiplied by three (referring to the three vehicles), one hundred and twenty becomes the standard interval.
If compared to the "three lower" practices performed in the present age, they are the same, but the "three penetrations" (*santong*) differ.

The *Fufa zang zhuan* (Biographies of the Dharma-Transmitters) further states that for the sake of allowing sentient beings suffering in the evil realms to find rest, [the teaching was entrusted to] Kanishka (*Jiniluzha*).

Because the king had committed great slaughter, he died and entered the body of a thousand-headed fish; a wheel of swords revolved around his body, cutting him as it turned and he was reborn as it cut.

If he heard the sound of a bell, the wheel of swords would remain suspended in the air. Through such causes and conditions, he sent his body to a place where the bell was struck incessantly so that his suffering might cease.
As stated in the *Ekottara Āgama*: "When the bell is struck, all the sufferings of the various evil realms [are stilled]."
All these matters shall be suspended; the formal procedures are listed below.

○ Regarding the performance of various *karmavācanā* rituals such as the *śayanāsana* (bedding and seating) and *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), the ascending and descending of the hall, the arrival of officials, venerable elders, and donors from various mountains at the monastery, and the morning and evening meals and gruel—on each occasion, the tower bell shall be struck according to a specific number of times.
The timing and urgency of these bells have already been clarified above. As for the "Dawn Bell," it shatters the long night and awakens those in sleep.
The "Twilight Bell" provides relief to the ignorant and deluded on the dark paths; it brings an end to the bitterness and suffering of the six realms and the three miserable states.
Regarding the bell before the Sangha Hall, there is no fixed time limit; the *weina* (chant leader) presides over it, and the hall attendant reports back to the *weina*.
When sounding it for the opening of a lecture, strike three times; for the end of the lecture, two times; for the meal of rice gruel, eight times.
According to the *Sāhasrikavīrya-sūtra* (Three Thousand Dignified Manners), among the seven subsequent rules:

for a high-ranking official, a great fire, a great flood, or bandits—these four occasions—the signal is given by striking three times to assemble the śrāmaṇeras, twice to assemble the upāsakas, and once to call the private attendants.
○ Regarding the various protocols for the sounding of drums: the *gong* (fa-tang gu) is used for the formal assembly (*kṣānti*), the invitation to leave (*an-zi*), and all *karman* rituals;

the drum for opening lectures and preaching the Dharma is struck three times, followed by two rotations of the upper pivot and another three strikes. For the small seat (*xiao-zuo*) and the serving of hot water or tea specifically for guests, each is struck once with a long roll;
for retiring from the seat, it is struck three times. If seats or drums are borrowed, they are sounded according to this same rule.

In the hall, the drum is struck for the intervals between sessions, for the morning and evening meals, and for the two periods of service. It is struck three times and then nine times; upon reaching the upper pivot, it is again struck three times and nine times.
If the *Tripitaka* is being rotated, the *Tripitaka* drum is sounded. If the bath is opened, there is the bath drum; for tea and soup, there is the tea-drinking drum;

and for the watch-changes, there is the watch drum. One must ensure that the time is known. Regarding the communal rules: when the assembly is gathered for lectures or when opening the small period of silence (*kṣaṇa-śānti*).
First, strike the corridor board three times to announce the opening of the bath; then strike it three more times for the bath itself.
For major communal labor (*daipuqing*) and for meals (*zhai* and *zhou*), strike the large wooden fish drum; for kitchen staff labor, strike the small wooden fish drum.

To open the period of great silence and for meals, ring the large board (the "large board" refers to the long board) three times. If tea is to be served, one must strike the board slowly to signal the participants to perform the rites of receiving tea.
In the third period, the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) strikes the board for tea; the dormitory hall (qintang) strikes its board;
the storehouse office (kusi) strikes the board in front of the storehouse hall to notify the assembly; and the various quarters strike the boards along the lower corridors.

The Great Hall possesses a large gong (daqing), which is struck when the abbot offers incense or when performing liturgical recitations and prostrations before the Buddha. For the offering of incense in the various halls, there are bells at each location.
I permit this incestuous violation of the laws and regulations, and thus record its brief account for all time to come;
by this, what was called the "ringing of bells and the eating from tripods" regarding the rites and music of the Three Dynasties can be clearly seen.
○ Monthly Essentials:
On the first day of the first month, during the Shangyuan Festival, many temples perform repentance rites (*chánfǎ*) in their halls;

it is appropriate for offerings to be made to the Buddhas and devas, so that each may with single-minded sincerity pray for the blessings of the coming year. Below are two models for the formal letters of congratulation sent by officials and patrons.

Regarding the sequence of entering and exiting and the propriety of the monastic gate’s rituals—whether light or grave—one must not violate established precedents. Following the Vinaya according to local custom, one should neither be overly rigid nor overly restrictive.

On the full moon of the second month, the anniversary of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, the Hall Attendant and the Ritual Practitioner shall collect funds from the assembly and deliver them to the Treasury Office.
In providing offerings to the Abbot and the Head Seat, it is appropriate to open the spring lectures to instruct and admonish the brethren;

when it is neither too hot nor too cold, this is precisely the season to spur oneself on. How can one allow time to pass in vain? One must instead attend to the fields and supervise agricultural affairs.
During the Cold Food Festival in the third month, the ancestral hall and shrine shall be arranged with offerings according to custom;
sutras shall be chanted, the hall swept and sprinkled, and the gathering of tea, bamboo shoots, and the clearing of mountain forests shall be prohibited.
In the fourth month, the treasury office of the Tathāgata’s birth prepares the Vimala Garden for the Buddha-Bathing ceremony and makes offerings;

the Abbot calls for the chanting of scriptures and the serving of snacks (*dianxin*) to the assembly. The Rector issues the notice boards for those performing the *śīla* recitation and the summer retreat (*an-guo*), as well as the charts for the liturgical services.
On the evening of the fifteenth day, the "Small Seat" hot soup is served (according to Chan regulations, this occurs on the fourteenth).

On the sixteenth day, the summer retreat (varṣā) is commenced; alternatively, three days prior to the formal commencement of the retreat at the Vinaya Hall, sand and water are first consecrated with mantras and reserved for the Great Hall.

On the actual day of the retreat, these are sprinkled throughout to establish the boundaries. Three days later, after the serving of tea and soup and the completion of scripture readings and prayers, the Abbot initiates the formal lecture.
In the fifth month, the Green Sprout Assembly (*qīngmíu huì*) shall be established;

whether by distributing sutra slips, gathering the assembly to read the sutras, preparing offerings, or traveling to the fields to practice the Way, it is appropriate for the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) to deliver evening lectures according to local custom until dusk.

One should encourage the students through recitation and diligent study. Furthermore, those who are mature and experienced within the various monasteries and pagoda sites should also be treated with kindness and respect.
The sixth month is intensely hot; prepare *zhongxia* noodles for the lecture assembly (*jiangxian*). Open and close the session according to the needs of the practitioners.

For the ninety-day cultivation period (*jiuxun daoxiu*), set a fixed term to attain realization. The abbot and head seat (*shouzuo*) should increase their exhortation and urging. This is no trivial matter;
it requires the preparation of various provisions such as soy sauce, vinegar, wheat flour, and fermented soybeans (*douzhi*).
In the seventh month, one should perform the repentance for one's parents, recite the Brahmajāla Sūtra, and offer the Pārvana (Lanpen) offerings to conclude the summer retreat (*varṣa*);
these rites are detailed in the *Pravāraṇā* ritual manual. One must carefully select a person to serve as the overseer of receipts.
In the eighth month, brothers should go out to visit spiritual friends (jñānins) and attend upon their elders during the cold season; do not fail to observe the prescribed rules.
You should personally attend to the lighting of the lamps and strive diligently in this regard.

On the first day of the ninth month, observe the memorial service for the Vinaya Master (vinayadhara), or open an autumn lecture series, or expound upon the textual scriptures; the supervising official (adhyakṣa) shall oversee these matters.
The various stewards shall plow the fields and lands.

On the third day of the tenth month, the anniversary of the Patriarch Nanshan’s passing is observed; it is appropriate to prepare the ponds, construct embankments and dams, organize labor for construction projects, and procure vegetables and other provisions for the year’s needs.

In the first month of the eleventh lunar month, during the winter solstice festival, one may perform offerings; it is precisely at this time that one should examine the ancestral scriptures by the side of the hearth according to the local custom.

In the first month of the twelfth lunar month, one prepares offerings for the Buddha’s Enlightenment Day; the abbot shall calculate the accounts of money and grain and oversee the transport [of supplies].
One may measure out rice, wheat, and the five flavors; it is appropriate to establish precedents for each matter according to the protocols for the two orders' processions.
One should sweep and sprinkle the halls and pavilions, practice the annual repentance rites, and prepare the ceremonial items for the New Year's greetings in advance.
*Regulations for the Garden of Vinaya*, Scroll Ten (End) The Ritual for Study and Recitation An ancient said:
"Proficiency in one's craft arises from diligence and is ruined by idle play. Among people today, few exert themselves spontaneously; it is not that they lack a strategy.
If one exerts oneself too strenuously, one will not be able to achieve mastery in one's studies.

Since ancient times, the practice of holding lectures during the spring and autumn seasons has been discontinued after the middle of summer to conclude the formal rites. Three days later, once the prayers for blessings are finished, on the fourth day before the fast, the Abbot initiates the morning lecture.
Three days thereafter, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) should initiate the evening lecture. On the fifth day, immediately upon departing...
For those engaged in study and recitation, a plaque for the lecture session shall be hung in the Dharma Hall.

Every time before the morning assembly or after ascending to the hall, the Abbot shall order the attendants to strike the "stillness bell" (jingzhong) three times. When dusk falls, the students shall carry lamps to the Dharma Hall;

those who have been designated as subjects for the lecture should each exert themselves with diligence. The Xitang and the senior monks (qijiu) should also take their seats to assist in forming the assembly.
The attendant on duty for the day delivers the *yinzi* (invitation signal) to the *weina* (ritual director), who then chants "Two Fires.
Following this, the abbot proceeds to his seat in the Dharma Hall. The *weina* strikes the *yin* bell twice to silence the assembly.

(In some traditions, the two administrative officers, the *tang* and the *bin*, take turns serving hot tea every night. After the shout of "Three," the *weina* strikes the *yin* bell twice again; the attendant on duty then [proceeds with the service].

The attendant on duty goes before the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable of the Hall) to inquire after his well-being and takes the covered box for the lecture-slips (*fǔjiǎng*), placing it upon the abbot’s desk.
After the abbot has inquired after his own well-being, he opens the box and, with a casual hand, draws one slip from the mixture and hands it to the attendant on duty.
The attendant unfolds it, presents it to the abbot, and then calls out loudly: "Attendant [Name] shall give the lecture."
Then, take the drawn lot and show it to the person who will oversee the lecture (*fùrén*), place it back into the lot casket, and return it before the *wéinà*.
(In some places, the two lots for the introductory text and the formal discourse are drawn together at once; having determined them, they are announced to the assembly and presented in sequence.
Meanwhile, the hall attendant (*tángsī xíngzhě*) places two candles on the table before the person overseeing the lecture, and that person then covers the previous day’s *zhǔchí* (abbot).

When the text for the lecture has been covered, the next person in order should prepare to lecture by studying it with meticulous precision and deep reflection, delivering striking words that cause the assembly to listen with awe, so that even those who are negligent may feel shame.
Once the covering of the text is finished, the *weina* (ritual master) strikes the gavel twice;
the duty-day official then returns before the *weina*, where they draw lots from a container to determine the order of the lectures, and together they proceed before the Abbot.
Having picked up the lot, he chants: "The Vinaya Master [Name] leads the citation of the ritual text. Then, the lots are placed back into the casket as described above.

Once the citation of the ritual text is finished, the casket is retrieved and the procedure is repeated. The person or persons designated by the lot—whether one, two, or three—are commanded to go forth and perform the rites as above.
The Rector (Vina) strikes the signal gong twice; the person designated by the lot then takes...
Having read the text, place it before the *karmadāna* (Venerable of the Hall) and point to the place where the recitation begins.

Then, standing with palms joined facing inward before the large central incense burner, recite the text you have read. The words must be clear and distinct; the delivery should be detailed, slow, and rhythmic, such that the beginning and ending are worthy of observation.
If many passages are being recited, the *karmadāna* shall strike the signal board twice to lead the recitation. When the text is finished, strike the board once more.

When the person has finished reciting and the sound has ceased, they step forward once more to the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) to inquire after him and take back the recitation manual, returning to their original seat.
Next, the person designated as the "examiner" (*ce-cen-wen*) is selected; he likewise recites as described above until all positions have been completed.

The Abbot and the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) then compare the examiner’s performance with those who recited well; those who recite excellently are rewarded with paper, brushes, ink, fans, and other such items.
Those who fail to recite properly shall also be penalized to serve as a warning to those who are indolent in their studies. Once the recitation is finished, the Abbot shall return to his quarters.
The Rector (Vina) shall strike the signal bell twice to lead the Chanting Master (Cejwen) out;

the Chanting Master shall then return, and the Head Monks on duty shall each return to their respective offices. Those in the three departments should each advance in their practice, following this routine every night. If the Abbot...

The Abbot shall take charge of the affairs; the Head Seat shall oversee the proceedings. During the latter half of summer, when the weather is cool, one should observe whether the lectures are being held or paused, acting as the Abbot does.
However, with the aim of cultivating talent, one must exert diligent effort;
for a foot-long jade disc is not a treasure if it is allowed to waste away in vain. Is this not so?

When new arrivals and fellow monks first arrive, they should thoroughly study the *Lüzong Huìyuán* (Compendium of the Vinaya School) and various prefaces, seeking instruction from the Master to understand the pathways of the teachings.
Only then may they cite the relevant sections;

"citing the sections" means that when the abbot delivers his lecture on a given day, the student’s learning and reflection must both reach the source, encountering the principle at every turn, before they may then repeat and explain it.
If Master Wen were merely lecturing orally, how could the meaning be seen within these written characters?
